channel.title: sedzinfo · R tutorials
channel.description: Tutorials in R with the code on every page: psychometrics, adaptive testing, scale validation, statistics, machine learning and data visualisation with real data.

item.title: Where the Earth Erupts: Volcanoes of the World
item.description: Where the world’s volcanoes are, which ones erupt, how big the eruptions get, the deadliest eruptions on record, how many people live close to a volcano, and where Greece stands.
item.content:encoded:
Where the world’s volcanoes are, which ones erupt, how big the eruptions get, the deadliest eruptions on record, how many people live close to a volcano, and where Greece stands.

What is this?

Most people know a few volcanoes: Vesuvius, Etna, Krakatau, perhaps Santorini. They are a small part of the whole. More than a thousand volcanoes have erupted in the last 10,000 years, and some of them erupt again every year. This story asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world are the volcanoes?
  2. Which volcanoes erupt, and how often?
  3. How big do eruptions get?
  4. Which were the deadliest eruptions?
  5. How many people live close to a volcano, and where does Greece stand?

Where the Earth Shakes looks at earthquakes, Waves from the Sea at tsunamis, and Natural Disasters puts the hazards side by side.

The data come from two sources, downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • The Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program (GVP), which keeps the Volcanoes of the World database, no key needed (GVP): the list of volcanoes that have erupted in the Holocene (the last 10,000 years or so), where they are and what kind they are; their eruptions, with the year they began and how explosive they were; and the number of people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 kilometres of each volcano.
  • NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), whose Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database lists the eruptions that did the most harm, with the number of deaths where it is known (NCEI volcanoes).

The map also draws the boundaries between the plates of the Earth’s crust, from Peter Bird’s model (Bird 2003), in the version of the GitHub repository fraxen/tectonicplates.

The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measures how big an explosive eruption was, on a scale that starts at 0 for a gentle eruption and is open-ended, with 8 for the largest eruptions in history. It is mainly based on the volume of ash thrown out, and also on the height of the eruption cloud. Each step up is about ten times more ash, apart from the first (USGS; Newhall and Self 1982).

A volcano here is a volcano of the GVP’s list. A large volcanic field, with hundreds of small vents, counts as one volcano.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(jsonlite)

The data

Code 
# the layers of the GVP's web service, as tables
gvp <- function(layer) {
  read.csv(
    paste0(
      "https://webservices.volcano.si.edu/geoserver/GVP-VOTW/ows?service=WFS&version=2.0.0",
      "&request=GetFeature&typeName=GVP-VOTW:", layer, "&outputFormat=csv"
    ),
    encoding = "UTF-8"
  )
}
# the volcanoes of the Holocene: place, type, tectonic setting and last eruption
volcanoes <- gvp("Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Volcanoes")
# the eruptions of the Holocene: one row for each eruption, with the year it began and its VEI
eruptions <- gvp("Smithsonian_VOTW_Holocene_Eruptions")
# the people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 km of each volcano
people <- gvp("E3WebApp_HoloceneVolcanoes")
# NOAA's significant eruptions: 200 to a page
noaa_page <- function(page) {
  fromJSON(paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/volcanoes?page=", page))
}
first_page <- noaa_page(1)
significant <- bind_rows(c(
  list(first_page$items),
  lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages)[-1], function(page) noaa_page(page)$items)
))
# the boundaries of the plates (Bird 2003), as lines
plates <- fromJSON(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json",
  simplifyVector = FALSE
)
Code 
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts
oranges <- c("#feedde", "#fdd0a2", "#fdae6b", "#fd8d3c", "#f16913", "#d94801", "#8c2d04")
# the colour of a volcano that has erupted in the time of the complete records (the dark orange of
# the scale) and of the plate boundaries
erupted_color <- "#d94801"
plate_color <- "#6b6b6b"
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# millions of people: one decimal below 10 million
million <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) >= 1e7, number(x / 1e6), one(x / 1e6))
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# country names that take "the" in a sentence
with_the <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% c("United States", "United Kingdom"), paste("the", x), x)
# the first letter of a sentence in capitals
cap <- function(x) paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substring(x, 2))
# a volcano name as people say it: "Ruiz, Nevado del" is Nevado del Ruiz
flip <- function(x) sub("^(.*), (.*)$", "\\2 \\1", x)
# a year, as in the text: years before the year 1 are BCE
year_text <- function(y) ifelse(y < 0, paste(-y, "BCE"), as.character(y))
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
Code 
# the eruptions that are certain: the GVP also lists eruptions that are only possible
confirmed <- eruptions[eruptions$Activity_Type == "Confirmed Eruption" & !is.na(eruptions$StartDateYear), ]
n_uncertain <- sum(eruptions$Activity_Type != "Confirmed Eruption")
# the country of each eruption: the country of its volcano
confirmed$country <- volcanoes$Country[match(confirmed$Volcano_Number, volcanoes$Volcano_Number)]
# the year of the data is not complete: its eruptions so far are left out of the rates
current_year <- max(confirmed$StartDateYear)
last_full_year <- current_year - 1
so_far <- sum(confirmed$StartDateYear == current_year)
# the records are complete from 1960 (explained below)
complete_from <- 1960
modern <- confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= complete_from & confirmed$StartDateYear <= last_full_year, ]
n_years <- last_full_year - complete_from + 1
# NOAA's rows are events with a date of their own: one volcano can have several in a year
same_year <- sum(duplicated(significant[, c("name", "year")]))

The list of eruptions has 11,109 rows, but not all of them are certain. 1,169 are marked by the GVP as uncertain, and they are left out: this page counts the 9,940 confirmed eruptions with a year, over the whole Holocene. An eruption counts in the year it began, and one that goes on for years counts once.

The records of eruptions are far more complete in recent times, so the page counts eruptions only from 1960. Newhall and Self, who invented the VEI, wrote that only the largest eruptions have a complete record back to the early 19th century, and that other important explosive events went unrecorded before about 1960 (Newhall and Self 1982). Section 2 shows the numbers. From 1960 to 2025 the list has 2,231 confirmed eruptions, 33.8 a year. For 2026 only 28 eruptions are listed so far, the year is not over, and it is left out of every rate and every trend.

The deaths are not always known. NOAA lists 903 significant eruptions, from 4360 BCE to 2026, but only 480 have a number of deaths. An empty cell means that the number is not known, not that nobody died, so the deaths below are a minimum. NOAA’s total deaths count the eruption and its secondary effects, whenever possible; where it has no total, this page takes the direct deaths. Each row of the database is an event with its own date, so the same volcano can appear more than once in a year (66 times here), and the deadliest eruptions below are rows of the database, which may be one phase of a longer eruption.

Code 
# the deaths of an eruption: the total if there is one, and never less than the direct deaths
significant$dead <- ifelse(
  is.na(significant$deathsTotal) & is.na(significant$deaths),
  NA,
  pmax(significant$deathsTotal, significant$deaths, na.rm = TRUE)
)
with_deaths <- significant[!is.na(significant$dead), ]

1. Where in the world are the volcanoes?

Code 
n_volcanoes <- nrow(volcanoes)
# volcanoes by country (a volcano on a border has both countries in its name: they stay together)
by_country <- volcanoes |>
  count(Country, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / n_volcanoes)
top_countries <- head(by_country, 10)
top_ten_share <- sum(top_countries$n) / n_volcanoes * 100
# the tectonic setting that the GVP gives each volcano: the first part, before the crust
volcanoes$setting <- sub(" /.*", "", volcanoes$Tectonic_Setting)
settings <- table(volcanoes$setting)
setting_share <- function(x) percent(100 * settings[[x]] / sum(settings))
# volcanoes whose last eruption is known (the year is empty when it is not)
n_since <- function(year) sum(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year >= year, na.rm = TRUE)
in_country <- function(name) by_country$n[by_country$Country == name]
type_top <- volcanoes |> count(Primary_Volcano_Type, sort = TRUE)
n_undersea <- sum(volcanoes$Elevation < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

Along the plate boundaries, and in a few countries. The GVP lists 1,209 volcanoes that have erupted in the Holocene. The 10 countries with the most have 59% of them: the United States (165), Japan (105) and Indonesia (101) lead, followed by Russia, Chile and Ethiopia. 69% of the volcanoes sit in what the GVP calls a subduction zone, a place where one plate of the crust slides under another, 18% in a rift zone, where plates pull apart, and 12% inside a plate, away from its edges. On the map the volcanoes follow the plate boundaries.

Code 
volcanoes$recent <- !is.na(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year) & volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year >= complete_from
volcanoes$label <- paste0(
  volcanoes$Volcano_Name,
  " (",
  volcanoes$Country,
  ")<br>",
  ifelse(
    is.na(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year),
    "last eruption not known",
    paste("last eruption:", year_text(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year))
  )
)
# the plate boundaries as one line with gaps, rounded to a tenth of a degree
boundary_lines <- do.call(rbind, lapply(plates$features, function(f) {
  xy <- do.call(rbind, lapply(f$geometry$coordinates, unlist))
  rbind(round(xy[, 1:2, drop = FALSE], 1), c(NA, NA))
}))
older <- volcanoes[!volcanoes$recent, ]
recent <- volcanoes[volcanoes$recent, ]
plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "lines",
    lon = boundary_lines[, 1],
    lat = boundary_lines[, 2],
    line = list(color = plate_color, width = 1),
    name = "Plate boundaries",
    hoverinfo = "skip"
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "markers",
    lon = older$Longitude,
    lat = older$Latitude,
    text = older$label,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    marker = list(color = gray, size = 5, line = list(color = "#8a8a8a", width = 0.4)),
    name = paste("No eruption since", complete_from)
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    type = "scattergeo",
    mode = "markers",
    lon = recent$Longitude,
    lat = recent$Latitude,
    text = recent$label,
    hoverinfo = "text",
    marker = list(color = erupted_color, size = 6, line = list(color = "white", width = 0.4)),
    name = paste("Erupted since", complete_from)
  ) |>
  chart(
    paste0("The ", number(n_volcanoes), " volcanoes of the Holocene"),
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World; plates: Bird (2003), via fraxen/tectonicplates.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = TRUE,
      coastlinecolor = "#d0d0d0",
      coastlinewidth = 0.5,
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#f3f3f3",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
      lataxis = list(range = c(-70, 85))
    ),
    legend = c(legend_top, list(itemsizing = "constant")),
    margin = list(t = 70, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )

Interactive chart: The 1,209 volcanoes of the Holocene

334 of the volcanoes have erupted since 1960, 439 since 1900. For 360 the year of the last eruption is not known: the evidence of an eruption in the Holocene is there, but not its date.

Code 
bars <- top_countries[order(top_countries$n), ] # the largest at the top
bars$Country <- factor(bars$Country, levels = bars$Country)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~n,
  y = ~Country,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$n == max(bars$n), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(n, " (", percent(share), ")"),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} volcanoes<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "Countries with the most volcanoes",
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Share of the world in brackets.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.5 * max(bars$n)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 60, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )

Interactive chart: Countries with the most volcanoes

The United States is first, with 165 volcanoes, 14% of the world’s; Japan has 105 and Indonesia 101. In Europe, Iceland has 35, Italy 13 and Greece 5. The 113 volcanoes of the list whose summit is below the sea are counted too, but the seafloor is far less surveyed than the land, and the list is surely less complete there.

2. Which volcanoes erupt, and how often?

Code 
by_year <- as.data.frame(table(factor(modern$StartDateYear, levels = complete_from:last_full_year)))
by_year$year <- complete_from:last_full_year
by_year$n <- by_year$Freq
trend_chance <- chance(by_year$n, by_year$year)
first_ten <- mean(by_year$n[by_year$year < complete_from + 10])
last_ten <- mean(by_year$n[by_year$year > last_full_year - 10])
n_erupted <- n_distinct(modern$Volcano_Number)
# the eruptions of each volcano since 1960
by_volcano <- modern |>
  group_by(Volcano_Number, Volcano_Name, country) |>
  summarise(eruptions = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(eruptions))
# volcanoes that erupted since 1960, by country
erupting <- modern |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(volcanoes = n_distinct(Volcano_Number), eruptions = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(volcanoes), desc(eruptions))
erupting$in_list <- by_country$n[match(erupting$country, by_country$Country)]
# the GVP's "country" of volcanoes under the sea that belong to no country
erupting$country[erupting$country == "Undersea Features"] <- "Undersea (no country)"
top_erupting <- head(erupting, 10)
# the eruptions in 50 years and in decades since 1600, per year: the part before the complete records
# is shown in grey
decades <- confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= 1600 & confirmed$StartDateYear <= last_full_year, ]
decades$decade <- 10 * (decades$StartDateYear %/% 10)
per_decade <- decades |>
  count(decade) |>
  mutate(years = pmin(decade + 9, last_full_year) - decade + 1, per_year = n / years)
per_year_in <- function(from, to) {
  nrow(confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= from & confirmed$StartDateYear <= to, ]) / (to - from + 1)
}

About 34 eruptions begin each year, and the number has not changed since 1960. From 1960 to 2025, between 23 and 49 eruptions began in a year, 34.1 a year on average in the first ten years and 32.0 in the last ten. A rank test of all the years finds no clear trend: the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 25 in 100. And 329 different volcanoes erupted at least once, 27% of the list: most volcanoes are quiet, and a few erupt again and again.

Code 
ggplot(per_decade, aes(x = decade, y = per_year, fill = decade >= complete_from)) +
  geom_col(width = 8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = erupted_color, "FALSE" = gray), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1600, 2000, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "The records get more complete",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Eruptions that began each year, average of each decade (dark: from ",
      complete_from,
      ")"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Confirmed eruptions."
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

Before 1960 the list is not a count of eruptions, but of what people recorded. In 1600–1699 the list has 3.4 eruptions a year, in 1800–1899 15.0, in 1900–1959 27.8, and since 1960 33.8. Volcanoes did not wake up in the 20th century: the records improved.

Code 
bars <- top_erupting[order(top_erupting$volcanoes), ]
bars$country <- factor(bars$country, levels = bars$country)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~volcanoes,
  y = ~country,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$volcanoes == max(bars$volcanoes), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(volcanoes, " of ", in_list),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} volcanoes erupted<br>%{customdata} eruptions<extra></extra>",
  customdata = ~eruptions,
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Volcanoes that erupted, ", complete_from, "–", last_full_year),
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Confirmed eruptions; \"of\": volcanoes of the country in the list.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.6 * max(bars$volcanoes)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 130, t = 60, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )

Interactive chart: Volcanoes that erupted, 1960–2025

A few countries have most of the eruptions. Since 1960, Indonesia had 54 different volcanoes erupt, the United States (39), Japan (37) and Russia (24) come next, and the ten countries of the chart have 67% of all the volcanoes that erupted. The volcanoes with the most eruptions are Piton de la Fournaise in France (54), Bezymianny in Russia (50) and Klyuchevskoy in Russia (44). Whether the GVP splits a long period of activity into many eruptions or counts one affects such numbers, so they are best read as rough.

3. How big do eruptions get?

Code 
vei_total <- table(factor(modern$ExplosivityIndexMax, levels = 0:8))
vei_known <- sum(vei_total)
vei_missing <- nrow(modern) - vei_known
vei_share <- function(levels) percent(100 * sum(vei_total[as.character(levels)]) / vei_known)
vei_n <- function(levels) sum(vei_total[as.character(levels)])
big <- confirmed[!is.na(confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax) & confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax >= 6 &
  confirmed$StartDateYear >= 1800, ]
big <- big[order(big$StartDateYear), ]
big$country <- with_the(big$country)
# the largest eruptions of the Holocene (VEI 7 and 8) in the list
huge <- confirmed[!is.na(confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax) & confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax >= 7, ]
since_1800 <- confirmed[confirmed$StartDateYear >= 1800 & confirmed$StartDateYear <= last_full_year &
  !is.na(confirmed$ExplosivityIndexMax), ]

Most eruptions are small; a few are enormous. Of the 2,225 eruptions since 1960 with a VEI, 83% are VEI 0 to 2, 14% are VEI 3, 2% VEI 4, and only 7 VEI 5 or more (6 at VEI 5, 1 at VEI 6, none higher). 6 have no VEI in the list.

Code 
sizes <- data.frame(vei = 0:7, n = as.integer(vei_total[as.character(0:7)]))
plot_ly(
  sizes,
  x = ~vei,
  y = ~n,
  type = "bar",
  marker = list(color = colorRampPalette(oranges)(8)),
  text = ~n,
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "VEI %{x}: %{y} eruptions<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Eruptions by size, ", complete_from, "–", last_full_year),
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. Confirmed eruptions with a VEI.",
    x_axis = list(title = "Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI)", dtick = 1),
    y_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(sizes$n)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 20, t = 60, b = 80, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.25
  )

Interactive chart: Eruptions by size, 1960–2025

The largest eruptions are rare: 5 of VEI 6 or more since 1800, and none above VEI 7. The table lists them.

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    year = big$StartDateYear,
    volcano = flip(big$Volcano_Name),
    country = big$country,
    vei = big$ExplosivityIndexMax
  ),
  col.names = c("Year", "Volcano", "Country", "VEI"),
  align = "rllr"
)
Year Volcano Country VEI
1812 Tambora Indonesia 7
1883 Krakatau Indonesia 6
1902 Santa Maria Guatemala 6
1912 Novarupta the United States 6
1991 Pinatubo Philippines 6

The biggest are much older. The list has 7 eruptions of VEI 7 or more in the whole Holocene, Santorini (1610 BCE), Kurile Lake (6440 BCE), Kikai (4350 BCE), Cerro Blanco (2300 BCE), Rinjani (1257), Tambora (1812) and Crater Lake (5680 BCE). The GVP dates Tambora’s eruption from 1812 to 1815, and NOAA gives the year of its great explosion, 1815; the table gives the year each eruption began. The date of an old eruption is an estimate: the GVP gives each one a margin of error, and some dates are marked as uncertain.

Big eruptions are rare, and small ones are the easiest to miss. From 1960 the list has 33.6 of them a year, but only 0.1 of VEI 5 or more, about one in 9 years. The VEI is also missing more often for older eruptions: for 5% of the eruptions from 1800 to 1959, against 0.3% since.

4. Which were the deadliest eruptions?

Code 
worst <- with_deaths[order(-with_deaths$dead), ]
top_dead <- head(worst, 10)
top_dead$label <- paste0(flip(top_dead$name), " ", year_text(top_dead$year))
total_dead <- sum(with_deaths$dead)
top_five_share <- 100 * sum(head(worst$dead, 5)) / total_dead
since_1900 <- with_deaths[with_deaths$year >= 1900, ]
n_1900 <- sum(significant$year >= 1900)
dead_1900 <- sum(since_1900$dead)
by_dead_country <- with_deaths |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(dead = sum(dead), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(dead))
n_100k <- sum(with_deaths$dead >= 10000)
# eruptions with a given number of deaths, since 1900, whose VEI is below 4
low_vei <- since_1900[!is.na(since_1900$vei) & since_1900$vei <= 3, ]
low_vei <- low_vei[order(-low_vei$dead), ]
tam <- worst[1, ]

4 eruptions have killed more than 25,000 people each. NOAA’s list has 480 eruptions with a known number of deaths, 335,768 deaths together. The five deadliest, Tambora 1815, Krakatau 1883, Ilopango 450, Pelee 1902 and Nevado del Ruiz 1985, account for 53% of them. The deadliest, Tambora in 1815, has 60,000 deaths on record, of which NOAA puts 11,000 directly on the eruption and the rest on its secondary effects.

Code 
bars <- top_dead[order(top_dead$dead), ]
bars$label <- factor(bars$label, levels = bars$label)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~dead,
  y = ~label,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$dead == max(bars$dead), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(number(dead), ifelse(is.na(vei), "", paste0(" (VEI ", vei, ")"))),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:,} deaths<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "The ten deadliest eruptions on record",
    "NOAA NCEI, Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database; VEI: the database. Total deaths where known.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.8 * max(bars$dead)), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 60, b = 60, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )

Interactive chart: The ten deadliest eruptions on record

The deadliest are not always the biggest. Of the ten, Nevado del Ruiz and Unzendake had a VEI of 3 or less, and the Nevado del Ruiz 1985 eruption, with 23,080 deaths, was VEI 3. How big an eruption is and how many people it kills are two different things.

Code 
timeline <- with_deaths[with_deaths$year >= 1500, ]
timeline$labelled <- timeline$dead >= 20000

The deaths on record are concentrated in a few countries. Indonesia has 43% of the deaths on the list, El Salvador (9%), Martinique (9%) and Colombia (8%) follow. And the list is not constant over time: since 1900 NOAA lists 530 significant eruptions, 344 of them with a number of deaths, 94,831 deaths in all, 28% of the total.

Code 
ggplot(timeline, aes(x = year, y = dead)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = labelled), size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(
    data = timeline[timeline$labelled, ],
    aes(label = paste0(flip(name), " ", year)),
    colour = "grey20",
    size = 3.2,
    vjust = -0.9,
    check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("TRUE" = red, "FALSE" = dark_gray), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(
    breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000),
    labels = c("1", "10", "100", "1,000", "10,000"),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Few eruptions kill many",
    subtitle = "Deaths in each eruption with a known number, since 1500, on a log scale",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA NCEI, Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database.\nEruptions without a known number of deaths are not shown."
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())

5. How many people live close to a volcano, and where does Greece stand?

Code 
people$country <- people$Country
known <- people[!is.na(people$Within_100km), ]
n_known <- nrow(known)
near <- function(km) known[[paste0("Within_", km, "km")]]
share_over <- function(km, n) percent(100 * mean(near(km) >= n))
close <- known[order(-known$Within_30km), ]
top_close <- head(close, 10)
hundred <- known[order(-known$Within_100km), ]
greece <- known[known$Country == "Greece", ]
greece <- greece[order(-greece$Within_30km), ]
# the volcanoes of Greece in the list, the last eruption first
greece_list <- volcanoes[volcanoes$Country == "Greece", ]
greece_list <- greece_list[order(-greece_list$Last_Eruption_Year), ]
santorini <- known[known$VolcanoName == "Santorini", ]
italy_top <- known[known$Country == "Italy", ]
italy_top <- italy_top[order(-italy_top$Within_30km), ]

Many volcanoes have millions of people near them, but the figures cannot simply be added up. The GVP counts, for each volcano, the people who live within 5, 10, 30 and 100 km. A person who lives near two volcanoes is counted for both, so the numbers of different volcanoes must not be added; this page compares volcanoes, and does not total the people. The GVP gives the numbers for 1,172 of the 1,209 volcanoes.

Code 
bars <- top_close[order(top_close$Within_30km), ]
bars$name <- paste0(flip(bars$VolcanoName), ", ", bars$Country)
bars$name <- factor(bars$name, levels = bars$name)
plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~ Within_30km / 1e6,
  y = ~name,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(bars$Within_30km == max(bars$Within_30km), red, gray)),
  text = ~ paste0(one(Within_30km / 1e6), " million"),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = paste0(
    "%{y}<br>%{x:.1f} million people within 30 km<br>",
    "%{customdata:,.0f} people within 100 km<extra></extra>"
  ),
  customdata = ~Within_100km,
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "Most people within 30 km of a volcano",
    "Smithsonian GVP, Volcanoes of the World. People within 30 km.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.6 * max(bars$Within_30km) / 1e6), showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE),
    margin = list(l = 240, t = 60, b = 60, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )

Interactive chart: Most people within 30 km of a volcano

In 76 volcanoes, more than a million people live within 30 km. The top of the list is Tatun Volcanic Group in Taiwan (6.7 million), Michoacan-Guanajuato in Mexico (5.8 million) and Tangkuban Parahu in Indonesia (5.7 million). Some of the volcanoes at the top are volcanic fields, which cover a large area and count as one volcano. Within 100 km, 30% of the volcanoes have a million people or more, and 4% have ten million or more; the most is 41 million, near Gede-Pangrango in Indonesia. And the other end: 39% of the volcanoes have fewer than 1,000 people within 30 km. The GVP’s counts come from a gridded population map whose year the data do not give, so they may not match today’s population.

Greece has 5 volcanoes in the list: Santorini (last eruption 1950), Nisyros (last eruption 1888), Kolumbo (last eruption 1650), Milos (last eruption 140) and Methana (last eruption 258 BCE). That is far fewer than Italy’s 13 or Iceland’s 35.

Code 
greece_eruptions <- confirmed[confirmed$country %in% "Greece", ]
santorini_eruptions <- greece_eruptions[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name == "Santorini", ]
minoan <- santorini_eruptions[which.max(santorini_eruptions$ExplosivityIndexMax), ]
last_santorini <- max(santorini_eruptions$StartDateYear)
kolumbo <- significant[significant$name == "Kolumbo", ]
kolumbo_year <- greece_eruptions$StartDateYear[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name == "Kolumbo"][1]
kolumbo_vei <- greece_eruptions$ExplosivityIndexMax[greece_eruptions$Volcano_Name == "Kolumbo"][1]
kolumbo_dead <- sum(kolumbo$dead, na.rm = TRUE)
santorini_dead <- with_deaths[with_deaths$name == "Santorini", ]

Santorini’s recent eruptions were small, but its largest was far older. The GVP lists 11 confirmed eruptions of Santorini in the Holocene, the last in 1950, with a VEI of 2; the largest, dated to 1610 BCE, was VEI 7, one of the 7 of VEI 7 or more in the Holocene in the list. Kolumbo, whose summit is 18 metres below the sea, erupted in 1650 (VEI 4), and NOAA’s database gives its 4 entries of that year 140 deaths together. Within 30 km of Santorini live 12,336 people, and within 100 km 67,468. Of the 4 volcanoes with a population count, the most people live near Methana (48,917 within 30 km). By the same measure Campi Flegrei, in Italy, has 3.0 million.

So, what does it mean?

  1. Volcanoes are where the plates meet, and in a few countries. The 10 countries with the most volcanoes have 59% of the 1,209 in the list, and 69% sit in subduction zones. The United States, Japan and Indonesia lead.
  2. About 34 eruptions begin a year, and the number has not changed since 1960. The apparent rise before that is a rise in what was recorded.
  3. Most eruptions are small. 83% of the eruptions since 1960 are VEI 0 to 2; 5 since 1800 were VEI 6 or more.
  4. The deadliest eruptions are not always the biggest. The five deadliest on record have 53% of the deaths of the eruptions with a known number, Tambora 1815, Krakatau 1883, Ilopango 450, Pelee 1902 and Nevado del Ruiz 1985.
  5. Many volcanoes have people near them. In 76 volcanoes of the list, more than a million people live within 30 km; Greece has 5 volcanoes in the list, and Santorini is the one that erupted last.

What this does not show. A list of eruptions is a list of what people recorded: it is incomplete before about 1960, and eruptions on the seafloor are the hardest to see. The VEI measures the explosion, not the harm, and it is missing for some eruptions. NOAA lists only significant eruptions, and for many of them the deaths are not known, so the totals are minimums, and a death toll is partly a matter of who counted and how. The numbers of people near volcanoes come from a population map whose year the data do not give, and each person near several volcanoes is counted several times. Nothing here says when or where the next eruption will be: a count of past eruptions is not a forecast.

For earthquakes, see Where the Earth Shakes; for tsunamis, Waves from the Sea; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

Sources

  • Global Volcanism Program, Smithsonian Institution, Volcanoes of the World, compiled by E. Venzke (database; the page uses the Holocene volcanoes, Holocene eruptions and population layers of the GVP’s web service). Cite as Global Volcanism Program, Volcanoes of the World (v. 5), distributed by Smithsonian Institution, compiled by Venzke, E., for example v. 5.3.1, 2025. The web service does not say which version it serves. Use is governed by the Smithsonian’s terms of use, which invite personal, educational and other non-commercial use.
  • NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Significant Volcanic Eruptions Database, doi:10.7289/V5JW8BSH, through its HazEL service. The pages read state no licence; the database is the work of a US federal agency.
  • Bird, P. (2003), An updated digital model of plate boundaries, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 4(3); in the GeoJSON version of fraxen/tectonicplates (Hugo Ahlenius, Nordpil), under the Open Data Commons Attribution License.
  • Newhall, C. G. and Self, S. (1982), The volcanic explosivity index (VEI): an estimate of explosive magnitude for historical volcanism, Journal of Geophysical Research 87(C2), 1231–1238.
  • USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory, The Volcanic Explosivity Index: a tool for comparing the sizes of explosive volcanic eruptions.

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · jsonlite

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Waves from the Sea: Where Tsunamis Start and Where They Strike Since 1900
item.description: Tsunamis since 1900 in NOAA’s global database: where they start, how far their waves travel, how tall they get, which were the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.
item.content:encoded:
Tsunamis since 1900 in NOAA’s global database: where they start, how far their waves travel, how tall they get, which were the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.

What is this?

A tsunami is a series of waves that starts when something moves a great deal of water at once, most often an earthquake under the sea. In the open ocean the waves are low and fast. Near a coast they grow, and they can flood it. This story looks at the tsunamis of the last 125 years and asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world do tsunamis start?
  2. Where do the waves strike, and how far do they travel?
  3. How big are they, and how often does one kill?
  4. Which were the deadliest?
  5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

For the earthquakes behind most tsunamis, see Earthquakes; for those that come from eruptions, Volcanoes; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

The data come from the Global Historical Tsunami Database of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), kept by its National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) (database). It lists tsunamis from 2000 BC to today, collected from reports, tide gauges and surveys. Its hazard-service interface gives it as two tables, downloaded here when the page is rendered, with no key:

  • The events: one row for each tsunami, with where its source was, what caused it, how reliable the report is, the highest water, and the deaths. We use the tsunamis since 1900, the first year of instrumentally located earthquakes (NOAA).
  • The runups: one row for each place where a tsunami’s waves were measured, with the height of the water, the distance from the source and the country. A runup is the maximum height of the water above the normal sea level (NOAA).

The meaning of every code below (validity, cause, region, kind of measurement) is from the help pages of NOAA’s own search tool (HazEL).

The record is of reports, not of every wave. A tsunami enters the database when someone saw it, measured it or wrote about it. Small waves far from people are missed, and how well they are recorded has changed over the years (section 5).

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("curl", "dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(curl)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(jsonlite)

The data

Code 
# one table of NOAA's hazard service: the first page says how many pages there are, and the rest
# are asked for at the same time, five at once, because one page takes a few seconds
noaa <- function(table, filter = "") {
  base <- paste0("https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/tsunamis/", table, "?", filter, "&page=")
  items <- function(response) {
    if (is.null(response) || response$status_code != 200) {
      return(NULL)
    }
    fromJSON(rawToChar(response$content))$items
  }
  first <- fromJSON(paste0(base, 1))
  pages <- list(first$items)
  todo <- seq_len(first$totalPages)[-1]
  for (attempt in 1:3) {
    if (length(todo) == 0) break
    got <- list()
    pool <- new_pool(total_con = 5, host_con = 5)
    for (p in todo) {
      local({
        page <- p
        curl_fetch_multi(
          paste0(base, page),
          done = function(r) got[[as.character(page)]] <<- items(r),
          fail = function(e) NULL,
          pool = pool
        )
      })
    }
    multi_run(pool = pool)
    pages <- c(pages, got)
    todo <- setdiff(todo, as.integer(names(got)[!sapply(got, is.null)]))
  }
  stopifnot(length(todo) == 0)
  bind_rows(pages)
}
# the tsunamis since 1900
events_all <- noaa("events", "minYear=1900&maxYear=2026")
# the places where waves were measured; this table cannot be cut by year, so all of it is downloaded
runups_all <- noaa("runups")
Code 
# the codes of NOAA (HazEL help pages)
validity <- c(
  "-1" = "erroneous entry",
  "0" = "only a seiche",
  "1" = "very doubtful",
  "2" = "questionable",
  "3" = "probable",
  "4" = "definite"
)
# the regions of the source, in NOAA's names, and the sea or ocean that they are in
regions <- c(
  "30" = "Red Sea and Persian Gulf",
  "40" = "Black Sea and Caspian Sea",
  "50" = "Mediterranean Sea",
  "60" = "Indian Ocean",
  "70" = "Southeast Atlantic",
  "71" = "Southwest Atlantic",
  "72" = "Northwest Atlantic",
  "73" = "Northeast Atlantic",
  "74" = "Caribbean Sea",
  "75" = "East coast of USA and Canada",
  "76" = "Gulf of Mexico",
  "77" = "West coast of Africa",
  "78" = "Central Africa",
  "80" = "Hawaii",
  "81" = "Australia, New Zealand and South Pacific",
  "82" = "New Guinea, Solomon Is. and Vanuatu",
  "83" = "Indonesia (Pacific) and Malaysia",
  "84" = "China, Koreas, Philippines, Taiwan",
  "85" = "Japan",
  "86" = "Kamchatka and Kuril Islands",
  "87" = "Alaska and Aleutian Islands",
  "88" = "West coast of North and Central America",
  "89" = "West coast of South America"
)
pacific_codes <- 80:89
# the causes, in the groups of this page
cause_group <- function(code) {
  case_when(
    code %in% 1:3 ~ "Earthquake",
    code %in% 4:7 ~ "Volcano",
    code == 8 ~ "Landslide",
    code == 9 ~ "Weather",
    TRUE ~ "Other or unknown"
  )
}
cause_levels <- c("Earthquake", "Volcano", "Landslide", "Weather", "Other or unknown")
events_all$status <- validity[as.character(events_all$eventValidity)]
first_year <- 1900
last_year <- max(events_all$year)
Code 
# the events to keep: probable or definite tsunamis
events <- events_all |>
  filter(eventValidity >= 3) |>
  mutate(
    cause = factor(cause_group(causeCode), levels = cause_levels),
    region = regions[as.character(regionCode)],
    ocean = case_when(
      is.na(regionCode) ~ NA_character_,
      regionCode %in% pacific_codes ~ "Pacific Ocean",
      regionCode == 60 ~ "Indian Ocean",
      regionCode %in% 70:78 ~ "Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean and Gulf",
      regionCode == 50 ~ "Mediterranean Sea",
      TRUE ~ "Black, Caspian and Red Seas, Persian Gulf"
    ),
    deadly = deaths >= 1 | deathsAmountOrder >= 1
  )
# the runups: the waves of the kept events, in places where the report was not doubtful
runups_since <- runups_all |> filter(year >= first_year)
runups <- runups_since |>
  filter(tsunamiEventId %in% events$id, doubtful == "n")
# a country name in a sentence
country_name <- function(x) {
  y <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(x))
  y[x == "USA"] <- "United States"
  y[x == "USA TERRITORY"] <- "US territories"
  y[x == "RUSSIA"] <- "Russia"
  y[x == "TURKEY"] <- "Turkey"
  y
}
# a place name in a table
place_name <- function(x) {
  y <- tools::toTitleCase(tolower(x))
  gsub("\\b(Ak|Se|Nw|Ne|Sw|Bc|Hi|Wa)\\b", "\\U\\1", y, perl = TRUE)
}
full_years <- first_year:(last_year - 1)
n_full <- length(full_years)
Code 
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the causes: earthquake, volcano, landslide and weather were checked for colour blindness (all pairs);
# the rest is grey
cause_colors <- c(
  "Earthquake" = "#2c7fb8",
  "Volcano" = "#d62728",
  "Landslide" = "#f0a000",
  "Weather" = "#6a3d9a",
  "Other or unknown" = "#9e9e9e"
)
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: water
blues <- c("#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#4292c6", "#2171b5", "#084594")
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
with_the <- function(x) ifelse(x == "United States", "the United States", x)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
Code 
n_all <- nrow(events_all)
n_kept <- nrow(events)
count_status <- function(codes) sum(events_all$eventValidity %in% codes)
n_with_xy <- sum(!is.na(events$latitude) & !is.na(events$longitude))
n_lake <- sum(!events$oceanicTsunami)
total_ex <- events |> filter(!is.na(deaths), !is.na(deathsTotal), deaths != deathsTotal)
haiti <- events |> filter(year == 2010, grepl("HAITI", locationName))
n_runups_all <- nrow(runups_all)
n_runups_since <- nrow(runups_since)
n_runups <- nrow(runups)
n_runup_events <- n_distinct(runups$tsunamiEventId)
n_runups_doubtful <- sum(runups_since$tsunamiEventId %in% events$id & runups_since$doubtful != "n")
n_runups_dropped_events <- sum(!runups_since$tsunamiEventId %in% events$id)

Only probable and definite tsunamis are kept. NOAA rates every report from -1 to 4. Since 1900 the database has 1,667 entries: 860 definite, 315 probable, 221 questionable, 188 very doubtful, 22 that only caused a seiche (a wave that sloshes in a lake or bay) and 61 erroneous. This page keeps the 1,175 definite and probable ones, 70% of the entries. The rest are too uncertain to count as tsunamis. Of those kept, 75 started in a lake, a reservoir or a river rather than the sea; they stay, and are named where they matter.

Deaths are those of the tsunami alone. The database gives two figures: the deaths of the tsunami, and a total for the whole event, which includes the earthquake or eruption that caused it. For the earthquake of Haiti in 2010 the total is 316,000 and the tsunami’s own figure 7. The two differ for 47 of the tsunamis that have both, so this page uses the tsunami’s own deaths, and only where a number is recorded (section 4).

The runups are those of the kept tsunamis, in places where the report was not doubtful. The runups table has 35,150 rows for all of history, and its filters do not cut it by year, so all of it is downloaded. 31,769 are of tsunamis since 1900. Of these, 561 belong to tsunamis that are not probable or definite, and 1,127 more are marked by NOAA as doubtful, or as waves that probably came from the weather or from an eruption’s air waves rather than from the sea. That leaves 30,081 places, for 1,027 tsunamis.

Places without a position are not on the map. 73 of the kept tsunamis have no latitude and longitude, so the map shows 1,102.

The latest year is incomplete. The database has tsunamis up to 2026, a year that is not over, so the counts over time (section 5) use the 126 full years, 1900 to 2025.

1. Where in the world do tsunamis start?

Code 
n_per_year <- sum(events$year < last_year) / n_full
by_cause <- events |>
  count(cause) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n), deaths = tapply(events$deaths, events$cause, sum, na.rm = TRUE)[as.character(cause)])
cause_n <- function(g, column = "n") by_cause[[column]][by_cause$cause == g]
with_region <- events[!is.na(events$regionCode), ]
ocean_share <- with_region |>
  count(ocean) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n))
ocean_in <- function(g) ocean_share$share[ocean_share$ocean == g]
by_region <- with_region |>
  count(regionCode, region) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(pacific = regionCode %in% pacific_codes)
by_country <- events |>
  count(country, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(name = country_name(country), share = 100 * n / sum(n))
top_countries <- head(by_country, 5)
earthquake_with_slide <- sum(events$causeCode == 3)
# the Mediterranean
med <- events |> filter(regionCode == 50)
med_country <- function(x) sum(med$country == x)
med_dead <- med |>
  filter(oceanicTsunami, !is.na(deaths)) |>
  slice_max(deaths, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
med_lakes <- med |> filter(!oceanicTsunami)
med_height <- median(med$maxWaterHeight, na.rm = TRUE)
pacific_height <- median(events$maxWaterHeight[events$regionCode %in% pacific_codes], na.rm = TRUE)

The Pacific Ocean: 72% of the tsunamis. Since 1900, 1,175 probable or definite tsunamis have been recorded, 9.2 a year. Of those with a region, 72% started in a region of the Pacific, 12% in the Atlantic, the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico, 8% in the Mediterranean and 6% in the Indian Ocean. By country of the source, Japan (184), United States (101), Indonesia (79), Russia (76) and Papua New Guinea (53) come first.

Code 
set.seed(2026)
on_map <- events |>
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) |>
  # the commonest cause first, so that the rarer ones are drawn on top of it
  arrange(cause)
map <- plot_ly()
for (g in cause_levels) {
  d <- on_map[on_map$cause == g, ]
  map <- add_trace(
    map,
    data = d,
    type = "scattergeo",
    lon = ~longitude,
    lat = ~latitude,
    mode = "markers",
    name = paste0(g, " (", nrow(d), ")"),
    marker = list(color = cause_colors[[g]], size = 6, opacity = 0.75, line = list(color = "white", width = 0.4)),
    text = ~ paste0(
      year,
      " ",
      place_name(locationName),
      ", ",
      country_name(country),
      "<br>",
      ifelse(is.na(eqMagnitude), "", paste0("Earthquake magnitude ", eqMagnitude, "<br>")),
      ifelse(is.na(maxWaterHeight), "", paste0("Highest water ", maxWaterHeight, " m"))
    ),
    hoverinfo = "text"
  )
}
map |>
  chart(
    paste0("Where tsunamis started, by cause, ", first_year, "–", last_year),
    "NOAA NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database; probable and definite tsunamis.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = FALSE,
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#e8e8e8",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
      lataxis = list(range = c(-70, 85))
    ),
    legend = c(legend_top, list(y = 0.99, yanchor = "bottom")),
    margin = list(t = 80, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )

Interactive chart: Where tsunamis started, by cause, 1900–2026

Earthquakes start 77% of them. 902 of the tsunamis were caused by an earthquake (67 of them by an earthquake and a landslide together), 113 by a landslide alone, 75 by the weather, 68 by a volcano, and 17 by something else or something unknown. On the map, most of them lie along the coasts of the Pacific, from Chile round to Japan and Indonesia. The weather tsunamis are what NOAA’s help pages call tsunami-like waves: they are produced by storms and other disturbances of the air, not by a movement of the sea floor. The table gives the toll of each cause:

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    cause = as.character(by_cause$cause),
    n = number(by_cause$n),
    share = percent(by_cause$share),
    deaths = number(unname(by_cause$deaths))
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c("Cause", "Tsunamis", "Share", "Deaths recorded"),
  align = "lrrr"
)
Cause Tsunamis Share Deaths recorded
Earthquake 902 77% 291,875
Volcano 68 6% 1,019
Landslide 113 10% 4,151
Weather 75 6% 101
Other or unknown 17 1% 1
Code 
top_regions <- head(by_region, 12)
top_regions <- top_regions[order(top_regions$n), ] # the largest at the top
top_regions$region <- factor(top_regions$region, levels = top_regions$region)
plot_ly() |>
  add_bars(
    data = top_regions[top_regions$pacific, ],
    x = ~n,
    y = ~region,
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Regions of the Pacific",
    marker = list(color = red),
    text = ~n,
    textposition = "outside",
    cliponaxis = FALSE,
    hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} tsunamis<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_bars(
    data = top_regions[!top_regions$pacific, ],
    x = ~n,
    y = ~region,
    orientation = "h",
    name = "Other regions",
    marker = list(color = gray),
    text = ~n,
    textposition = "outside",
    cliponaxis = FALSE,
    hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} tsunamis<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Tsunamis by region of the source, top 12"),
    "NOAA NCEI tsunami database.",
    x_axis = list(showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE, range = c(0, 1.12 * max(top_regions$n))),
    y_axis = list(automargin = TRUE),
    legend = legend_top,
    margin = list(l = 10, t = 80, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.05
  )

Interactive chart: Tsunamis by region of the source, top 12

The Mediterranean has 96 tsunamis, 8% of the world’s. Greece has 41 of them, Italy 24 and Turkey 9. The median highest water of a Mediterranean tsunami is 1.2 m, against 0.4 m in the Pacific. The deadliest of the sea itself was in 1908, at Messina Strait, Ionian Sea, where 2,000 died. 3 of the Mediterranean entries are in lakes or reservoirs, such as the Vajont dam in Italy in 1963.

2. Where do the waves strike, and how far do they travel?

Code 
# the farthest place that each tsunami reached
reach <- runups |>
  filter(!is.na(distFromSource)) |>
  group_by(tsunamiEventId) |>
  summarise(far = max(distFromSource))
far_km <- 3000
far_events <- reach |> filter(far >= far_km)
n_far <- nrow(far_events)
far_info <- events |> filter(id %in% far_events$tsunamiEventId)
far_pacific <- 100 * mean(far_info$regionCode %in% pacific_codes, na.rm = TRUE)
far_earthquake <- 100 * mean(far_info$cause == "Earthquake")
far_magnitude <- median(far_info$eqMagnitude, na.rm = TRUE)
far_by_country <- runups |>
  filter(distFromSource >= far_km) |>
  distinct(tsunamiEventId, country) |>
  count(country, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(name = country_name(country))
us_far <- runups |>
  filter(distFromSource >= far_km, country == "USA") |>
  distinct(tsunamiEventId, area) |>
  count(area)
hawaii_far <- us_far$n[us_far$area == "HI"]
farthest <- runups |> slice_max(distFromSource, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
runups_by_country <- runups |>
  count(country, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(name = country_name(country), share = 100 * n / sum(n))

Most tsunamis stay near home; the few that cross an ocean are earthquakes of the Pacific. Of the 1,014 tsunamis with a measured distance, 27% were measured at least 1,000 km from their source, and 180 (18%) at least 3,000 km away. 93% of those 180 began in a region of the Pacific and 98% were earthquakes, with a median magnitude of 7.8. The waves that travelled farthest were those of the earthquake of 2004, measured at Baltra Island in Ecuador, 19,266 km from the source.

Code 
far_top <- head(far_by_country, 10)
far_top <- far_top[order(far_top$n), ]
far_top$name <- factor(far_top$name, levels = far_top$name)
plot_ly(
  far_top,
  x = ~n,
  y = ~name,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(far_top$country == "USA", red, gray)),
  text = ~n,
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x} tsunamis<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Tsunamis that struck from ", number(far_km), " km or more"),
    "NOAA NCEI tsunami database (runups); top 10.",
    x_axis = list(showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE, range = c(0, 1.12 * max(far_top$n))),
    y_axis = list(automargin = TRUE),
    margin = list(l = 10, t = 70, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.05
  )

Interactive chart: Tsunamis that struck from 3,000 km or more

The United States, mostly Hawaii, is struck from afar the most. 132 tsunamis reached the United States from 3,000 km or more, and 125 of them reached Hawaii. It lies in the middle of the Pacific, so the waves of earthquakes all round the ocean can arrive there. Then come US territories (75), Japan (58) and Canada (55).

The number of places where waves were measured says as much about the measuring as about the waves. The runups table has 11,740 places in Japan (39% of all), 4,191 in the United States and 2,458 in Indonesia. A country with few places may have few measurements rather than few waves.

3. How big are they, and how often does one kill?

Code 
with_height <- events |> filter(!is.na(maxWaterHeight))
n_height <- nrow(with_height)
height_breaks <- c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, Inf)
height_names <- c("Under 1 m", "1 to 3 m", "3 to 10 m", "10 to 30 m", "30 m or more")
with_height$class <- cut(with_height$maxWaterHeight, height_breaks, right = FALSE, labels = height_names)
height_counts <- as.integer(table(with_height$class))
height_share <- function(i) 100 * height_counts[i] / n_height
tall <- with_height |> filter(maxWaterHeight >= 30)
tallest <- with_height |> slice_max(maxWaterHeight, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
tall_by_cause <- table(tall$cause)
tall_slide_codes <- sum(tall$causeCode %in% c(3, 5, 7, 8))
tall_lake <- sum(!tall$oceanicTsunami)
tall_since_2000 <- sum(tall$year >= 2000)
n_far_slide <- sum(far_info$cause == "Landslide")
cause_name_of <- function(code) c("3" = "an earthquake and a landslide", "8" = "a landslide")[as.character(code)]
n_deadly <- sum(events$deadly, na.rm = TRUE)
n_counted <- sum(!is.na(events$deaths))
n_code_only <- sum(is.na(events$deaths) & events$deathsAmountOrder >= 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_1000 <- sum(events$deathsAmountOrder == 4, na.rm = TRUE)
n_100 <- sum(events$deathsAmountOrder >= 3, na.rm = TRUE)

More than half of the tsunamis are under a metre, and a few are over 30. Of the 998 tsunamis with a measured height of water, 56% are under 1 m, 18% 1 to 3 m, 16% 3 to 10 m, 7% 10 to 30 m and 4% (42) 30 m or more. The height is the highest water of the event above the normal sea level: for a tide gauge it is half the height from trough to crest, and for a survey the highest point reached on land (NOAA).

Code 
plot_ly(
  x = factor(height_names, levels = height_names),
  y = height_counts,
  type = "bar",
  marker = list(color = blues),
  text = height_counts,
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y} tsunamis<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    "Highest water of each tsunami",
    paste0("NOAA NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database; the ", number(n_height), " tsunamis with a measured height."),
    y_title = "Tsunamis",
    y_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(height_counts))),
    margin = list(t = 60, b = 80, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.2
  )

Interactive chart: Highest water of each tsunami

The tallest waves are not those of the great earthquakes. Of the 42 tsunamis of 30 m or more, 28 were caused by a landslide alone, 6 by a volcano and 8 by an earthquake; 36 involved a landslide, 20 of them in a lake, a reservoir or a river, and 20 have happened since 2000. Of the 113 tsunamis caused by a landslide alone, 0 were measured 3,000 km or more away (section 2). The tallest of all was in SE. Alaska, AK in 1958, 524.6 m, from an earthquake and a landslide, which killed 5 people.

Most tsunamis kill nobody on record, but a few kill thousands. 165 of the 1,175 tsunamis (14%) have at least one death recorded: 1.3 a year. NOAA records a number of deaths for 156 of them, and for 9 only a class (for example “few, 1 to 50”). 41 tsunamis killed more than 100 people and 16 more than 1,000, one every 7.9 years.

4. Which were the deadliest?

Code 
dead <- events |>
  filter(!is.na(deaths)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
total_dead <- sum(dead$deaths)
top10 <- head(dead, 10)
top2_share <- 100 * sum(dead$deaths[1:2]) / total_dead
by_country_dead <- dead |>
  group_by(country) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths), events = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths)) |>
  mutate(name = country_name(country), share = 100 * deaths / total_dead)
cause_phrase <- function(code) {
  c("1" = "Earthquake", "2" = "Questionable earthquake", "3" = "Earthquake and landslide", "6" = "Volcano", "8" = "Landslide")[as.character(code)]
}
top10_lake <- top10 |> filter(!oceanicTsunami)

Two tsunamis caused 83% of the deaths on record. From 1900 to 2026, 297,147 deaths are recorded, in 156 tsunamis with a number of deaths. The earthquake off Sumatra on 26 December 2004 killed 227,899 and the one off Honshu, Japan, in 2011, 18,423. Indonesia has 81% of all the recorded deaths, Japan 8%.

Code 
dc <- head(by_country_dead, 8)
dc <- dc[order(dc$deaths), ]
dc$name <- factor(dc$name, levels = dc$name)
plot_ly(
  dc,
  x = ~deaths,
  y = ~name,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(dc$country == "INDONESIA", red, gray)),
  text = ~ number(deaths),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:,.0f} deaths in %{customdata} tsunamis<extra></extra>",
  customdata = ~events,
  showlegend = FALSE
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Recorded tsunami deaths by country, top 8"),
    "NOAA NCEI tsunami database; country of the source.",
    x_axis = list(showgrid = FALSE, showticklabels = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE, range = c(0, 1.45 * max(dc$deaths))),
    y_axis = list(automargin = TRUE),
    margin = list(l = 10, t = 70, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.05
  )

Interactive chart: Recorded tsunami deaths by country, top 8

The ten deadliest, with the highest water that each reached:

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    year = top10$year,
    place = paste0(place_name(top10$locationName), ", ", country_name(top10$country)),
    cause = cause_phrase(top10$causeCode),
    deaths = number(top10$deaths),
    height = ifelse(is.na(top10$maxWaterHeight), "", one(top10$maxWaterHeight))
  ),
  col.names = c("Year", "Place", "Cause", "Deaths", "Highest water (m)"),
  align = "rllrr"
)
Year Place Cause Deaths Highest water (m)
2004 Off W. Coast of Sumatra, Indonesia Earthquake 227,899 50.9
2011 Honshu Island, Japan Earthquake 18,423 39.3
1952 Kamchatka, Russia Earthquake 10,000 23.0
1976 Moro Gulf, Philippines Earthquake 6,800 9.0
2018 Sulawesi, Indonesia Earthquake and landslide 4,340 10.7
1933 Sanriku, Japan Earthquake 3,022 29.0
1960 Southern Chile, Chile Earthquake 2,226 25.0
1907 NW. Sumatra, Indonesia Earthquake 2,188 15.0
1908 Messina Strait, Ionian Sea, Italy Earthquake and landslide 2,000 13.0
1963 Vajont Dam, Vajont River, Italy Landslide 2,000 235.0

The tsunami of 1963 at Vajont Dam, Vajont River was in a reservoir, behind a dam, and not in the sea. These figures are a floor: 1,019 tsunamis have no number of deaths in the database, and the database does not say whether they had none or whether the number is unknown.

5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

Code 
yearly <- events |>
  filter(year < last_year) |>
  count(year) |>
  right_join(data.frame(year = full_years), by = "year") |>
  mutate(n = coalesce(n, 0L))
big <- events |> filter(causeCode %in% 1:3, eqMagnitude >= 7.5, year < last_year)
yearly_big <- big |>
  count(year) |>
  right_join(data.frame(year = full_years), by = "year") |>
  mutate(n = coalesce(n, 0L))
span <- 25
early <- first_year:(first_year + span - 1)
late <- (last_year - span):(last_year - 1)
mean_years <- function(x, years) mean(x$n[x$year %in% years])
decade_of <- function(x) 10 * (x %/% 10)
by_decade <- events |>
  mutate(decade = decade_of(year)) |>
  count(decade, name = "all") |>
  left_join(
    events |> filter(causeCode %in% 1:3, eqMagnitude >= 7.5) |> mutate(decade = decade_of(year)) |> count(decade, name = "big"),
    by = "decade"
  )
by_decade$big[is.na(by_decade$big)] <- 0
by_decade$label <- ifelse(by_decade$decade == decade_of(last_year), paste0(by_decade$decade, "–", substr(last_year, 3, 4)), paste0(by_decade$decade, "s"))
# how well the tsunamis are measured, by half century
half <- cut(events$year, c(1900, 1950, 2000, Inf), right = FALSE, labels = c("1900–1949", "1950–1999", paste0("2000–", last_year)))
measured <- tapply(!is.na(events$maxWaterHeight), half, mean) * 100

More tsunamis are recorded than a century ago, but that does not show that more happen. From 1900 to 1924 the database has 5.2 tsunamis a year; from 2001 to 2025, 17.2. A rank test over the 126 full years puts the chance of a pattern this strong without a rise at less than 1 in 100. The same holds for the tsunamis of the great earthquakes alone (magnitude 7.5 or more, 1.4 a year at first and 3.4 lately; the chance is less than 1 in 100). But the records are not equally complete: a measured height is given for 69% of the tsunamis of 1900–1949, 88% of 1950–1999 and 93% of 2000–2026. Later tsunamis are better documented, so part of the rise may be better recording. The data cannot say how much of it is real.

Code 
plot_ly(by_decade, x = ~label) |>
  add_bars(y = ~all, name = "All tsunamis", marker = list(color = gray), hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y} tsunamis<extra></extra>") |>
  add_bars(
    y = ~big,
    name = "From earthquakes of magnitude 7.5+",
    marker = list(color = red),
    hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y} tsunamis<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  chart(
    "Tsunamis in each decade",
    paste0("NOAA NCEI Global Historical Tsunami Database. The ", by_decade$label[nrow(by_decade)], " is not over."),
    y_title = "Tsunamis",
    legend = legend_top,
    barmode = "group",
    margin = list(t = 90, b = 90),
    note_y = -0.14
  )

Interactive chart: Tsunamis in each decade

So, what does it mean?

  1. Tsunamis follow the earthquakes, and most of them are in the Pacific. 72% of the tsunamis with a region started in the Pacific; 77% of all of them were caused by an earthquake.
  2. A few cross an ocean. 180 tsunamis, 18% of those measured, struck 3,000 km or more from their source, and Hawaii received 125 of them.
  3. The tallest waves come from landslides, the deadliest from earthquakes. 28 of the 42 tsunamis of 30 m or more were landslides alone, and the highest water was 524.6 m.
  4. Deaths are concentrated in a few events. Two tsunamis, off Sumatra in 2004 and off Japan in 2011, account for 83% of the deaths on record.
  5. More are recorded now, and the data cannot say whether more happen. 5.2 a year at first and 17.2 lately, while the share with a measured height went from 69% to 93%.

What this does not show. The database lists the tsunamis that were reported, not all the waves of the sea, and it does not say how likely a tsunami is in any one place. The map shows the sources, not the coasts that are in danger. Doubtful reports are left out, and so is everything before 1900, though the database goes back to 2000 BC. Deaths are a floor, and the heights mix the tide gauge, the eyewitness and the survey. The numbers of places for each country depend on how well each country measures its tsunamis.

For the earthquakes behind most tsunamis, see Earthquakes; for eruptions, Volcanoes; for all the hazards together, Natural Disasters.

Sources

  • NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, NCEI/WDS Global Historical Tsunami Database, doi:10.7289/V5PN93H7: the events and the runups, from the hazard-service interface, without a key. Access is unrestricted; NOAA gives no warranty for the data (the use constraints of the dataset record).
  • NOAA NCEI, Introduction to Global Historical Tsunami Data: the definition of a runup and the notes on the data.
  • NOAA NCEI, Hazard Tsunami Search (HazEL): the help pages with the codes of validity, cause, region, deaths and kind of measurement.

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · curl · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · jsonlite

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Where Tornadoes Strike: The United States, Canada and What Cannot Be Compared
item.description: Where tornadoes happen: the United States state by state since 1950, how Canada’s count compares, when they strike, how strong and how deadly they are, the worst events, and whether there are more of them.
item.content:encoded:
Where tornadoes happen: the United States state by state since 1950, how Canada’s count compares, when they strike, how strong and how deadly they are, the worst events, and whether there are more of them.

What is this?

A tornado is a narrow, violently rotating column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground. People think of the American Plains, and the United States does report more tornadoes than any other country we can count. But there is no single open database of the world’s tornadoes, so this story does what the data allow: it counts the United States closely, sets Canada beside it, and says plainly what cannot be compared. It asks five questions:

  1. Where do tornadoes happen?
  2. When do they strike?
  3. How strong and how deadly are they?
  4. Which were the worst?
  5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

This is one of a series on natural disasters: see the overview and Floods.

The data come from two places, downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • The United States: the tornado database of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Storm Prediction Center (SPC), one row for each tornado since 1950, with its date and time, the state, the start and end points, the length and width of its path, the rating, and the people injured and killed (SPC severe weather database). It is made of the reports that the National Weather Service’s offices send in (format description). The file used here is the one with single tracks: a tornado that crosses a state line is one row, in the state where it touched down.
  • Canada: the event summaries of the Northern Tornadoes Project, founded at Western University in 2017, which investigates tornadoes by ground, drone, aerial and satellite surveys (Northern Tornadoes Project).

The rating of a tornado is not a measurement of its wind. Since February 2007 the National Weather Service rates a tornado on the Enhanced Fujita scale, from EF0 to EF5, from the damage that it leaves: an EF0 is estimated at 65 to 85 miles per hour (the gust of three seconds), an EF1 at 86 to 110, an EF2 at 111 to 135, an EF3 at 136 to 165, an EF4 at 166 to 200 and an EF5 at more than 200 (National Weather Service). Before 2007 the original Fujita scale (F0 to F5) was used, in the same way. This page writes EF0 to EF5 for both. A tornado is rated by what it destroys, so one that crosses empty land can get a low rating whatever its wind.

Europe is missing, on purpose. The European Severe Weather Database, kept by the European Severe Storms Laboratory, lets a guest browse only recent events; the full data need a request for restricted access (ESWD). A study of its reports from 1950 to 2015 finds that tornadoes do occur in Europe, with injuries, deaths and damage, “although their reported frequencies and intensities are lower compared with the United States” (Antonescu et al. 2017). That is all this page can say about Europe from what it has read.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# the SPC file of single tornado tracks since 1950, named after the last year it holds: try the
# latest years first
this_year <- as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y"))
tor <- NULL
for (y in this_year:2020) {
  tor <- tryCatch(
    read.csv(paste0("https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/1950-", y, "_actual_tornadoes.csv")),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(tor)) break
}
# the Northern Tornadoes Project's event summaries (Canada), a thousand rows at a time
ntp_url <- paste0(
  "https://services.arcgis.com/rGKxabTU9mcXMw7k/arcgis/rest/services/",
  "NTP_Event_Summaries_stakeholder/FeatureServer/0/query"
)
ntp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0, 9000, by = 1000), function(offset) {
  r <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
    ntp_url,
    "?where=1%3D1&outFields=Year,event_type,province&returnGeometry=false&resultOffset=",
    offset,
    "&resultRecordCount=1000&f=json"
  ))
  if (length(r$features) == 0) NULL else r$features$attributes
}))
Code 
first_year <- min(tor$yr)
last_year <- max(tor$yr)
first_ten <- first_year:(first_year + 9)
last_ten <- (last_year - 9):last_year
# the rating: -9 means that the tornado has no rating
ratings <- c("EF0", "EF1", "EF2", "EF3", "EF4", "EF5")
tor$rating <- factor(ifelse(tor$mag < 0, "Unrated", ratings[pmax(tor$mag, 0) + 1]), levels = c("Unrated", ratings))
n_unrated <- sum(tor$mag < 0)
unrated_modern <- tor[tor$mag < 0 & tor$yr >= 2007, ]
estimated <- sum(tor$fc == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
state_name <- function(s) ifelse(s %in% state.abb, state.name[match(s, state.abb)], s)
# the states: 50 states, with their area (the R datasets) and the census division they are in
areas <- data.frame(
  st = state.abb,
  state = state.name,
  km2 = state.area * 2.589988,
  division = as.character(state.division)
)
tor_states <- tor[tor$st %in% areas$st, ]
# the time of day: the SPC puts all times, but a few, on central standard time (3 in the column tz);
# the sun's time at the place is the clock in Greenwich (central standard time plus six hours) plus one
# hour for every 15 degrees of longitude
hms <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(tor$time, ":"))
tor$clock <- as.numeric(hms[, 1]) + as.numeric(hms[, 2]) / 60
tor$sun_hour <- floor((tor$clock + 6 + tor$slon / 15) %% 24)
timed <- tor[tor$tz == 3 & tor$slon != 0, ]
n_other_clock <- sum(tor$tz != 3)

# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# a change in per cent, with its sign (the bold font of the charts has no minus sign: a dash there)
change_text <- function(x, minus = "−") paste0(ifelse(x >= 0, "+", minus), round(abs(x)), "%")
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
# a date as "27 April 2011"
long_date <- function(x) format(as.Date(x), "%e %B %Y") |> trimws()
Code 
# the unrated tornadoes in the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale, and the tornadoes that the SPC rated
# afterwards from the damage (fc = 1, from 1953 to 1982)
n_all <- nrow(tor)
unrated_years <- tor |>
  filter(yr >= 2007) |>
  group_by(yr) |>
  summarise(share = 100 * mean(mag < 0))
first_unrated <- min(tor$yr[tor$mag < 0 & tor$yr >= 2007])
rated_early <- tor[tor$fc == 1, ]

Some tornadoes have no rating. 1,546 of the 73,458 tornadoes (2.1%) are coded -9, “unknown”. For 1953 to 1982 the SPC has filled in an estimated rating, from the property loss and the length of the path, for 1,863 tornadoes that had none; the file marks them. The 1,546 that remain unrated come from 2007 on, and from 2019 on they are 10% to 20% of the tornadoes of a year. The documentation does not say why. This page counts them in the totals, shows them apart in the tables, and, where a trend depends on the ratings, tests what happens if all of them were strong (section 5).

Times are those of the sun. The SPC converts the time of a tornado to central standard time, whatever the state (37 tornadoes are on another clock). A tornado in Georgia at 17:00 central standard time struck at six in the evening by the clock there. To compare places, section 2 turns each time into the sun’s time at the place where the tornado began, from its longitude: an hour for every 15 degrees.

1. Where do tornadoes happen?

Code 
last_eight <- (last_year - 7):last_year
us_a_year <- tor |>
  filter(yr %in% last_eight) |>
  nrow() / length(last_eight)
ntp$Year <- as.integer(ntp$Year)
canada_tornadoes <- ntp[ntp$event_type %in% c("tornado_over_land", "tornado_over_water") & ntp$Year %in% last_eight, ]
canada_a_year <- nrow(canada_tornadoes) / length(last_eight)
canada_provinces <- sort(table(canada_tornadoes$province), decreasing = TRUE) / length(last_eight)
canada_water <- 100 * mean(canada_tornadoes$event_type == "tornado_over_water")
# the states since 2006, the years of the Enhanced Fujita scale
since <- 2006
years_since <- last_year - since + 1
by_state <- tor_states |>
  filter(yr >= since) |>
  group_by(st) |>
  summarise(all = n(), ef2 = sum(mag >= 2), ef3 = sum(mag >= 3)) |>
  left_join(areas, by = "st") |>
  mutate(
    per_10k = all / years_since / km2 * 1e4,
    ef2_per_10k = ef2 / years_since / km2 * 1e4,
    a_year = all / years_since
  )
by_count <- by_state |> arrange(desc(all))
by_density <- by_state |> arrange(desc(per_10k))
by_strong <- by_state |> arrange(desc(ef2_per_10k))
top_density <- by_density$state[1:3]
# the state with the most tornadoes, and its density
texas <- by_state[by_state$st == "TX", ]
rank_texas_density <- which(by_density$st == "TX")
n_states <- nrow(by_state)

The United States reports about 1,346 tornadoes a year; Canada’s project finds about 112, and for Europe there is no open count. From 2018 to 2025 the United States had 1,346 a year on average and Canada 112 (15% of them over water, which the Canadian figures count). The two numbers are not a fair comparison. They come from different ways of finding tornadoes, and a tornado that nobody reports or surveys is not counted anywhere.

    )

In the United States, Texas has the most tornadoes, but the most for their size are in Mississippi. Texas had the most tornadoes from 2006 to 2025, 119 a year, but it is large. Per area, Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois come first, with 5.40, 4.92 and 4.51 tornadoes a year for every 10,000 square kilometres; Texas is only 24th of the 50 states, with 1.72. For the strong tornadoes (EF2 and above) the order is Mississippi, Alabama and Kentucky: 0.90, 0.81 and 0.54. Hover over a state to see its numbers.
