Most of the violent ones, the EF4 and EF5, began in two census divisions: the West North Central division (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) had 32% of them and the West South Central division (Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma and Texas) 24%.

2. When do they strike?

Code 
month_share <- function(x) 100 * tabulate(x$mo, 12) / nrow(x)
all_months <- month_share(tor)
strong_months <- month_share(tor[tor$mag >= 3, ])
peak_month <- which.max(all_months)
three_months <- function(s) sapply(1:12, function(m) sum(s[(m - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1]))
best_three <- which.max(three_months(all_months))
best_three_share <- max(three_months(all_months))
winter_share <- sum(all_months[c(12, 1, 2)])
strong_winter <- sum(strong_months[c(12, 1, 2)])
hour_share <- 100 * tabulate(timed$sun_hour + 1, 24) / nrow(timed)
peak_hour <- which.max(hour_share) - 1
afternoon <- sum(hour_share[(15:19) + 1]) # 15:00 to 19:59
night <- timed$sun_hour <= 5
night_tornadoes <- 100 * mean(night)
night_deaths <- 100 * sum(timed$fat[night]) / sum(timed$fat)
night_strong <- 100 * mean(night[timed$mag >= 3]) # the share of the EF3 and above that began at night
hour_label <- function(h) paste0(sprintf("%02d", h), ":00")

May is the peak month, and each part of the country peaks at its own time. 22% of all tornadoes since 1950 began in May, and 54% in the three months of April to June. The strong ones (EF3 and above) are more spread out over the year than the weak ones: 11% of them came in December, January and February, against 8% of all tornadoes.

The calendar shows, for each census division, the share of its tornadoes that came in each month. The divisions are ordered from the one with the most tornadoes.

In the East South Central division (Alabama, Kentucky, Mississippi and Tennessee) the busiest month is April (22% of its tornadoes); in the West North Central division (Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota and South Dakota) it is June (27%). Late afternoon and evening. By the sun’s time at the place where they began, the busiest hour of the day is 16:00 to 17:00, and 52% of all tornadoes began between 15:00 and 20:00.

Few begin at night, and they are somewhat deadlier. Between midnight and 06:00 began 7% of the tornadoes, and 9% of the deaths were from them. Among the EF3 and stronger tornadoes, 8% began at night.

3. How strong and how deadly are they?

Code 
by_rating <- tor |>
  group_by(rating) |>
  summarise(n = n(), deaths = sum(fat), injured = sum(inj)) |>
  mutate(
    share = 100 * n / sum(n),
    death_share = 100 * deaths / sum(deaths),
    per_thousand = 1000 * deaths / n
  )
of_rating <- function(r, column) by_rating[[column]][by_rating$rating == r]
rated_n <- sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating != "Unrated"])
weak_share <- 100 * sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating %in% c("EF0", "EF1")]) / rated_n
violent_n <- sum(by_rating$n[by_rating$rating %in% c("EF4", "EF5")])
violent_tor_share <- 100 * violent_n / sum(by_rating$n)
violent_death_share <- sum(by_rating$death_share[by_rating$rating %in% c("EF4", "EF5")])
total_deaths <- sum(tor$fat)
total_injured <- sum(tor$inj)
deaths_ef0 <- of_rating("EF0", "deaths")

Most tornadoes are weak; most of the deaths come from the strongest. Of the tornadoes that have a rating, 81% were EF0 or EF1. The 656 EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of all of them, and 61% of the 6,341 people killed from 1950 to 2025 died in them. An EF5 killed on average 22 people, an EF0 one in 1,389 (the chart and the table count the unrated too).

A rating describes damage, not size. The tornadoes with no rating killed 2 people.   ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = red, `FALSE` = gray), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1950, 2020, 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(
    title = "People killed by tornadoes each year",
    subtitle = "United States, red: the three worst years",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA Storm Prediction Center"
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

The worst years were 2011, 1953 and 1974, with 553, 523 and 366 deaths. The data say how many died, not how many tornadoes struck places where people live: that is a question of where tornadoes land, and of warnings and shelter, which this page does not follow.

5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

Code 
count_after <- function(x, years) mean(x[by_year$yr %in% years])
trend_row <- function(name, x) {
  data.frame(
    name = name,
    start = count_after(x, first_ten),
    end = count_after(x, last_ten),
    chance = chance(x, by_year$yr),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}
# the days of the year with at least one tornado of rating EF1 or above, and the days with ten or more
ef1_days <- tor[tor$mag >= 1, ] |>
  count(yr, date) |>
  group_by(yr) |>
  summarise(days = n(), big_days = sum(n >= 10))
ef1_days <- left_join(data.frame(yr = by_year$yr), ef1_days, by = "yr")
ef1_days[is.na(ef1_days)] <- 0
changes <- rbind(
  trend_row("All tornadoes", by_year$n),
  trend_row("EF1 or above", by_year$ef1),
  trend_row("EF2 or above", by_year$ef2),
  trend_row("EF3 or above", by_year$ef3),
  trend_row("People killed", by_year$deaths),
  trend_row("Days with an EF1 or above", ef1_days$days),
  trend_row("Days with ten or more EF1 or above", ef1_days$big_days)
)
changes$change <- 100 * (changes$end / changes$start - 1)
of_change <- function(name, column) changes[[column]][changes$name == name]
# what if every unrated tornado were EF1 or above?
chance_if_strong <- chance(by_year$ef1 + by_year$unrated, by_year$yr)
before_2007 <- by_year$yr < 2007
chance_before <- chance(by_year$ef1[before_2007], by_year$yr[before_2007])
chance_after <- chance(by_year$ef1[!before_2007], by_year$yr[!before_2007])
ef2_peak <- by_year$yr[which.max(by_year$ef2)]
ef0 <- by_year$n - by_year$ef1 - by_year$unrated
ef0_start <- count_after(ef0, first_ten)
ef0_end <- count_after(ef0, last_ten)

More are reported, but the rise is mostly in the weak tornadoes. In 1950–1959 the SPC database had 479 tornadoes a year, in 2016–2025 1,318: 175% more, and a rank test of all the years finds the rise (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is less than 1 in 100). Much of the rise is in the weakest tornadoes: EF0 tornadoes went from 105 a year to 534. A study of the database found that the doubling of the count from the 1950s to the 2000s “is likely not related to meteorological causes alone”, and that the count of F1 and stronger tornadoes was steadier than that of F2 and stronger (Verbout et al. 2006); another says that changes in how tornadoes are reported “have made it difficult” to read the trend, and leaves out the weakest (Brooks et al. 2014). Counting from EF1 up, the rise is smaller: 374 a year at the start and 632 at the end (+69%), and the test does not clearly find a trend (6 in 100).

The table compares the first and the last ten years. The last column is the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as that of all the years without a trend.

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    name = changes$name,
    start = number(changes$start),
    end = number(changes$end),
    change = change_text(changes$change),
    chance = changes$chance
  ),
  col.names = c(
    "",
    paste0(min(first_ten), "–", max(first_ten)),
    paste0(min(last_ten), "–", max(last_ten)),
    "Change",
    "By chance, in 100"
  ),
  align = "lrrrr"
)
1950–1959 2016–2025 Change By chance, in 100
All tornadoes 479 1,318 +175% less than 1
EF1 or above 374 632 +69% 6
EF2 or above 189 142 −25% less than 1
EF3 or above 50 28 −43% less than 1
People killed 142 51 −64% 4
Days with an EF1 or above 120 110 −9% less than 1
Days with ten or more EF1 or above 7 18 +167% less than 1
Code 
panels <- c("All tornadoes", "EF1 or above", "EF2 or above", "EF3 or above")
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = panels[1], yr = by_year$yr, n = by_year$n),
  data.frame(panel = panels[2], yr = by_year$yr, n = by_year$ef1),
  data.frame(panel = panels[3], yr = by_year$yr, n = by_year$ef2),
  data.frame(panel = panels[4], yr = by_year$yr, n = by_year$ef3)
)
long$panel <- factor(long$panel, levels = panels)
ten_year <- changes[match(panels, changes$name), ]
bands <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels), x0 = min(first_ten) - 0.4, x1 = max(first_ten) + 0.4, y = ten_year$start, who = "first"),
  data.frame(panel = factor(panels, levels = panels), x0 = min(last_ten) - 0.4, x1 = max(last_ten) + 0.4, y = ten_year$end, who = "last")
)
ggplot(long, aes(x = yr, y = n)) +
  geom_line(colour = dark_gray, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = dark_gray, size = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(
    data = bands,
    aes(x = x0, xend = x1, y = y, yend = y, colour = who),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(first = blue, last = red), guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1950, 2020, 20)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "More tornadoes, or only more found?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Tornadoes in each year. Blue: the average of ",
      min(first_ten),
      "–",
      max(first_ten),
      "; red: of ",
      min(last_ten),
      "–",
      max(last_ten)
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: NOAA Storm Prediction Center. Unrated tornadoes are in the first panel only."
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )

The strongest tornadoes are fewer, but be careful with that. The EF2 and stronger tornadoes fell from 189 a year to 142 (by chance less than 1 in 100), the EF3 and stronger from 50 to 28 (less than 1 in 100). Their peak year was 1973. But ratings are judgements of damage, they changed from one scale to the other in 2007, and from 2007 the unrated tornadoes grew in number, so this page does not conclude that the strong tornadoes have become rarer. The unrated tornadoes matter for the count of EF1 and above: if every one of them is counted in it, the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend becomes 1 in 100, against 6. For the years before 2007 alone it is 95 in 100, and for 2007 on 3 in 100. People killed fell from 142 a year to 51 (4 in 100); these data do not say why.

What changed more is how the tornadoes come. The days with at least one tornado of EF1 or above fell from 120.4 a year to 110.0, while the days with ten or more of them rose from 6.7 to 17.9 (the chances of the two patterns, less than 1 and less than 1 in 100). That is what a study of the database found, after setting aside the weakest tornadoes: the mean annual number “has remained relatively constant”, but the variability has increased since the 1970s, with fewer days with tornadoes and more days with many (Brooks et al. 2014).

So, what does it mean?

  1. A few states have the most tornadoes for their size, and they are not the largest. Mississippi, Alabama and Illinois had the most per area from 2006 to 2025, and Texas, the state with the most tornadoes, only 24th. Canada’s project finds about 112 a year, against 1,346 in the United States, but the two are not counted the same way.
  2. They come in the afternoon and evening, mostly in spring. 22% of them began in May, and each part of the country has its own busiest month.
  3. Most are weak and most deaths come from the strongest. EF4 and EF5 tornadoes were 0.9% of the tornadoes and 61% of the deaths.
  4. The worst years and days are far from the average. 27 April 2011 had 210 tornadoes in one day, and 2011 killed 553 people.
  5. More are counted, but that is not the same as more. The tornadoes of EF2 and above did not rise; what has changed is that the tornadoes of EF1 and above come on fewer days and in bigger groups.

What this does not show. There is no worldwide count: the data cover the United States and, in outline, Canada, and say nothing of the many countries where tornadoes are not systematically recorded, so this page cannot say that the United States has the most tornadoes in the world, only the most that are counted. Reports depend on who is there to see a tornado, and the ratings on what it destroyed. Averages by state hide the differences inside a state, and a rank test says whether a pattern is likely to be chance, not what causes it. And the counts say nothing of the people who live where tornadoes land.

For floods, see Floods; for all the hazards together, the overview.

Sources

  • NOAA National Weather Service Storm Prediction Center, Severe weather database files (1950–2025), file 1950-2025_actual_tornadoes.csv, and its format description. The information on National Weather Service web pages is in the public domain (NWS disclaimer).
  • National Weather Service, The Enhanced Fujita Scale (EF Scale).
  • Northern Tornadoes Project, Western University: Open Data, the layer NTP Event Summaries (non-commercial use is permitted, per the project’s page).
  • European Severe Storms Laboratory, European Severe Weather Database (not used: access beyond recent events is by request).
  • Antonescu, B., Schultz, D. M., Holzer, A. and Groenemeijer, P. (2017), Tornadoes in Europe: An underestimated threat, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 98, 713–728.
  • Brooks, H. E., Carbin, G. W. and Marsh, P. T. (2014), Increased variability of tornado occurrence in the United States, Science 346, 349–352.
  • Verbout, S. M., Brooks, H. E., Leslie, L. M. and Schultz, D. M. (2006), Evolution of the U.S. tornado database: 1954–2003, Weather and Forecasting 21, 86–93.
  • R Core Team, the datasets package: state.area, state.name, state.division.

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · jsonlite

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Where the Water Rises: Large Floods in Every Part of the World
item.description: Where in the world floods happen, kill and displace the most people, when each part of the world floods, the worst floods on record, and whether floods have become more frequent or deadlier, from two open flood records.
item.content:encoded:
Where in the world floods happen, kill and displace the most people, when each part of the world floods, the worst floods on record, and whether floods have become more frequent or deadlier, from two open flood records.

What is this?

Wherever rain falls and a river runs, a flood is possible, so the records show floods in every part of the world. But they do not happen equally often, and they do not kill equally often. This story asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world do the large floods happen?
  2. Where do floods kill the most people?
  3. When does each part of the world flood?
  4. Which were the worst floods?
  5. Are floods more frequent or deadlier than they were?

It is one of a series on natural hazards: see Natural Disasters for the overview, and Tornadoes for another hazard of the weather.

No single record of floods is complete, so the page uses two, which count different things, and downloads them when it is rendered:

  • The Global Flood Records of the DFO Flood Observatory (University of Colorado), one row for each large flood from January 1985 to December 2023: when it started and ended, the countries it hit, its estimated cause, the people killed and the people displaced (DFO, data). DFO gives a flood an entry when it “appears to be large”: significant damage to buildings or farmland, a long time since the last similar flood, or deaths. It builds the record from news and government reports (DFO notes on the archive). The rows say where the flood was, not how many people lived there.
  • EM-DAT, the international disaster database of the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED, UCLouvain), as yearly totals for each country since 2000: floods that are confirmed by at least two sources and meet one of its entry criteria, which are 10 or more deaths, 100 or more people affected, a call for international help or a declaration of an emergency (EM-DAT FAQ). The totals come from the Humanitarian Data Exchange.
  • The population and the land area of each country, and the continent it is in, from Our World in Data (population, land area, continents).

What counts as a flood. EM-DAT uses “flood” as a general term for water that overflows a river onto dry land, for higher-than-normal water along a coast or around a lake, and for flash floods, where water ponds where the rain fell; it includes glacial lake outburst floods (Our World in Data). Dead in EM-DAT means the dead plus the missing; in DFO, the missing are not counted. Affected in EM-DAT means injured, affected or homeless (EM-DAT). A tropical cyclone is a large storm that forms over warm sea and brings wind, heavy rain and a rise of the sea; a monsoon is a season of heavy rain that comes with a seasonal change in the wind.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "jsonlite", "readxl"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(jsonlite)
library(readxl)

The data

Code 
# a chart of Our World in Data as a table: one row for each country or region and each year
owid <- function(chart) {
  read.csv(paste0(
    "https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/",
    chart,
    ".csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true"
  ))
}
continents <- owid("continents-according-to-our-world-in-data")
population <- owid("population")
land <- owid("land-area-km")
# the DFO Global Flood Records, version 0.9.0 (CC0): one row for each large flood
dfo_url <- "https://zenodo.org/records/19288171/files/Global_Flood_Records.csv"
dfo_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
download.file(dfo_url, dfo_file, quiet = TRUE)
dfo <- read.csv(dfo_file, encoding = "UTF-8", check.names = FALSE)
# the column names, in the order of the file
names(dfo) <- c("id", "glide", "start", "end", "country", "area", "source", "cause", "dead", "displaced", "severity", "magnitude")
# the EM-DAT country profiles: the yearly figures of each country, from the page of the dataset on the
# Humanitarian Data Exchange, which gives the address of the latest file
hdx <- fromJSON("https://data.humdata.org/api/3/action/package_show?id=emdat-country-profiles")$result
emdat_url <- hdx$resources$url[grepl("xlsx$", hdx$resources$url)][1]
emdat_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(emdat_url, emdat_file, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
# the second row of the sheet holds codes, not data
emdat <- read_xlsx(emdat_file, col_types = "text")[-1, ]
names(emdat) <- c("year", "country", "iso", "group", "subgroup", "type", "subtype", "events", "affected", "dead", "damage", "damage_adjusted", "cpi")
Code 
# the countries: rows with a country code that Our World in Data puts on a continent (its regions
# have no code or one that starts with OWID_, except Kosovo's)
continents <- continents[nzchar(continents$code) & (!grepl("^OWID_", continents$code) | continents$code == "OWID_KOS"), ]
country_codes <- continents$code
# the continents of Our World in Data count all of Russia in Europe: Russia is on its own here
group_of <- function(code) {
  continent <- continents$owid_region[match(code, continents$code)]
  ifelse(code == "RUS", "Russia", ifelse(continent == "Europe", "Europe without Russia", continent))
}
# the name of a country in a sentence (with the same names as Our World in Data)
name_of <- function(code) continents$entity[match(code, continents$code)]
with_the <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    x %in% c("Central African Republic", "Democratic Republic of Congo", "United States", "United Kingdom", "Gambia", "Netherlands", "Philippines", "Dominican Republic"),
    paste("the", x),
    x
  )
}
# the land area of each country (the latest year that the World Bank has) and its population
land_now <- land[land$code %in% country_codes & !is.na(land$ag_lnd_totl_k2), ] |>
  group_by(code) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1) |>
  ungroup()
land_of <- function(code) land_now$ag_lnd_totl_k2[match(code, land_now$code)]
pop_key <- setNames(population$population_historical, paste(population$code, population$year))
pop_of <- function(code, year) unname(pop_key[paste(code, year)])
Code 
# the dates: month, day and year of two digits ("1/6/24")
dfo$start_date <- as.Date(dfo$start, "%m/%d/%y")
dfo$year <- as.integer(format(dfo$start_date, "%Y"))
dfo$month <- as.integer(format(dfo$start_date, "%m"))
dfo$area <- as.numeric(gsub(",", "", dfo$area))
dfo$row <- seq_len(nrow(dfo))
n_records <- nrow(dfo)
last_dfo_year <- 2023 # the last year that the archive covers
n_after <- sum(dfo$year > last_dfo_year)
# a flood can hit more than one country: the countries are written in one cell, separated by commas
# and with names of the United Nations; they are given the names of Our World in Data here
renamed <- c(
  "Azores Islands" = "Portugal",
  "Bolivia (Plurinational State of)" = "Bolivia",
  "Canary Islands" = "Spain",
  "Côte d’Ivoire" = "Cote d'Ivoire",
  "Réunion" = "Reunion",
  "Democratic Republic of the Congo" = "Democratic Republic of Congo",
  "Democratic People's Republic of Korea" = "North Korea",
  "Germany Federal Republic" = "Germany",
  "Hong Kong Special Administrative Region" = "Hong Kong",
  "Iran (Islamic Republic of)" = "Iran",
  "Lao People's Democratic Republic" = "Laos",
  "Micronesia (Federated States of)" = "Micronesia (country)",
  "Netherlands (Kingdom of the)" = "Netherlands",
  "Republic of Korea" = "South Korea",
  "Republic of Moldova" = "Moldova",
  "Russian Federation" = "Russia",
  "State of Palestine" = "Palestine",
  "Syrian Arab Republic" = "Syria",
  "Taiwan (Province of China)" = "Taiwan",
  "Timor-Leste" = "East Timor",
  "Türkiye" = "Turkey",
  "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland" = "United Kingdom",
  "United Republic of Tanzania" = "Tanzania",
  "United States of America" = "United States",
  "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)" = "Venezuela",
  "Viet Nam" = "Vietnam"
)
parts <- strsplit(gsub("\\s+", " ", gsub("'", "'", dfo$country)), ",\\s*")
places <- data.frame(row = rep(dfo$row, lengths(parts)), name = trimws(unlist(parts)))
places$name <- ifelse(places$name %in% names(renamed), renamed[places$name], places$name)
places$code <- continents$code[match(places$name, continents$entity)]
places$group <- group_of(places$code)
gone <- sort(unique(places$name[is.na(places$code)]))
n_gone <- length(unique(places$row[is.na(places$code)]))
n_multi <- sum(lengths(parts) > 1)
# the cause: written freely in the file (with typing mistakes and names of storms), sorted here
cause_of <- function(x) {
  x <- tolower(x)
  case_when(
    grepl("monso|monoo", x) ~ "Monsoon rain",
    grepl("cyclone|tropical|typhoon|hurricane", x) ~ "Cyclone",
    grepl("dam|levy|levee", x) ~ "Dam or levee failure",
    grepl("snow|\\bice\\b|avalan", x) ~ "Snowmelt or ice",
    grepl("rain|torrential", x) ~ "Heavy rain",
    TRUE ~ "Other or not given"
  )
}
dfo$cause_group <- cause_of(dfo$cause)
# tsunamis are not floods (EM-DAT sorts them with the earthquakes): DFO has four records with the cause
# "tsunami", and one more that it calls a tidal surge, of 26 December 2004 in Thailand, the day of the
# tsunami of the Indian Ocean
dfo$tsunami <- grepl("tsunami", tolower(dfo$cause)) | (dfo$start_date == as.Date("2004-12-26") & dfo$country == "Thailand")
n_tsunami <- sum(dfo$tsunami)
thai <- dfo[dfo$tsunami & dfo$country == "Thailand", ]
# the floods used on this page: not tsunamis, and in the years that the archive covers
floods <- dfo[!dfo$tsunami & dfo$year <= last_dfo_year, ]
places <- places[places$row %in% floods$row, ]
places_ok <- places[!is.na(places$code), ]
first_dfo_year <- min(floods$year)
n_floods <- nrow(floods)
Code 
for (v in c("year", "events", "affected", "dead")) emdat[[v]] <- as.numeric(emdat[[v]])
# the Canary Islands have a code of their own in EM-DAT
emdat$iso[emdat$iso == "SPI"] <- "ESP"
emdat_date <- as.Date(sub(".*_(\\d{4}_\\d{2}_\\d{2})\\.xlsx$", "\\1", emdat_url), "%Y_%m_%d")
# the floods, with the glacial lake outburst floods that EM-DAT lists apart
em_flood <- emdat[emdat$type %in% c("Flood", "Glacial lake outburst flood"), ]
n_glof <- sum(em_flood$type == "Glacial lake outburst flood")
first_em_year <- min(emdat$year)
partial_year <- max(emdat$year) # the year that is not over
n_partial <- sum(em_flood$events[em_flood$year == partial_year])
em_flood <- em_flood[em_flood$year < partial_year, ]
last_em_year <- max(em_flood$year)
# the rows whose country Our World in Data does not have (the former Serbia and Montenegro)
em_lost <- em_flood[!em_flood$iso %in% country_codes, ]
em_flood <- em_flood[em_flood$iso %in% country_codes, ]
# a missing figure of deaths (or of people affected) is a figure that nobody reported, not a zero
share_no_dead <- 100 * mean(is.na(em_flood$dead))
share_no_affected <- 100 * mean(is.na(em_flood$affected))
n_years_em <- last_em_year - first_em_year + 1
Code 
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map and the calendar (water: blue)
blues <- c("#eff3ff", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c", "#08306b")
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# millions of people: whole numbers from 10 million, one decimal below
million <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) >= 1e7, number(x / 1e6), one(x / 1e6))
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}

The archive and the countries. The DFO archive has 5,503 records; 2 of them start in January 2024, after the end of the years it covers, and are left out. 424 records name more than one country, and a flood counts once for each country it hit. 18 records name only Czechoslovakia, Serbia Montenegro, Soviet Union and Yugoslavia, which no longer exist as countries, and are left out of the figures by country.

Tsunamis are not floods. DFO’s records have 5 tsunamis: 4 with the cause “tsunami”, and the record of 26 December 2004 in Thailand, which DFO calls a “tidal surge” and gives 160,000 dead: the date of the earthquake and tsunami in the Indian Ocean, which left 227,898 people dead or missing in all the countries on its shores (NOAA). EM-DAT counts the Thai tsunami with the earthquakes, with 8,345 dead and missing. These 5 are left out, which leaves 5,496 floods from 1985 to 2023.

EM-DAT: the years, and the empty cells. The yearly figures of EM-DAT that this page uses start in 2000, and they are those of the version of 25 November 2026. 2026 is not over, and its 61 floods so far are left out: the figures run from 2000 to 2025. In 24% of the rows of floods (a country, a year and a kind of flood) no number of dead is given, and in 6% no number of people affected. EM-DAT cannot tell an unreported number from none (EM-DAT FAQ), so a total here is a minimum, and the rows without a figure are counted as zero. A flood that hit several countries is a record in each. 5 rows for former countries are left out. EM-DAT includes 7 country-years of glacial lake outburst floods, which are kept.

1. Where in the world do the large floods happen?

Code 
# the groups: the continents, with Russia on its own
groups_all <- c("Africa", "Asia", "Europe without Russia", "North America", "Oceania", "South America", "Russia")
# the floods of each group: a flood that hit two groups counts in both
by_group <- places_ok |>
  distinct(row, group) |>
  count(group, name = "n_floods")
group_land <- tibble(code = country_codes, km2 = land_of(country_codes), group = group_of(country_codes)) |>
  filter(!is.na(km2)) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(km2 = sum(km2))
by_group$km2 <- group_land$km2[match(by_group$group, group_land$group)]
by_group$per_area <- by_group$n_floods / by_group$km2 * 1e6
by_group <- by_group[order(-by_group$n_floods), ]
of_group <- function(g, column) by_group[[column]][by_group$group == g]
n_distinct_floods <- n_distinct(places_ok$row)
# the countries
by_country <- places_ok |>
  count(code, name = "n_floods") |>
  mutate(name = name_of(code), km2 = land_of(code), per_area = n_floods / km2 * 1e6) |>
  arrange(desc(n_floods))
top_count <- head(by_country, 5)
# per square kilometre, the countries of more than 10,000 square kilometres (the smallest ones
# would lead with a handful of floods)
min_km2 <- 25000
n_small <- sum(by_country$km2 < min_km2, na.rm = TRUE)
top_area <- by_country |>
  filter(km2 >= min_km2) |>
  arrange(desc(per_area)) |>
  head(5)
in_country <- function(name, column) by_country[[column]][by_country$name == name]
# the share of the floods of each part of the world in the first three groups
share_asia <- 100 * of_group("Asia", "n_floods") / n_distinct_floods
# a second record: the events that EM-DAT counts in each country from 2000 to the last year that
# both records have
both_from <- 2000
both_to <- min(last_dfo_year, last_em_year)
em_count <- em_flood |>
  filter(year >= both_from, year <= both_to) |>
  group_by(code = iso) |>
  summarise(n_em = sum(events))
dfo_count <- places_ok |>
  filter(row %in% floods$row[floods$year >= both_from]) |>
  count(code, name = "n_dfo")
top_em <- head(em_count$code[order(-em_count$n_em)], 10)
top_dfo <- head(dfo_count$code[order(-dfo_count$n_dfo)], 10)
shared_top <- intersect(top_em, top_dfo)
only_em <- setdiff(top_em, top_dfo)
only_dfo <- setdiff(top_dfo, top_em)
europe <- places_ok[places_ok$group %in% c("Europe without Russia"), ]
n_europe <- n_distinct(europe$row)
greece_n <- sum(places_ok$code == "GRC")
greece_years <- em_flood[em_flood$iso == "GRC", ] |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE))
greece_worst <- greece_years[which.max(greece_years$dead), ]

Asia: more than two in five of the large floods. DFO’s 5,496 large floods from 1985 to 2023 include 5,479 in at least one country that has a continent (a flood that crosses a border counts in each continent it touches). 43% of these floods were in Asia: 2,361 floods, one for every 13,160 square kilometres of land. In South America there were 501, in North America 886, in Africa 913, in Europe without Russia 481, in Oceania 249 and in Russia 115. Per square kilometre, Europe without Russia has 2.7 times as many large floods as Africa does, which may say as much about how much news reaches DFO as about floods: its notes say that news from poorer countries tends to arrive later and in less detail (DFO notes on the archive).

Code

Interactive chart: Large floods, 1985–2023

The most large floods are in a few large countries. The most large floods were in the United States (509), China (380), India (316), Indonesia (247) and the Philippines (215): large countries, with a lot of land for a flood to hit. Per square kilometre of land, the list changes. Of the countries of more than 25,000 square kilometres, Haiti, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, the Dominican Republic and Burundi come first, with 1,488, 1,115, 885, 788 and 740 large floods per million km²; the United States has 56. The 38 countries of less than 25,000 square kilometres are not ranked, because a handful of floods would put them first.

Interactive chart: Large floods in each country, 1985–2023

EM-DAT, a different record, finds much the same countries. Counting the floods that EM-DAT records in each country from 2000 to 2023, and the large floods of DFO in the same years, 8 of the 10 countries with the most floods are the same in both records. Pakistan and Colombia come in the top 10 of EM-DAT only, Australia and Russia in the top 10 of DFO only.

Europe. 481 large floods hit Europe without Russia, 33 of them Greece, which also has 22 floods in EM-DAT from 2000 to 2025. 2017 is the year with the most dead and missing in the floods of Greece in EM-DAT (23).

2. Where do floods kill the most people?

Code 
# EM-DAT, the years from first_em_year to last_em_year: the floods of each country, their dead and the
# people affected, and the average population of the country in those years
em_country <- em_flood |>
  group_by(code = iso) |>
  summarise(n_em = sum(events), dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE), affected = sum(affected, na.rm = TRUE))
average_pop <- population[population$code %in% country_codes & population$year %in% first_em_year:min(last_em_year, max(population$year)), ] |>
  group_by(code) |>
  summarise(pop = mean(population_historical))
em_country$pop <- average_pop$pop[match(em_country$code, average_pop$code)]
em_country$name <- name_of(em_country$code)
# deaths a year for each million people, and the share of the people affected each year
em_country$per_million <- em_country$dead / em_country$pop * 1e6 / n_years_em
em_country$affected_share <- 100 * em_country$affected / em_country$pop / n_years_em
total_dead <- sum(em_country$dead)
top_dead <- em_country |>
  arrange(desc(dead)) |>
  head(10)
# per million people: the countries of more than one million people
min_pop <- 1e6
top_rate <- em_country |>
  filter(pop >= min_pop) |>
  arrange(desc(per_million)) |>
  head(10)
top_affected <- em_country |>
  filter(pop >= min_pop) |>
  arrange(desc(affected_share)) |>
  head(5)
of_dead <- function(name, column) em_country[[column]][em_country$name == name]
world_dead_rate <- total_dead / sum(em_country$pop) * 1e6 / n_years_em

Most of the dead are in a few large countries. From 2000 to 2025, EM-DAT counts 142,432 dead and missing in floods. India (36,103), China (13,447) and Pakistan (11,356) come first, and the ten countries with the most dead have 63% of all of them: India alone has 25%. But a large country has a lot of people to lose. Per million people, a different list leads: Haiti (12.6 a year), Afghanistan (5.3 a year) and Nepal (5.1 a year), against 0.8 a year for all the countries together.

Code 
left_panel <- top_dead |>
  transmute(panel = "Dead and missing, total", name, value = dead, label = number(dead))
right_panel <- top_rate |>
  transmute(panel = "A year for each million people", name, value = per_million, label = one(per_million))
dots <- rbind(left_panel, right_panel)
dots$panel <- factor(dots$panel, levels = c("Dead and missing, total", "A year for each million people"))
dots$name <- sub("Democratic Republic of Congo", "DR Congo", dots$name)
dots$key <- paste(dots$panel, dots$name, sep = "___")
dots$key <- factor(dots$key, levels = rev(dots$key))
dots$highlight <- dots$name %in% c(top_dead$name[1], top_rate$name[1])
ggplot(dots, aes(x = value, y = key, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.6, colour = "grey20") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) sub(".*___", "", x)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.3))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = red, "FALSE" = gray), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Where floods killed most, ", first_em_year, "–", last_em_year),
    subtitle = "EM-DAT: dead and missing in floods",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = paste0("Data: EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via the Humanitarian Data Exchange; population: Our World in Data.\nRight: countries of over ", number(min_pop / 1e6), " million people")
  ) +
  theme_page(12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),

    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )

The people affected: a different list again. Deaths are one measure; EM-DAT also counts the people affected (injured, affected or homeless, counted again each time they are hit). In an average year of 2000–2025, the countries of over 1 million people with the largest share of their people affected are South Sudan (3.0%), Cambodia (2.9%), Slovenia (2.9%), Bangladesh (2.8%) and Thailand (2.8%). Read these with care: how many people are “affected” depends on who counts, and EM-DAT takes the number that its source gives (EM-DAT).

3. When does each part of the world flood?

Code 
# the share of the floods of each group that start in each month (a flood that crosses two groups
# counts in both)
season <- places_ok |>
  distinct(row, group) |>
  mutate(month = floods$month[match(row, floods$row)]) |>
  count(group, month, name = "n") |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()
season <- merge(expand.grid(group = groups_all, month = 1:12), season, all.x = TRUE)
season$share[is.na(season$share)] <- 0
# the three months in a row in which each group floods the most (December to February included)
three <- function(shares) sapply(1:12, function(m) sum(shares[(m - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1]))
best <- season |>
  arrange(group, month) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(start = which.max(three(share)), share = max(three(share)))
season_months <- function(g) {
  s <- best$start[best$group == g]
  (s - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1
}
season_text <- function(g) {
  m <- season_months(g)
  paste(month.name[m[1]], "to", month.name[m[3]])
}
season_share <- function(g) percent(best$share[best$group == g])
# the causes: the share of the floods of a group that DFO puts down to each
cause_share <- function(g, cause, from = 1:12) {
  rows <- places_ok$row[places_ok$group == g]
  rows <- unique(rows)
  fl <- floods[floods$row %in% rows & floods$month %in% from, ]
  100 * mean(fl$cause_group == cause)
}
asia_months <- floods[floods$row %in% unique(places_ok$row[places_ok$group == "Asia"]), ]
asia_jjas <- 100 * mean(asia_months$month %in% 6:9)
asia_jul <- 100 * mean(asia_months$month == 7)
monsoon_share <- 100 * mean(asia_months$cause_group == "Monsoon rain")
monsoon_in_jjas <- 100 * mean(asia_months$cause_group[asia_months$month %in% 6:9] == "Monsoon rain")
heavy_in_jjas <- 100 * mean(asia_months$cause_group[asia_months$month %in% 6:9] == "Heavy rain")
all_causes <- floods |>
  count(cause_group) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
of_cause <- function(x) all_causes$share[all_causes$cause_group == x]

Each part of the world floods in its own wet season. The calendar shows, for each group, the share of its large floods that start in each month, from 1985 to 2023. If floods came evenly through the year, each month would have 8% to 9%.

Code 
season$class <- cut(
  season$share,
  c(-Inf, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15, Inf),
  labels = c("Under 5%", "5–7.5%", "7.5–10%", "10–12.5%", "12.5–15%", "15% or more"),
  right = FALSE
)
ggplot(season, aes(x = month, y = factor(group, levels = rev(groups_all)), fill = class)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = blues[2:7], drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12, labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "When each continent floods",
    subtitle = paste0("Share of its large floods that start in each month, ", first_dfo_year, "–", last_dfo_year),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Data: DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0"
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8)))

Asia floods in the summer of the north. 53% of the large floods of Asia start from June to September, 18% in July alone. DFO puts 19% of them down to monsoon rain. Of the floods that start from June to September, 29% are put down to monsoon rain and 56% to heavy rain, so DFO’s word for the cause is not a count of monsoon floods. In South America and Oceania the floods come in the other half of the year: South America floods most from January to March (41% of its floods), Oceania from January to March (53%). Africa’s season is August to October (33%), North America’s August to October (34%) and Europe’s, without Russia, September to November (32%); Russia’s floods come in May to July (49%).

What causes them, in DFO’s words. DFO writes down one main cause for each flood. For all the floods of the record, 77% are down to heavy or torrential rain, 9% to a cyclone (including a tropical storm), 8% to monsoon rain, 3% to snowmelt or ice, and 1% to the failure of a dam or levee. The rest is another cause, or none is given. The names are written freely in the file, with typing mistakes and storm names, and are sorted here by the words they contain.

4. Which were the worst floods?

Code 
# EM-DAT's dead for the floods and the storms (the group that holds tropical cyclones, which DFO
# counts as floods) of each country and year
em_deadly <- emdat[emdat$type %in% c("Flood", "Glacial lake outburst flood", "Storm"), ] |>
  group_by(iso, year) |>
  summarise(dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
em_dead_of <- function(codes, y) {
  sum(em_deadly$dead[em_deadly$iso %in% codes & em_deadly$year %in% c(y, y + 1)])
}
# the floods with the most dead in DFO, and the dead that EM-DAT has for the same countries in the
# year of the flood and the year after (EM-DAT starts in 2000)
worst <- floods |>
  arrange(desc(dead)) |>
  head(25)
worst$codes <- lapply(worst$row, function(r) places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r])
worst$em_dead <- ifelse(
  worst$year >= first_em_year,
  mapply(function(codes, y) em_dead_of(codes, y), worst$codes, worst$year),
  NA
)
worst$where <- sapply(worst$codes, function(codes) and_list(with_the(name_of(codes))))
worst$where_plain <- sapply(worst$codes, function(codes) and_list(name_of(codes)))
# a record whose dead are more than ten times those of EM-DAT for the same countries and years
worst$doubtful <- !is.na(worst$em_dead) & worst$dead > 10 * worst$em_dead
doubtful <- worst[worst$doubtful, ]
worst_ok <- worst[!worst$doubtful, ]
top_worst <- head(worst_ok, 10)
all_dead <- sum(floods$dead[!floods$row %in% doubtful$row])
top_share <- 100 * sum(top_worst$dead) / all_dead
# the people displaced: a number larger than the population of the countries of the flood is wrong
floods$pop_of_places <- sapply(floods$row, function(r) {
  codes <- places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r]
  if (length(codes) == 0 || floods$year[floods$row == r] > max(population$year)) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }
  sum(pop_of(codes, floods$year[floods$row == r]), na.rm = TRUE)
})
too_many <- floods[!is.na(floods$pop_of_places) & floods$displaced > floods$pop_of_places, ]
too_many_text <- paste0(
  sapply(too_many$row, function(r) and_list(with_the(name_of(places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r])))),
  " ",
  too_many$year,
  ": ",
  million(too_many$displaced),
  " million displaced, ",
  million(too_many$pop_of_places),
  " million people"
)
displaced_ok <- floods[!floods$row %in% too_many$row, ]
top_displaced <- displaced_ok |>
  arrange(desc(displaced)) |>
  head(8)
top_displaced$codes <- lapply(top_displaced$row, function(r) places_ok$code[places_ok$row == r])
top_displaced$where_plain <- sapply(top_displaced$codes, function(codes) and_list(name_of(codes)))
top_displaced$share <- 100 * top_displaced$displaced / sapply(seq_len(nrow(top_displaced)), function(i) {
  sum(pop_of(top_displaced$codes[[i]], top_displaced$year[i]), na.rm = TRUE)
})
# the flood of Storm Daniel in Greece, in DFO and EM-DAT
daniel <- floods[floods$start_date == as.Date("2023-09-05") & grepl("Greece", floods$country), ]
daniel_em <- emdat[emdat$iso == "GRC" & emdat$year == 2023 & emdat$type == "Flood", ]
libya <- floods[floods$year == 2023 & floods$country == "Libya", ]
libya_em <- emdat[emdat$iso == "LBY" & emdat$year == 2023 & emdat$type == "Storm", ]

A handful of floods kill most of the people. Leaving out the 4 doubtful records named below, DFO’s floods have 507,360 dead. The 10 floods in the table, 0.2% of all the floods, have 60% of them. The table is the floods with the most dead in DFO’s record, after two checks: the tsunami is out (see the data), and so are the records that give more than ten times the dead that EM-DAT has, for the same countries in the year of the flood and the year after, in floods and storms together: Uganda, September 2020 (12,000 dead in DFO, 40 in EM-DAT), Costa Rica and Nicaragua, November 2016 (4,000 dead in DFO, 44 in EM-DAT), Tanzania, December 2000 (3,600 dead in DFO, 41 in EM-DAT) and Nicaragua and Honduras, October 2005 (2,000 dead in DFO, 73 in EM-DAT). EM-DAT starts in 2000, so the floods before it cannot be checked this way.

15 Nov 2007 Bangladesh Cyclone 3,447 5,560 3,000,000
23 May 2004 Dominican Republic and Haiti Heavy rain 3,300 6,225 13,000

5 of these 10 floods came with a cyclone: the cause column shows it. EM-DAT counts a tropical cyclone as a storm, not as a flood; this is why the table compares DFO with EM-DAT’s floods and storms together. The totals are also two ways of counting: DFO does not count the missing, EM-DAT does.

The floods that drove the most people from their homes were the monsoon floods of South Asia. DFO’s “displaced” is the people left homeless or evacuated, and it makes estimates when the news gives only words such as “thousands” (DFO notes on the archive). 3 records give more displaced than all the people of the countries in the flood (Guyana 2008: 1.2 million displaced, 0.8 million people, Nicaragua 2001: 27 million displaced, 5.1 million people and New Caledonia 1989: 0.5 million displaced, 0.2 million people) and are left out here.

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    start = format(top_displaced$start_date, "%d %b %Y"),
    where = top_displaced$where_plain,
    cause = top_displaced$cause_group,
    displaced = million(top_displaced$displaced),
    share = percent(top_displaced$share, 1)
  ),
  col.names = c("Start", "Where", "Cause (DFO)", "Displaced (millions)", "Share of the people of the countries"),
  align = "lllrr"
)
Start Where Cause (DFO) Displaced (millions) Share of the people of the countries
20 Jun 2004 India and Bangladesh Monsoon rain 40 3.1%
11 Jul 1999 Bangladesh and India Monsoon rain 33 2.8%
05 Jul 1998 Bangladesh and India Monsoon rain 25 2.2%
18 Sep 2000 India Monsoon rain 24 2.3%
25 May 1993 China Heavy rain 17 1.4%
21 Jun 2002 India and Bangladesh Monsoon rain 15 1.2%
04 Jul 1995 Bangladesh Monsoon rain 15 12.2%
12 Jul 2007 India Monsoon rain 11 0.9%

Storm Daniel, September 2023. The storm brought record rain to Greece on 5 and 6 September, with a reported 750 mm in 24 hours at a station in Zagora, and heavy floods in Libya a few days later, where two old dams burst above the city of Derna (WMO). In DFO’s record, the flood of Greece, Türkiye and Bulgaria has 11 dead and 340 displaced; EM-DAT has 17 dead and missing in Greece in 1 flood in 2023. The flood of Libya (cause in DFO: dam failure) has 5,300 dead in DFO, and EM-DAT has no flood in Libya in 2023, only a storm, with 13,200 dead and missing. The two records differ, as the numbers of such a disaster do: the Libyan Red Crescent reported up to 10,000 people missing in the first days, and the WMO says that “the number of casualties was not immediately confirmed”.

5. Are floods more frequent or deadlier than they were?

Code 
# DFO: the large floods that start in each year
dfo_year <- floods |>
  count(year, name = "n")
# EM-DAT: the floods, the dead and the people affected each year
em_year <- em_flood |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(n = sum(events), dead = sum(dead, na.rm = TRUE), affected = sum(affected, na.rm = TRUE))
world_pop <- population[population$entity == "World", ]
# the population of the world is known up to the last year of Our World in Data's file
em_year$per_million_world <- em_year$dead / world_pop$population_historical[match(em_year$year, world_pop$year)] * 1e6
rate_years <- em_year[!is.na(em_year$per_million_world), ]
last_pop_year <- max(rate_years$year)
dfo_early <- dfo_year[dfo_year$year < 2000, ]
dfo_late <- dfo_year[dfo_year$year >= 2000, ]
peak <- dfo_year[which.max(dfo_year$n), ]
after_peak <- dfo_year[dfo_year$year > peak$year, ]
low_after <- min(after_peak$n)
low_after_years <- after_peak$year[after_peak$n == low_after]
low_first <- dfo_year[which.min(dfo_year$n), ]
em_peak <- em_year[which.max(em_year$n), ]
# what a rank test says of a trend: "no clear trend" unless the chance of the pattern without a trend is
# under 5 in 100
trend_text <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p >= 0.05) "no clear trend" else if (cor(x, years, method = "kendall") > 0) "a rise" else "a fall"
}
em_dead_peak <- em_year[which.max(em_year$dead), ]

There is no clear trend in the floods since 2000, and the older years do not compare. The count of large floods in DFO’s record went from 45 in 1987 to 297 in 2003, and down to 102 in 2013, 2014 and 2015: swings of that size over a few years say more about how floods were found and written down than about floods (from 2000 to 2023 a rank test finds no trend in this count: by chance, 12 in 100). DFO warns that the quality and the quantity of the information about a flood is “not always in proportion to its actual magnitude”, and that news from some countries arrives later and with less detail (DFO notes on the archive). EM-DAT warns of the same, the more so for the years before 2000: the rise in the number of disasters recorded from the 1960s on “largely reflects improvements in reporting, communication technology, and the growth of the database itself”, and it advises leaving the years before 2000 out of any study of trends (EM-DAT FAQ). So the figures for EM-DAT keep to 2000 onwards.

From 2000 to 2025, EM-DAT records 124 to 224 floods a year, with 224 in 2006 and 2021, and a rank test finds no clear trend: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 93. For the dead it finds no clear trend (by chance, 91 in 100); the dead range from 2,875 to 9,820 a year, most in 2013. For the dead of floods per million people in the world, from 2000 to 2023, the last year of the population data, it finds no clear trend (1.0 in 2000, 0.9 in 2023; by chance, 20 in 100). For the people affected it finds a fall (by chance, 1 in 100), but a few years dominate the total, such as 2010, with 189 million.

Code 
panels <- c(
  paste0("Large floods a year (DFO, from ", first_dfo_year, ")"),
  paste0("Floods a year (EM-DAT, from ", first_em_year, ")"),
  paste0("Dead and missing a year (EM-DAT, from ", first_em_year, ")")
)
series <- rbind(
  data.frame(panel = panels[1], year = dfo_year$year, value = dfo_year$n),
  data.frame(panel = panels[2], year = em_year$year, value = em_year$n),
  data.frame(panel = panels[3], year = em_year$year, value = em_year$dead)
)
series$panel <- factor(series$panel, levels = panels)
peaks <- series |>
  group_by(panel) |>
  slice_max(value, n = 1)
ggplot(series, aes(x = year, y = value)) +
  geom_line(colour = dark_gray, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = dark_gray, size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = peaks, colour = red, size = 2.6) +
  geom_text(data = peaks, aes(label = paste(year, "·", number(value))), colour = "grey20", hjust = -0.15, vjust = 0.5, size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1990, 2020, 10), limits = c(first_dfo_year - 1, last_dfo_year + 8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) number(x), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.15)), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "More floods, or more reporting?",
    subtitle = "Red: the year with the most",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: DFO Global Flood Records v0.9.0; EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via the Humanitarian Data Exchange"
  ) +
  theme_page(12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))

So, what does it mean?

  1. Asia has the most large floods. 43% of the large floods of the record, and the countries with the most are the United States, China and India. Per square kilometre, Haiti and Sri Lanka lead.
  2. A few large countries have most of the dead, and other countries have the most for each person. The ten countries with the most dead have 63% of the deaths in EM-DAT since 2000; per million people, Haiti leads, with 12.6 a year.
  3. Every part of the world has its wet season. Asia floods in June to September, South America and Oceania in the first months of the year.
  4. A few floods kill most of the people. The 10 deadliest floods have 60% of the dead of DFO’s floods, and 5 of them came with a cyclone.
  5. The records do not show a clear rise in floods or in flood deaths since 2000. Older counts rise and fall with the way floods were recorded.

What this does not show. Neither record is a count of all floods: DFO records the large floods that the news and government reports tell of, and EM-DAT those that meet its entry criteria, so a country with little news coverage or few reports may have more floods than it shows. A flood that kills nobody, in a country that does not ask for help, may appear in neither. The counts are of floods, not of how long they lasted or how much land they covered, and the estimates of the dead, the missing and the displaced differ between sources. Nothing here says what causes floods, or whether climate change is changing them: for that, a record must be built to measure it. And the table of the worst floods leaves out the records that did not agree with the other source, which may include a true record that EM-DAT lists differently.

For the overview of all the hazards, see Natural Disasters; for another hazard of the weather, Tornadoes; for the fire that follows the dry season, Where the World Burns.

Sources

  • DFO – Flood Observatory (University of Colorado), Global Flood Records, version 0.9.0, January 1985 to December 2023, Zenodo; the page of the records. Licence CC0 1.0.
  • DFO, Global Archive of Large Flood Events – Notes (archived copy of the notes on the columns of the archive, from the Internet Archive).
  • EM-DAT, the International Disaster Database, CRED / UCLouvain, Brussels, Belgium (emdat.be): Frequently asked questions, Data accessibility, Human impact variables; the yearly totals for each country are the EM-DAT country profiles of the Humanitarian Data Exchange. EM-DAT is free for non-commercial use under its Database License Agreement and is not open data; the country profiles are published under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and this page shows totals and counts worked out from them, not the data.
  • Our World in Data, natural disasters (the definition of a flood in EM-DAT), population (HYDE, Gapminder and UN World Population Prospects 2024; CC BY 4.0 and CC BY 3.0 IGO), land area (FAO, via the World Bank; CC BY 4.0) and continents (CC BY 4.0).
  • NOAA National Geophysical Data Center, December 26, 2004 Sumatra, Indonesia earthquake and tsunami – tenth anniversary update.
  • World Meteorological Organization, Storm Daniel leads to extreme rain and floods in Mediterranean, heavy loss of life in Libya (2023).

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · jsonlite · readxl

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Where the Earth Shakes: Earthquakes Around the World Since 1900
item.description: Earthquakes in the USGS catalogue: where in the world they strike, how often and how strong, how deep, the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.
item.content:encoded:
Earthquakes in the USGS catalogue: where in the world they strike, how often and how strong, how deep, the deadliest, and whether there are more of them than there used to be.

What is this?

An earthquake comes without warning, and the strongest can wreck a city in a minute. This story asks where they strike, and four more questions:

  1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?
  2. How often, and how strong?
  3. How deep are they?
  4. Which were the deadliest?
  5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

For the other hazards of the series, see Tsunamis, Volcanoes and the overview of natural disasters.

The data come from three places, downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • The earthquakes: the catalogue of the United States Geological Survey (USGS), called ComCat, which collects the earthquakes that seismic networks around the world report: the date, the place, the magnitude and the depth (ComCat, queried through its web service). The page uses every earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1900, and every one of magnitude 5 and above since 1973.
  • The deaths: the Significant Earthquake Database of the US National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI, part of NOAA), which lists destructive earthquakes with the number of people they killed (NCEI). The USGS catalogue has no deaths.
  • The map: the boundaries of the tectonic plates, from Peter Bird’s digital model (Bird 2003) in the version of Hugo Ahlenius and Nordpil (tectonicplates), and the outlines of the countries, from Natural Earth.

The magnitude is the size of the earthquake. Each whole number up is a tenfold increase in the ground motion that a seismograph records and 32 times more energy released (USGS). So a magnitude 7 earthquake releases 32 times the energy of a magnitude 6, and about a thousand times (32 × 32) that of a magnitude 5. This page writes magnitude 6 as M6, and “M6+” for magnitude 6 and above.

The depth is how far below the surface the rock starts to break, in kilometres. The USGS calls an earthquake shallow when it is between 0 and 70 km deep, intermediate between 70 and 300 km and deep between 300 and 700 km (USGS).

The tectonic plates are the large slabs that make up the outer shell of the Earth. They move against each other, and the earthquakes are not spread evenly: look at where the plates meet.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly", "sf", "jsonlite"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(sf)
library(jsonlite)

The data

Code 
# only complete years: from 1 January of this year, the catalogue is incomplete
last_year <- as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y")) - 1
# the USGS catalogue as a table: the earthquakes between two dates, of at least a magnitude
# (a query returns 20,000 earthquakes at most, so the magnitude 5 and above come in pieces)
usgs <- function(from, to, magnitude) {
  read.csv(paste0(
    "https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/query?format=csv",
    "&starttime=", from, "-01-01&endtime=", to, "-01-01",
    "&minmagnitude=", magnitude, "&orderby=time-asc&limit=20000"
  ))
}
# magnitude 6 and above, since 1900
big <- usgs(1900, last_year + 1, 6)
# magnitude 5 and above, since 1973, eight years at a time
starts <- seq(1973, last_year, by = 8)
ends <- c(starts[-1], last_year + 1)
middle <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(a, b) usgs(a, b, 5), starts, ends))
# the destructive earthquakes of NCEI, with deaths, since 1900, 200 to a page
noaa_url <- "https://www.ngdc.noaa.gov/hazel/hazard-service/api/v1/earthquakes?minYear=1900&minDeaths=1"
first_page <- fromJSON(noaa_url)
deadly <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(first_page$totalPages), function(i) {
  fromJSON(paste0(noaa_url, "&page=", i))$items[, c(
    "year", "locationName", "country", "eqMagnitude", "deaths", "deathsTotal", "latitude", "longitude"
  )]
}))
# the plate boundaries (Bird 2003), and the countries (Natural Earth, 1:50 million)
plates <- st_read(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tectonicplates/master/GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.json",
  quiet = TRUE
)
land <- st_read(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/geojson/ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson",
  quiet = TRUE
)[, c("NAME_LONG", "ADM0_A3", "CONTINENT")]
Code 
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the three depths, in order, whose neighbours were checked for colour blindness
depth_colors <- c(Shallow = "#d97706", Intermediate = "#be123c", Deep = "#5b3fb5")
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map of the countries
blues <- c("#eff3ff", "#c6dbef", "#9ecae1", "#6baed6", "#3182bd", "#08519c", "#08306b")
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
# the distance in kilometres between two points (longitude and latitude in degrees)
distance_km <- function(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2) {
  r <- pi / 180
  h <- sin((lat2 - lat1) * r / 2)^2 + cos(lat1 * r) * cos(lat2 * r) * sin((lon2 - lon1) * r / 2)^2
  12742 * asin(sqrt(h))
}
Code 
# only earthquakes: the catalogue also holds explosions, and more
all_types <- table(c(big$type, middle$type))
n_blasts <- sum(all_types[names(all_types) == "nuclear explosion"])
n_other <- sum(all_types[!names(all_types) %in% c("earthquake", "nuclear explosion")])
quakes <- function(x) {
  x <- x[x$type == "earthquake", ]
  x$year <- as.integer(substr(x$time, 1, 4))
  x
}
n_before <- nrow(big) + nrow(middle)
big <- quakes(big)
middle <- quakes(middle)
magnitude_types <- sort(table(middle$magType), decreasing = TRUE)
# the depth classes of the USGS
depth_class <- function(depth) {
  cut(depth, c(-Inf, 70, 300, Inf), labels = names(depth_colors), right = FALSE)
}
middle$depth_class <- depth_class(middle$depth)
big$depth_class <- depth_class(big$depth)
# depths that a location program sets when the data do not fix the depth (USGS: 10 and 33 km)
fixed_depth <- mean(middle$depth %in% c(10, 33))
other_depth <- max(table(middle$depth[!middle$depth %in% c(10, 33)])) / nrow(middle)
above_sea <- sum(middle$depth < 0)
# each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above: the country it is in; or the nearest country, if the
# sea is less than 200 km wide between the two; or nowhere. Planar geometry on longitude and latitude
# is accurate enough to find the nearest country; the distance itself is then worked out on the globe.
sf_use_s2(FALSE)
points <- st_as_sf(middle[, c("id", "longitude", "latitude")], coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
inside <- st_intersects(points, land)
on_land <- lengths(inside) > 0
nearest <- st_nearest_feature(points[!on_land, ], land)
lines <- st_nearest_points(points[!on_land, ], land[nearest, ], pairwise = TRUE)
ends_xy <- st_coordinates(st_cast(lines, "POINT"))
from_xy <- ends_xy[seq(1, nrow(ends_xy), by = 2), ]
to_xy <- ends_xy[seq(2, nrow(ends_xy), by = 2), ]
offshore_km <- distance_km(from_xy[, 1], from_xy[, 2], to_xy[, 1], to_xy[, 2])
middle$place_index <- NA_integer_
middle$place_index[on_land] <- vapply(inside[on_land], `[`, 1L, 1L)
reach <- 200
middle$place_index[!on_land][offshore_km <= reach] <- nearest[offshore_km <= reach]
land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG == "Russian Federation"] <- "Russia"
land$NAME_LONG[land$NAME_LONG == "South Georgia and the Islands"] <- "South Georgia"
middle$country <- land$NAME_LONG[middle$place_index]
middle$code <- land$ADM0_A3[middle$place_index]
middle$continent <- land$CONTINENT[middle$place_index]
# each earthquake of magnitude 6 and above since 1973: its distance from the nearest plate boundary
big_now <- big[big$year >= 1973, ]
points_now <- st_as_sf(big_now[, c("id", "longitude", "latitude")], coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
near_boundary <- st_nearest_feature(points_now, plates)
lines_now <- st_nearest_points(points_now, plates[near_boundary, ], pairwise = TRUE)
xy_now <- st_coordinates(st_cast(lines_now, "POINT"))
big_now$boundary_km <- distance_km(
  xy_now[seq(1, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 1], xy_now[seq(1, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 2],
  xy_now[seq(2, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 1], xy_now[seq(2, nrow(xy_now), by = 2), 2]
)
# the same distance for points spread evenly over the globe: how much of the world is near a boundary
set.seed(2026)
n_random <- 4000
random_points <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(lon = runif(n_random, -180, 180), lat = asin(runif(n_random, -1, 1)) * 180 / pi),
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
)
near_random <- st_nearest_feature(random_points, plates)
lines_random <- st_cast(st_nearest_points(random_points, plates[near_random, ], pairwise = TRUE), "POINT")
xy_random <- st_coordinates(lines_random)
random_km <- distance_km(
  xy_random[seq(1, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 1], xy_random[seq(1, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 2],
  xy_random[seq(2, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 1], xy_random[seq(2, nrow(xy_random), by = 2), 2]
)
sf_use_s2(TRUE)
# the deaths: the NCEI total where it has one
deadly$deaths_all <- ifelse(is.na(deadly$deathsTotal), deadly$deaths, deadly$deathsTotal)
deadly <- deadly[!is.na(deadly$deaths_all) & deadly$year <= last_year, ]
deadly$name <- ifelse(deadly$country == "USA", "United States", tools::toTitleCase(tolower(deadly$country)))
# the place as NCEI writes it, in words: the parts between colons, without compass points
place_text <- function(x) {
  parts <- strsplit(tolower(x), "\\s*:\\s*")
  vapply(parts, function(p) {
    p <- trimws(p)
    paste(tools::toTitleCase(p[!p %in% c("n", "s", "e", "w", "ne", "nw", "se", "sw", "")]), collapse = ", ")
  }, "")
}
deadly$place <- place_text(deadly$locationName)

Only earthquakes. The catalogue also holds explosions, mine collapses and landslides. Of the 102,788 events that the two downloads found, 494 were nuclear explosions and 69 were other things (an explosion, a rock burst, a volcanic eruption and so on). The page uses the other 102,225, labelled earthquakes. 14,358 of them are magnitude 6 and above since 1900 and 87,867 magnitude 5 and above since 1973, and the second group includes most of the first from 1973 on.

Only whole years. The page stops at the end of 2025, so that every year counts in full.

Many magnitudes. The catalogue gives each earthquake the magnitude that its source chose, of several kinds: from 1973 on, 47% of the magnitude 5 and above are of the kind called mb, and the others are of kinds such as Mw (the moment magnitude, the one that scientists prefer for large earthquakes). Section 5 shows what that means for counting earthquakes over the years.

Which country? The catalogue’s place is a piece of text, not a country code, so each earthquake of magnitude 5 and above is placed on the map of the countries. Only 20% fall inside a country: the rest happen under the sea. An earthquake at sea is given to the nearest country when it is within 200 km of its coast (56% of all of them); the other 24%, in the open sea, belong to no country. Countries are those of Natural Earth, which counts overseas territories (Puerto Rico, Guam) as places of their own, and a country’s earthquakes are the ones under it and near it.

The depth is the least certain number. It is the least constrained of all the parameters of an earthquake, says the USGS, and where the data do not fix it, the location program sets a default, often 10 or 33 km (ComCat). 40% of the magnitude 5 and above have exactly 10 or 33 km (the next most common depth has 3%), so the depths on this page are good for classes (shallow, intermediate, deep) and not for the exact kilometre. 27 of them are negative, which means above the reference level that the source used.

1. Where in the world do the earthquakes strike?

Code 
n_big <- nrow(big_now)
within <- function(km) percent(100 * mean(big_now$boundary_km <= km))
world_within <- function(km) percent(100 * mean(random_km <= km))
places <- middle |>
  filter(!is.na(country)) |>
  group_by(country, code, continent) |>
  summarise(n = n(), strong = sum(mag >= 6), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(n), country)
n_years <- last_year - 1973 + 1
n_places <- nrow(places)
top <- head(places, 15)
sea_share <- 100 * mean(is.na(middle$country))
place_of <- function(name, column) places[[column]][places$country == name]
rank_of <- function(name) match(name, places$country)
# Europe: the continent of Natural Earth, without Russia (most of its earthquakes are in Kamchatka and
# the Kuril Islands, in the east) and with Turkey, which Natural Earth puts in Asia, counted on its own
europe <- places |>
  filter(continent == "Europe", country != "Russia") |>
  head(4)

Along narrow belts, and mostly under the sea. The 7,327 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above from 1973 to 2025 do not fall at random: 65% of them are within 100 km of a plate boundary and 92% within 300 km. Of the surface of the globe, only 10% is within 100 km of a boundary and 24% within 300 km (worked out for 4,000 points spread evenly over the globe). Where plates meet, one slides under the other, or they grind side by side, and the rock breaks.

Code

2. How often, and how strong?

Code 
modern <- 1990
# the magnitude classes: the lower end and the name
classes_m <- list(
  "5–5.9" = c(5, 6),
  "6–6.9" = c(6, 7),
  "7–7.9" = c(7, 8),
  "8 and above" = c(8, 11)
)
per_year <- sapply(classes_m, function(r) {
  sum(middle$mag >= r[1] & middle$mag < r[2] & middle$year >= modern) / (last_year - modern + 1)
})
big_per_year <- sapply(classes_m[3:4], function(r) {
  sum(big$mag >= r[1] & big$mag < r[2]) / (last_year - 1900 + 1)
})

largest$place_short <- sub("^[0-9.]+ km [A-Z]+ of ", "", largest$place)

n8_years <- big |>
  filter(mag >= 8) |>
  count(year)

About 1,500 a year of magnitude 5 and 0.9 of magnitude 8. 3. How deep are they?

Code

  "5–5.9" = middle[middle$mag < 6, ],
  "6–6.9" = middle[middle$mag >= 6 & middle$mag < 7, ],

  data.frame(size = s, k = names(depth_colors), share = sapply(names(depth_colors), function(k) share_of(by_size[[s]], k)))

Not the strongest earthquakes. The ten deadliest were of magnitude 7.0 to 9.1. Of the ten largest earthquakes of section 2, 4 killed 1,000 or more people (by NCEI’s list), and 4 have no deaths in it. Of the 1,546 earthquakes in NCEI’s list with a magnitude, 74% were below magnitude 7. How many die depends on where the earthquake strikes, who lives there and how they build, as well as on the magnitude, and the data here cannot separate those.

Which deaths? NCEI gives two figures: the deaths and a total. They differ for 42 earthquakes since 1900, and the largest difference is the 2004 earthquake (Indonesia, Sumatra, Aceh, Off West Coast): 1,001 deaths and 227,899 in total, with a tsunami linked to it in the database. The page uses the total where there is one.

5. Are there more of them than there used to be?

Code 
years_big <- 1900:last_year
count_by_year <- function(x, lo, years) {
  tab <- table(factor(x$year[x$mag >= lo], levels = years))
  data.frame(year = years, n = as.integer(tab))
}
m7 <- count_by_year(big, 7, 1900:last_year)
m6 <- count_by_year(big, 6, 1900:last_year)
m6_modern <- m6[m6$year >= 1973, ]
m5 <- count_by_year(middle, 5, 1973:last_year)
# the year after which the yearly counts of magnitude 6 and above are on another level (the split
# of the years that leaves the least spread within the two parts)
split_cost <- sapply(1976:(last_year - 3), function(y) {
  a <- m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year < y]
  b <- m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year >= y]
  sum((a - mean(a))^2) + sum((b - mean(b))^2)
})
step_year <- (1976:(last_year - 3))[which.min(split_cost)]
before_step <- mean(m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year < step_year])
after_step <- mean(m6_modern$n[m6_modern$year >= step_year])
m6_first <- mean(m6$n[m6$year <= 1904])
m6_next <- mean(m6$n[m6$year %in% 1905:1914])
m7_first <- mean(m7$n[m7$year <= 1904])
m7_all <- mean(m7$n)
m7_periods <- c(
  early = mean(m7$n[m7$year <= 1949]),
  middle = mean(m7$n[m7$year %in% 1950:1989]),
  late = mean(m7$n[m7$year >= 1990])
)
tests <- data.frame(
  what = c("M7+", "M7+", "M6+", "M5+"),
  from = c(1900, modern, step_year, step_year),
  chance = c(
    chance(m7$n, m7$year),
    chance(m7$n[m7$year >= modern], m7$year[m7$year >= modern]),
    chance(m6$n[m6$year >= step_year], m6$year[m6$year >= step_year]),
    chance(m5$n[m5$year >= step_year], m5$year[m5$year >= step_year])
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
means_of <- function(x, from, to) mean(x$n[x$year >= from & x$year <= to])
# one big earthquake brings its aftershocks: the Tohoku earthquake of 2011 and the following year
in_2011 <- big[big$year == 2011, ]
tohoku <- in_2011[which.max(in_2011$mag), ]
tohoku_time <- as.POSIXct(tohoku$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")
middle_time <- as.POSIXct(middle$time, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")
after <- middle_time > tohoku_time & middle_time <= tohoku_time + 365 * 86400 &
  distance_km(tohoku$longitude, tohoku$latitude, middle$longitude, middle$latitude) <= 500
after_n <- sum(after)
year_2011 <- m5$n[m5$year == 2011]
peak_year <- m5$year[which.max(m5$n)]

No clear trend in the big ones; the smaller ones are counted in steps. Earthquakes of magnitude 7 and above are the only ones that the catalogue seems to record in full since 1900 (see below). They averaged 12.4 a year from 1900 to 1949, 11.1 from 1950 to 1989 and 15.0 from 1990 to 2025: not a steady rise. From 1990 on, a rank test finds no trend in them (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is 64 in 100). Over all the years from 1900 the test leans slightly upwards (3 in 100), because of the dip in the middle of the century; the page does not take that for a lasting rise, since magnitudes were worked out differently in each period.

For the smaller earthquakes the catalogue is the problem, not the Earth. From 1900 to 1904 it holds 15.4 earthquakes of magnitude 6 and above a year, and from 1905 to 1914 55.8; for magnitude 7 and above the same years give 12.0 and 15.7, so only the strongest were recorded in those years. Even from 1973 the counts of magnitude 6 and above are not on one level: they average 93.1 a year before 1983 and 148.7 from 1983 on, a step of 60%. The page does not know why the catalogue steps there. So the tests for magnitude 6 and above and for 5 and above start in 1983, where the rank test finds no clear trend either (the last column):

Aftershocks can make a year. A large earthquake is followed by many smaller ones, and a simple count does not tell them from new earthquakes. After the Tohoku earthquake in Japan (magnitude 9.1, 2011-03-11), 779 earthquakes of magnitude 5 and above happened within 500 km in the following year, 29% of the 2,701 of the whole of 2011, and 779 is 46% of the average year since 1983. The year with the most of magnitude 5 and above was 2011, with 2,701.

Code

So, what does it mean?

  1. Earthquakes come in belts. 65% of the 7,327 of magnitude 6 and above since 1973 struck within 100 km of a plate boundary, which is near only 10% of the surface of the globe. 24% of those of magnitude 5 and above were farther than 200 km from any country.
  2. Indonesia, Papua New Guinea and Japan have the most. Greece is number 22 among 172 countries and territories, and the first in Europe without Russia.
  3. There are about 0.9 earthquakes of magnitude 8 a year and about 14 of magnitude 7, and each step down in magnitude is several times as common.
  4. Nearly all are shallow, 79% of those of magnitude 5 and above. The deaths come in a few events: the ten deadliest earthquakes killed 61% of the 2,531,015 recorded since 1900.
  5. There is no clear sign of more earthquakes in this catalogue. From 1990 on there is no trend in those of magnitude 7 and above; the smaller ones are counted in steps, and the page does not claim a trend for them.

What this does not show. The catalogue is of the earthquakes that instruments record, and the earlier years of it are patchy for all but the strongest. The magnitude is of several kinds, and the depth is uncertain. The countries come from the places of the earthquakes, not from where the shaking was felt. The deaths are those NCEI recorded for its significant earthquakes: some counts are estimates, and the tsunamis that follow some earthquakes are not told apart here. And earthquakes of the same size do not do the same harm.

For the waves that some of these earthquakes send across the sea, see Tsunamis; for the mountains that melt rock instead, Volcanoes; and for the hazards side by side, Natural Disasters.
