  • NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, NCEI/WDS Global Significant Earthquake Database, doi:10.7289/V5TD9V7K, read through its hazard service. Access to the data is unrestricted; NOAA gives no warranty for them.
  • Bird, P. (2003), An updated digital model of plate boundaries, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 4(3), 1027; GeoJSON version: Ahlenius, H., Nordpil, World tectonic plates and boundaries, Open Data Commons Attribution License.
  • Natural Earth, 1:50 million Admin 0 countries, via natural-earth-vector. Public domain.

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · sf · jsonlite

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Natural Disasters: Which Strike Most, Which Kill Most, and Where
item.description: Natural disasters in the EM-DAT database and in the catalogues of earthquakes and volcanoes: which happen most often, which kill and affect the most people, where they kill the most, and where the Earth itself is restless.
item.content:encoded:
Natural disasters in the EM-DAT database and in the catalogues of earthquakes and volcanoes: which happen most often, which kill and affect the most people, where they kill the most, and where the Earth itself is restless.

What is this?

Floods, storms, earthquakes, heatwaves and droughts: somewhere in the world, a disaster caused by nature is recorded about once a day, and a few of them kill tens of thousands of people. This page is the overview of a series on natural disasters, and asks five questions:

  1. Which disasters happen most often?
  2. Which kill the most, and has that changed?
  3. Which affect the most people?
  4. Where do disasters kill the most?
  5. Where is the Earth itself restless?

Each kind has a page of its own: earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, floods, tornadoes, and wildfires, in the world and in Greece.

The data are downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • EM-DAT, the International Disaster Database of the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED) at UCLouvain, as published by Our World in Data (Natural disasters): the disasters recorded in the world each year, by kind, and the people killed and affected in each country each year since 1900. EM-DAT records only disasters that meet its entry criteria, and defines a disaster as “a situation or event which overwhelms local capacity, necessitating a request to the national or international level for external assistance” (EM-DAT, definitions).
  • The population of each country, for deaths per person (Our World in Data).
  • Earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more since 1900, from the catalogue of the US Geological Survey (USGS); volcanoes, from the Smithsonian Institution’s Global Volcanism Program (Volcanoes of the World); and the boundaries of the Earth’s tectonic plates (Bird 2003).

The kinds of disaster are those of EM-DAT. A storm includes tropical cyclones (hurricanes and typhoons) and tornadoes; an earthquake includes its aftershocks and the tsunamis it causes; extreme temperature means heatwaves, cold waves and severe winters (EM-DAT classification). Deaths are the confirmed dead and the missing.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("plotly", "sf"))
library(plotly)
library(sf)

The data

Code 
# a chart of Our World in Data as a table: one row for each country or region and each year
owid<-function(chart) {
  result<-read.csv(paste0("https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/",chart,
                          ".csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true"))
  return(result)
}
# EM-DAT: the people killed and affected in each country each year, by kind of disaster, and the
# disasters recorded in the world each year, by kind
deaths<-owid("natural-disasters-deaths")
affected<-owid("natural-disasters-people-affected")
events<-owid("number-of-natural-disaster-events")
population<-owid("population")
continents<-owid("continents-according-to-our-world-in-data")
# the earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more since 1900 (USGS)
quakes<-read.csv(paste0(paste0("https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/qu","ery?format=csv"),
                        "&starttime=1900-01-01&minmagnitude=7&orderby=time-asc"))
# the volcanoes that have erupted in the last 12,000 years (Smithsonian); the geological summary of
# each volcano has line breaks inside its quotes, which read.csv reads correctly
volcanoes<-read.csv(paste0(paste0("https://webservices.volcano.si.edu/geoserver/",
                                  "GVP-VOTW/ows?service=WFS&version=2.0.0"),
                           paste0("&request=GetFeature&typeName=GVP-VOTW:Smithso",
                                  "nian_VOTW_Holocene_Volcanoes&outputFormat=csv")))
# the boundaries of the tectonic plates (Bird 2003, as GeoJSON)
plates<-st_read(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fraxen/tect",
                       "onicplates/master/GeoJSON/PB2002_boundaries.j","son"),quiet=TRUE)
Code 
# the kinds of disaster: the columns of EM-DAT's tables, their names in its table of events, and
# their names on this page
kinds<-data.frame(key=c("flood","extreme_temperature","extreme_weather","drought","earthquake",
                        "volcanic_activity","landslide","wildfire"),
                  event_name=c("Flood","Extreme temperature","Extreme weather","Drought",
                               "Earthquake","Volcanic activity","Landslide","Wildfire"),
                  label=c("Flood","Extreme temperature","Storm","Drought","Earthquake","Volcano",
                          "Landslide","Wildfire"))
# the charts with colours show the five deadliest kinds and put the other three together
kinds$group<-ifelse(kinds$key%in%c("volcanic_activity","landslide","wildfire"),"Other",kinds$label)
group_levels<-c("Flood","Extreme temperature","Storm","Drought","Earthquake","Other")
label_of<-setNames(kinds$label,kinds$key)
group_of<-setNames(kinds$group,kinds$key)
# a table of EM-DAT with one row for each place, year and kind; a year without a recorded disaster
# of
# a kind has no value there, which means that none was recorded: zero
to_long<-function(x,prefix) {
  y<-do.call(rbind,
             lapply(kinds$key,
                    function(k) {
    data.frame(entity=x$entity,
               code=x$code,
               year=x$year,
               kind=k,
               value=x[[paste0(prefix,k,"_yearly")]])
  }))
  y$value[is.na(y$value)]<-0
  result<-y
  return(result)
}
dead<-to_long(deaths,"total_dead_")
hit<-to_long(affected,"total_affected_")
first_year<-min(dead$year)
last_year<-max(dead$year)
recent<-2000:last_year
# the countries: rows with a code that Our World in Data puts on a continent (its regions have no
# code, or one that starts with OWID_)
country_codes<-continents$code[nzchar(continents$code)]
continent_of<-setNames(continents$owid_region,continents$code)
# the population of each place and year; the data end in 2023, and the years after it take the
# population of 2023
names(population)[names(population)=="population_historical"]<-"people"
last_population<-max(population$year)
carried<-do.call(rbind,
                 lapply((last_population+1):last_year,
                        function(y) {
  transform(population[population$year==last_population,],year=y)
}))
population<-rbind(population[population$year>=first_year,],carried)
Code 
red<-"#d62728"
gray<-"#bdbdbd"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the kinds of disaster, in the order of the stacked bars: the first five colours of a palette whose
# neighbours were checked for colour blindness, and grey for the rest
group_colors<-c(Flood="#2a78d6","Extreme temperature"="#eb6834",Storm="#1baf7a",Drought="#eda100",
                Earthquake="#e87ba4",Other="#bdbdbd")
# one hue, from light to dark, for the deaths per person on the map
reds<-c("#fee5d9","#fcbba1","#fc9272","#fb6a4a","#ef3b2c","#cb181d","#99000d")
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom",traceorder="normal")
# numbers in the text
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
percent<-function(x,digits=0) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits,trim=TRUE),"%")
  return(result)
}
one<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
two<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,2),nsmall=2,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
thousand<-function(x) {
  result<-number(x/1000)
  return(result)
}
and_list<-function(x) {
  if(length(x)<2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1))
  return(result)
}
# country names that take "the" in a sentence
with_the<-function(x) {
  result<-ifelse(x%in%
                 c("Democratic Republic of Congo","Central African Republic","United States",
                   "Philippines"),paste("the",x),x)
  return(result)
}

More disasters are recorded than before, which is not the same as more happening. EM-DAT recorded 6 disasters in 1900, 84 in 1970 and 405 in 2000, and since 2000 between 325 and 451 a year. Our World in Data warns that “the historical increase largely reflects improvements in data reporting” (Our World in Data), so this page counts disasters only from 2000. Deaths are another matter: the great disasters of the past were recorded too, and the page follows deaths since 1900.

The population of each country comes up to 2023; for 2024–2025 the page uses that of 2023.

1. Which disasters happen most often?

Code 
per_year<-sapply(kinds$event_name,
                 function(k) {
  sum(events$n_events[events$entity==k&events$year%in%recent])/length(recent)
})
often<-data.frame(label=kinds$label,per_year=per_year)
often<-often[order(-often$per_year),]
all_per_year<-mean(events$n_events[events$entity=="All disasters"&events$year%in%recent])
of_often<-function(label) {
  result<-often$per_year[often$label==label]
  return(result)
}

Floods, then storms. Since 2000, EM-DAT has recorded 393 disasters a year: 167 floods and 110 storms, 71% of them. Earthquakes, droughts and extreme temperatures come next, 27, 26 and 25 a year, then landslides (20), wildfires (13) and volcanic eruptions (5).

Code 
often$label<-factor(often$label,levels=rev(often$label))
plot_ly(often,x=~per_year,y=~label,type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(often$label%in%c("Flood","Storm"),red,gray)),
        text=~round(per_year),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:.0f} a year<extra></extra>",showlegend=FALSE) %>%
  chart(paste0("Disasters recorded a year, 2000–",last_year),
        "EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via Our World in Data.",
        x_axis=list(showticklabels=FALSE,showgrid=FALSE,zeroline=FALSE,
                    range=c(0,1.15*max(often$per_year))),margin=list(l=140,t=60,b=50,r=20),
        note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: Disasters recorded a year, 2000–2025

2. Which kill the most, and has that changed?

Code 
world_dead<-dead[dead$entity=="World",]
# the deaths of each kind since 2000, the most first
since_2000<-aggregate(value~kind,world_dead[world_dead$year%in%recent,],sum)
names(since_2000)[2]<-"deaths"
since_2000<-since_2000[order(-since_2000$deaths),]
of_since<-function(k) {
  result<-since_2000$deaths[since_2000$kind==k]
  return(result)
}
all_since<-sum(since_2000$deaths)
# deaths a year per 100,000 people in the world, by decade and kind
world_people<-population[population$entity=="World",c("year","people")]
decades<-merge(world_dead,world_people,by="year")
decades$decade<-10*(decades$year%/%10)
decades$group<-group_of[decades$kind]
# the people of each decade, each year counted once (in the rows of one kind)
one_kind<-decades[decades$kind==kinds$key[1],]
person_years<-tapply(one_kind$people,one_kind$decade,sum)
decades<-aggregate(value~decade+group,decades,sum)
decades$rate<-1e5*decades$value/person_years[as.character(decades$decade)]
decades<-decades[order(decades$decade,decades$group,method="radix"),c("decade","group","rate")]
rownames(decades)<-NULL
decade_total<-aggregate(rate~decade,decades,sum)
worst_decade<-decade_total$decade[which.max(decade_total$rate)]
rate_of<-function(d) {
  result<-decade_total$rate[decade_total$decade==d]
  return(result)
}
last_decade<-max(decade_total$decade)
# the deadliest years of single countries: since 1900 and since 2000
country_dead<-dead[dead$code%in%country_codes,]
# the deadliest kind of each country and year, the deadliest first
place_years<-split(country_dead,list(country_dead$entity,country_dead$year),drop=TRUE)
worst_ever<-do.call(rbind,lapply(place_years,function(x) x[which.max(x$value),]))
worst_ever<-worst_ever[order(-worst_ever$value,worst_ever$entity,worst_ever$year,method="radix"),]
rownames(worst_ever)<-NULL
worst_recent<-worst_ever[worst_ever$year%in%recent,]

Since 2000, earthquakes. Disasters killed 1,595 thousand people from 2000 to 2025: 796 thousand in earthquakes and the tsunamis they caused, 377 thousand in heatwaves and cold, 228 thousand in storms and 142 thousand in floods. A few events make most of these numbers. The deadliest years of single countries since 2000:

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(country=worst_recent$entity[1:10],
                        year=worst_recent$year[1:10],
                        kind=label_of[worst_recent$kind[1:10]],
                        deaths=number(worst_recent$value[1:10])),
             col.names=c("Country","Year","Kind","Deaths"),align="llll",row.names=FALSE)
Country Year Kind Deaths
Haiti 2010 Earthquake 222,570
Indonesia 2004 Earthquake 165,816
Myanmar 2008 Storm 138,366
China 2008 Earthquake 87,564
Pakistan 2005 Earthquake 73,338
Russia 2010 Extreme temperature 55,760
Turkey 2023 Earthquake 53,007
Sri Lanka 2004 Earthquake 35,399
Iran 2003 Earthquake 26,797
Italy 2003 Extreme temperature 20,089

Over the century, far fewer. In the 1920s, disasters killed 26.6 people a year for every 100,000 people in the world; in the 2020s so far, 0.75. The deadliest years ever recorded in one country were China in 1931 (flood, 3,700,000 dead), China in 1928 (drought, 3,000,000) and Bangladesh in 1943 (drought, 1,900,000). The last year in which disasters killed a million people or more in a single country was 1943.

Code 
decades$group<-factor(decades$group,levels=group_levels)
decades$label<-paste0(decades$decade,"s")
p<-plot_ly()
for(g in group_levels) {
  x<-decades[decades$group==g,]
  p<-add_bars(p,data=x,x=~label,y=~rate,name=g,
              marker=list(color=group_colors[[g]],line=list(color="white",width=1)),
              hovertemplate=paste0("%{x}, ",tolower(g),
                                   ": %{y:.2f} a year per 100,000<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("Disaster deaths a year per 100,000 people, by decade",
        paste0(paste0("EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain; population: HYDE, ",
                      "Gapminder, UN; via Our World in Data. 2020s: ","2020–"),last_year,"."),
        "Deaths a year per 100,000",barmode="stack",legend=legend_top,
        margin=list(t=110,b=80,l=60,r=10),note_y=-0.14)

Interactive chart: Disaster deaths a year per 100,000 people, by decade

3. Which affect the most people?

Code 
affected_since<-aggregate(value~kind,hit[hit$entity=="World"&hit$year%in%recent,],sum)
names(affected_since)[2]<-"people"
affected_since<-affected_since[order(-affected_since$people),]
of_affected<-function(k) {
  result<-affected_since$people[affected_since$kind==k]
  return(result)
}
billion<-function(x) {
  result<-one(x/1e9)
  return(result)
}

Floods and droughts. From 2000 to 2025, EM-DAT counted 1.9 billion people affected by floods, 1.8 billion by droughts and 0.9 billion by storms; earthquakes affected 159 million. These are not different people: someone hit by a flood in 2010 and again in 2020 is counted twice. EM-DAT counts as affected the people who needed immediate help, together with the injured and the homeless (EM-DAT, definitions).

Code 
affected_since$label<-factor(label_of[affected_since$kind],
                             levels=rev(label_of[affected_since$kind]))
plot_ly(affected_since,x=~people/1e6,y=~label,type="bar",orientation="h",
        marker=list(color=ifelse(affected_since$kind%in%c("flood","drought"),red,gray)),
        text=~number(people/1e6),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:,.0f} million<extra></extra>",showlegend=FALSE) %>%
  chart(paste0("People affected, millions, 2000–",last_year),
        "EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via Our World in Data.",
        x_axis=list(showticklabels=FALSE,showgrid=FALSE,zeroline=FALSE,
                    range=c(0,1.18*max(affected_since$people)/1e6)),
        margin=list(l=140,t=60,b=50,r=20),note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: People affected, millions, 2000–2025

4. Where do disasters kill the most?

Code 
min_people<-1e6 # countries with fewer people are left out of the rates: one event decides them
# the deaths of each country and year, and the kind that killed the most
recent_dead<-country_dead[country_dead$year%in%recent,]
recent_dead<-recent_dead[order(recent_dead$code,recent_dead$entity,recent_dead$year,method="radix"),
                         ]
per_year<-split(recent_dead,list(recent_dead$code,recent_dead$entity,recent_dead$year),drop=TRUE)
yearly<-do.call(rbind,
                lapply(per_year,
                       function(x) {
  data.frame(code=x$code[1],
             entity=x$entity[1],
             year=x$year[1],
             deaths=sum(x$value),
             worst_kind=x$kind[which.max(x$value)])
}))
yearly<-merge(yearly,population[,c("code","year","people")],by=c("code","year"))
yearly<-yearly[order(yearly$code,yearly$entity,yearly$year,method="radix"),]
# each country: its deadliest year and kind, its deaths a year per 100,000 people, its people now
per_country<-split(yearly,list(yearly$code,yearly$entity),drop=TRUE)
country_rates<-do.call(rbind,
                       lapply(per_country,
                              function(x) {
  data.frame(code=x$code[1],
             entity=x$entity[1],
             worst_year=x$year[which.max(x$deaths)],
             worst_kind=x$worst_kind[which.max(x$deaths)],
             rate=1e5*sum(x$deaths)/sum(x$people),
             people_now=x$people[which.max(x$year)],
             deaths=sum(x$deaths))
}))
country_rates<-country_rates[order(country_rates$code,country_rates$entity,method="radix"),]
rownames(country_rates)<-NULL
small<-country_rates[country_rates$people_now<min_people,]
country_rates<-country_rates[country_rates$people_now>=min_people,]
country_rates<-country_rates[order(-country_rates$rate),]
top_rates<-head(country_rates,5)
world_rate<-1e5*sum(world_dead$value[world_dead$year%in%recent])/
            sum(world_people$people[world_people$year%in%recent])
# each continent: the deaths since 2000 by kind
continents_world<-c("Africa","Asia","Europe","North America","South America","Oceania","World")
continent_dead<-dead[dead$entity%in%continents_world&dead$year%in%recent,]
continent_dead$group<-group_of[continent_dead$kind]
continent_dead<-aggregate(value~entity+group,continent_dead,sum)
names(continent_dead)[3]<-"deaths"
continent_dead<-continent_dead[order(continent_dead$entity,continent_dead$group,method="radix"),]
continent_dead$share<-100*continent_dead$deaths/
                      ave(continent_dead$deaths,continent_dead$entity,FUN=sum)
rownames(continent_dead)<-NULL
share_in<-function(place,g) {
  result<-continent_dead$share[continent_dead$entity==place&continent_dead$group==g]
  return(result)
}
# the deadliest kind in each continent (of all eight kinds), as text
plural<-c(flood="floods",extreme_temperature="heat and cold",extreme_weather="storms",
          drought="droughts",earthquake="earthquakes",volcanic_activity="volcanic eruptions",
          landslide="landslides",wildfire="wildfires")
killers<-dead[dead$entity%in%continents_world[1:6]&dead$year%in%recent,]
killers<-aggregate(value~entity+kind,killers,sum)
names(killers)[3]<-"deaths"
killers<-killers[order(killers$entity,killers$kind,method="radix"),]
killers$share<-100*killers$deaths/ave(killers$deaths,killers$entity,FUN=sum)
# the deadliest kind of each continent
killers<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(killers,killers$entity),function(x) x[which.max(x$share),]))
rownames(killers)<-NULL
killer_text<-and_list(paste0("in ",killers$entity,", ",plural[killers$kind]," (",
                             percent(killers$share),")"))
europe_heat<-dead[dead$entity=="Europe"&dead$kind=="extreme_temperature",]
heat_in<-function(year) {
  result<-europe_heat$value[europe_heat$year==year]
  return(result)
}
greece<-country_dead[country_dead$entity=="Greece"&country_dead$year%in%recent,]
greece_heat<-greece[greece$kind=="extreme_temperature",]

Where one event struck a country hard. From 2000 to 2025, disasters killed 0.85 people a year for every 100,000 in the world. Among the countries of a million people or more, Haiti lost 88.4 a year, almost all in its earthquake of 2010; then Libya (47.5, storm of 2023), Myanmar (12.5, storm of 2008), Sri Lanka (6.9, earthquake of 2004) and Somalia (6.2, drought of 2010). The 58 places with fewer than a million people are left out of the rates and the map: on a small island, a single storm makes the rate enormous.

Code 
classes<-c(0,0.1,0.5,1,2,5,10,Inf)
class_names<-c("Under 0.1","0.1–0.5","0.5–1","1–2","2–5","5–10","10 or more")
country_rates$class<-as.integer(cut(country_rates$rate,classes,right=FALSE))
steps<-do.call(c,
               lapply(seq_along(reds),function(i) {list(list((i-1)/7,reds[i]),list(i/7,reds[i]))}))
plot_ly(country_rates,type="choropleth",locations=~code,z=~class,zmin=0.5,zmax=7.5,
        colorscale=steps,marker=list(line=list(color="white",width=0.3)),
        text=~paste0(entity,": ",two(rate)," deaths a year per 100,000<br>",
                     number(deaths)," deaths in all; the worst year ",worst_year,
                     " (",tolower(label_of[worst_kind]),")"),
        hoverinfo="text",
        colorbar=list(title=list(text="Deaths a year<br>per 100,000"),tickvals=1:7,
                      ticktext=class_names,len=0.8,thickness=14)) %>%
  chart(paste0("Disaster deaths per 100,000 people a year, 2000–",last_year),
        paste0("EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain; population: HYDE, ",
               "Gapminder, UN; via Our World in Data. Grey: ",
               "under a million people, or no data."),
        geo=list(showframe=FALSE,showcoastlines=FALSE,showland=TRUE,landcolor="#e8e8e8",
                 projection=list(type="natural earth"),lataxis=list(range=c(-57,85))),
        margin=list(t=50,b=40,l=0,r=0),note_y=-0.02)

Interactive chart: Disaster deaths per 100,000 people a year, 2000–2025

Each continent has its own killer. Of the people killed by disasters since 2000, the most died, in Africa, floods (34%), in Asia, earthquakes (63%), in Europe, heat and cold (99%), in North America, earthquakes (88%), in Oceania, landslides (28%) and in South America, floods (55%).

In Europe, heat, and its deaths are of another kind. For 2022 and 2023, EM-DAT’s heat deaths in Europe, 61,671 and 47,688, are almost exactly the heat-related deaths that epidemiologists estimated for those years, 61,672 and 47,690, with statistical models of temperature and the deaths recorded in 35 countries (Ballester et al. 2023; Gallo et al. 2024): estimates of the deaths that the heat added, not deaths counted one by one, as those of an earthquake are. In Greece, 14,831 of the 15,134 disaster deaths since 2000 are such heat deaths, 14,783 of them in the years from 2022 to 2025; for the summer of 2022, the first study found the second highest rate of heat deaths in Europe in Greece, after Italy.

Code 
rows<-c("World","Africa","Asia","Europe","North America","South America","Oceania")
continent_dead$row<-factor(continent_dead$entity,levels=rev(rows))
p<-plot_ly()
for(g in group_levels) {
  x<-continent_dead[continent_dead$group==g,]
  p<-add_bars(p,data=x,x=~share,y=~row,name=g,orientation="h",
              marker=list(color=group_colors[[g]],line=list(color="white",width=1.5)),
              text=~ifelse(share>=12,percent(share),""),textposition="inside",
              insidetextanchor="middle",textfont=list(color="#1a1a1a"),
              hovertemplate=paste0("%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of the deaths, ",tolower(g),"<extra></extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart(paste0("Disaster deaths by kind, % of each continent, 2000–",last_year),
        "EM-DAT, CRED / UCLouvain, via Our World in Data.",
        x_axis=list(range=c(0,100),ticksuffix="%",showgrid=FALSE),barmode="stack",legend=legend_top,
        uniformtext=list(minsize=10,mode="hide"),margin=list(l=120,t=100,b=70,r=10),note_y=-0.1)

Interactive chart: Disaster deaths by kind, % of each continent, 2000–2025

5. Where is the Earth itself restless?

Code 
sf_use_s2(TRUE)
boundary<-st_union(st_geometry(plates))
quake_points<-st_as_sf(quakes,coords=c("longitude","latitude"),crs=4326)
erupted<-volcanoes[!is.na(volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year)&volcanoes$Last_Eruption_Year>=1900,]
volcano_points<-st_as_sf(erupted,coords=c("Longitude","Latitude"),crs=4326)
quake_km<-as.numeric(st_distance(quake_points,boundary))/1000
volcano_km<-as.numeric(st_distance(volcano_points,boundary))/1000
# how much of the Earth lies near a boundary: an even grid of points over the sphere (a Fibonacci
# lattice), each measured like the earthquakes
n_grid<-60000
i<-0:(n_grid-1)
grid<-st_as_sf(data.frame(lon=((i*180*(3-sqrt(5)))%%360)-180,lat=asin(-1+2*(i+0.5)/n_grid)*180/pi),
               coords=c("lon","lat"),crs=4326)
grid_km<-as.numeric(st_distance(grid,boundary))/1000
bands<-data.frame(km=c(100,200,300))
bands$earth<-sapply(bands$km,function(k) 100*mean(grid_km<=k))
bands$quakes<-sapply(bands$km,function(k) 100*mean(quake_km<=k))
bands$volcanoes<-sapply(bands$km,function(k) 100*mean(volcano_km<=k))
in_band<-function(k,column) {
  result<-bands[[column]][bands$km==k]
  return(result)
}

Along the edges of the plates. The outer shell of the Earth is broken into plates that move against each other (Bird 2003). The map shows the 1,620 earthquakes of magnitude 7 or more since 1900 and the 439 volcanoes that have erupted since 1900: they line the boundaries of the plates, above all around the Pacific Ocean. Within 300 km of a boundary, a band that covers 24% of the Earth’s surface, lie 89% of those earthquakes and 87% of those volcanoes.

Code 
# the boundaries as one line, broken (NA) between their segments
segments<-st_coordinates(plates)
breaks<-c(which(diff(segments[,"L1"])!=0),nrow(segments))
lines_lon<-unlist(lapply(seq_along(breaks),
                         function(k) {
  from<-if(k==1) 1 else breaks[k-1]+1
  c(segments[from:breaks[k],"X"],NA)
}))
lines_lat<-unlist(lapply(seq_along(breaks),
                         function(k) {
  from<-if(k==1) 1 else breaks[k-1]+1
  c(segments[from:breaks[k],"Y"],NA)
}))
plot_geo() %>%
  add_trace(type="scattergeo",mode="lines",lon=lines_lon,lat=lines_lat,
            line=list(color=dark_gray,width=1),name="Plate boundary",hoverinfo="skip") %>%
  add_trace(type="scattergeo",mode="markers",lon=quakes$longitude,lat=quakes$latitude,
            marker=list(color="#2a78d6",size=3+3*(quakes$mag-7),opacity=0.6,
                        line=list(color="white",width=0.5)),name="Earthquake, magnitude 7+",
            text=paste0(quakes$place,"<br>",substr(quakes$time,1,10),", magnitude ",quakes$mag),
            hoverinfo="text") %>%
  add_trace(type="scattergeo",mode="markers",lon=erupted$Longitude,lat=erupted$Latitude,
            marker=list(color="#eb6834",symbol="triangle-up",size=7,
                        line=list(color="white",width=0.5)),
            name="Volcano that erupted since 1900",
            text=paste0(erupted$Volcano_Name,", ",erupted$Country,"<br>last eruption ",
                        erupted$Last_Eruption_Year),hoverinfo="text") %>%
  chart("Big earthquakes and active volcanoes since 1900",
        paste0("USGS earthquake catalogue; Smithsonian, ",
               "Global Volcanism Program; plate boundaries: ","Bird (2003)."),
        geo=list(showframe=FALSE,showcoastlines=TRUE,coastlinecolor="#c8c8c8",showland=TRUE,
                 landcolor="#f2f2f2",projection=list(type="natural earth"),
                 lataxis=list(range=c(-60,85))),legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=80,b=40,l=0,r=0),
        note_y=-0.02)

Interactive chart: Big earthquakes and active volcanoes since 1900

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(km=paste("Within",bands$km,"km"),
                        earth=percent(bands$earth),
                        quakes=percent(bands$quakes),
                        volcanoes=percent(bands$volcanoes)),
             col.names=c("Distance from a plate boundary","Share of the Earth's surface",
                         "Earthquakes of magnitude 7+","Volcanoes that erupted since 1900"),
             align="lrrr")
Distance from a plate boundary Share of the Earth’s surface Earthquakes of magnitude 7+ Volcanoes that erupted since 1900
Within 100 km 9% 59% 36%
Within 200 km 17% 83% 66%
Within 300 km 24% 89% 87%

Earthquakes under the sea also cause most tsunamis. Each has a page of its own: earthquakes, volcanoes and tsunamis.

So, what does it mean?

  1. Floods and storms are the commonest disasters: 167 and 110 a year of the 393 that EM-DAT records.
  2. Earthquakes have killed the most people since 2000, 796 thousand, then heat and cold, 377 thousand.
  3. Disasters kill far fewer people than a century ago: 0.75 a year per 100,000 people in the 2020s, against 26.6 in the 1920s.
  4. Floods and droughts affect the most people, billions since 2000; in Europe, by the estimates of recent years, heat kills more than any other disaster.
  5. The ground shakes and erupts along the edges of the plates: a quarter of the Earth’s surface holds nearly nine in ten of the big earthquakes.

What this does not show. EM-DAT records the disasters that meet its criteria, and more of them get recorded as time goes on; its recent heat deaths in Europe are estimates from statistical models, while those of an earthquake or a flood are counted. The people affected are counted once for every disaster that hits them. The rates per person leave out small countries, and one event can decide the rate of a country for decades. And the numbers count the dead and the affected, not what the survivors lost.

For the details, see the pages on earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, floods, tornadoes and wildfires.

Sources

  • EM-DAT, the International Disaster Database, CRED / UCLouvain, Brussels (www.emdat.be): EM-DAT data, 2026, as published by Our World in Data, Natural disasters, in its charts natural-disasters-deaths, natural-disasters-people-affected and number-of-natural-disaster-events. EM-DAT’s definitions, classification and licence.
  • Ballester, J. et al. (2023), Heat-related mortality in Europe during the summer of 2022, Nature Medicine 29, 1857–1866.
  • Gallo, E. et al. (2024), Heat-related mortality in Europe during 2023 and the role of adaptation in protecting health, Nature Medicine 30, 3101–3105.
  • Population: HYDE (2023), Gapminder (2022) and UN World Population Prospects (2024), as published by Our World in Data; its continents.
  • U.S. Geological Survey, Earthquake Catalog (ComCat), through its web service.
  • Global Volcanism Program, Smithsonian Institution, Volcanoes of the World: the list of Holocene volcanoes, through its web services.
  • Bird, P. (2003), An updated digital model of plate boundaries, Geochemistry, Geophysics, Geosystems 4(3), 1027; as GeoJSON by Hugo Ahlenius, Nordpil, fraxen/tectonicplates (Open Data Commons Attribution License).

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · sf

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Where the World Burns: Wildfires on Every Continent Since 2002
item.description: Wildfires on every continent in satellite data: how much of Africa, Europe and the rest of the world burns each year, whether the world burns more than it used to, what burns, when each continent burns, and the worst years.
item.content:encoded:
Wildfires on every continent in satellite data: how much of Africa, Europe and the rest of the world burns each year, whether the world burns more than it used to, what burns, when each continent burns, and the worst years.

What is this?

Every summer the fires of California, Canada, Australia or Greece make the news. They are a small part of the land that burns in the world: most of it burns in Africa, every year, in dry seasons that seldom make the news at all. This story compares the continents and asks five questions:

  1. Where in the world does land burn?
  2. Is the world burning more than it used to?
  3. What burns: forest, savanna, grassland or fields?
  4. When does each continent burn?
  5. Which were the worst years?

Greece Burning looks at one country close up; this page looks at the whole world.

The data come from the Global Wildfire Information System (GWIS), a joint initiative of the Group on Earth Observations and the EU’s Copernicus programme, funded mainly by the European Commission (GWIS). Our World in Data adds up its figures by continent (Wildfires), and they are downloaded from there when the page is rendered:

  • The land burnt each year since 2002 in every country, mapped by NASA’s MODIS sensors on the Terra and Aqua satellites, which find land that has just burnt in their images (the product MCD64A1, Giglio et al. 2018), with the kind of land that burnt: forest, savanna, shrubland and grassland, cropland or other land (GWIS country profiles).
  • The land burnt each week since 2012, from MODIS and the finer VIIRS sensors, and the carbon dioxide that the fires released each year since 2003 (GWIS seasonal trends).
  • The land area of each country, from the World Bank (land area), and the continent it is in (continents).

A hectare is a square of 100 metres by 100, so a million hectares are 10,000 square kilometres.

The satellites count every fire. They map the land that burnt, whatever started the fire: a wildfire, a farmer burning the stubble of a field, or a fire set on purpose to clear dry grass. And they miss some: small fires, and fires hidden by cloud or by the trees above them (Our World in Data).

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "plotly"))
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a chart of Our World in Data as a table: one row for each country or region and each year (or week)
owid <- function(chart) {
  read.csv(paste0(
    "https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/",
    chart,
    ".csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true"
  ))
}
# the land burnt each year, in hectares, by the kind of land (MODIS)
cover <- owid("annual-burned-area-by-landcover")
# the land burnt each week, in hectares (MODIS and VIIRS); the weeks are written as "2012-W01"
weekly <- owid("weekly-area-burnt-by-wildfires")
# the carbon dioxide that the fires released each year, in tonnes (MODIS and VIIRS)
co2 <- owid("annual-carbon-dioxide-emissions")
# the land area of each country, in square kilometres (World Bank), and the continent it is in
land <- owid("land-area-km")
continents <- owid("continents-according-to-our-world-in-data")
Code 
# the kinds of land: the columns of the data and their names on this page
covers <- c(
  forest = "Forest",
  savannas = "Savanna",
  shrublands_grasslands = "Shrubland and grassland",
  croplands = "Cropland",
  other = "Other land"
)
cover$all <- rowSums(cover[names(covers)])
first_year <- min(cover$year)
last_year <- max(cover$year)
first_five <- first_year:(first_year + 4)
last_five <- (last_year - 4):last_year
# the continents of Our World in Data, which counts all of Russia in Europe, with Russia on its own
by_group <- function(x, time = "year") {
  values <- setdiff(names(x), c("entity", "code", time))
  europe <- x[x$entity == "Europe", ]
  russia <- x[x$entity == "Russia", ]
  russia <- russia[match(europe[[time]], russia[[time]]), ]
  rest <- europe
  rest[values] <- europe[values] - russia[values]
  rest$entity <- "Europe without Russia"
  others <- c("Africa", "Asia", "North America", "Oceania", "South America", "Russia")
  y <- rbind(x[x$entity %in% others, ], rest)
  names(y)[names(y) == "entity"] <- "group"
  y
}
yearly <- by_group(cover)
world <- cover[cover$entity == "World", ]
# the groups, from the one that burns the most land to the one that burns the least
groups <- names(sort(tapply(yearly$all, yearly$group, mean), decreasing = TRUE))
# the groups and the world in one table, the world first
with_world <- rbind(
  yearly[, c("group", "year", "all", names(covers))],
  data.frame(group = "World", world[, c("year", "all", names(covers))])
)
with_world$group <- factor(with_world$group, levels = c("World", groups))
# the countries: rows with a country code that Our World in Data puts on a continent (its regions,
# such as "Europe (excl. Russia)", have no code or one that starts with OWID_, like Kosovo's)
country_codes <- continents$code[nzchar(continents$code)]
group_of <- function(code) {
  continent <- continents$owid_region[match(code, continents$code)]
  ifelse(code == "RUS", "Russia", ifelse(continent == "Europe", "Europe without Russia", continent))
}
# each country: the land burnt in an average year, its land area (the latest year that the World Bank
# has) and its group
countries <- cover[cover$code %in% country_codes, ] |>
  group_by(code, entity) |>
  summarise(burnt = mean(all), crops = mean(croplands), .groups = "drop")
land_now <- land[land$code %in% country_codes & !is.na(land$ag_lnd_totl_k2), ] |>
  group_by(code) |>
  slice_max(year, n = 1)
countries$km2 <- land_now$ag_lnd_totl_k2[match(countries$code, land_now$code)]
countries$group <- group_of(countries$code)
# a hectare is 1% of a square kilometre, so hectares per square kilometre are a percentage
countries$share <- countries$burnt / countries$km2
Code 
red <- "#d62728"
gray <- "#bdbdbd"
dark_gray <- "#6b6b6b" # also the colour of the notes
# the kinds of land, in the order of the stacked bars, whose neighbours were checked for colour
# blindness; the other land, a sliver, is grey
cover_colors <- c(
  forest = "#008300",
  savannas = "#eda100",
  shrublands_grasslands = "#1baf7a",
  croplands = "#eb6834",
  other = "#d9d9d9"
)
# one hue, from light to dark, for amounts: the map and the calendar
oranges <- c("#feedde", "#fdd0a2", "#fdae6b", "#fd8d3c", "#f16913", "#d94801", "#8c2d04")
# the source of a plotly chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart <- function(
  p,
  title,
  source,
  y_title = "",
  y_axis = list(),
  x_axis = list(),
  annotations = list(),
  margin = list(t = 70, b = 90),
  note_y = -0.16,
  ...
) {
  note <- list(
    text = paste("Source:", source),
    xref = "paper",
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = note_y,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "top",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 11, color = dark_gray)
  )
  layout(
    p,
    title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, xanchor = "left", y = 0.97, yanchor = "top"),
    yaxis = c(list(title = y_title), y_axis),
    xaxis = c(list(title = ""), x_axis),
    margin = margin,
    annotations = c(annotations, list(note)),
    ...
  ) |>
    config(displaylogo = FALSE)
}
legend_top <- list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom")
# the look of the ggplot charts
theme_page <- function(base_size = 14) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
      plot.caption.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
# numbers in the text
number <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
percent <- function(x, digits = 0) paste0(format(round(x, digits), nsmall = digits, trim = TRUE), "%")
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1, trim = TRUE)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2, trim = TRUE)
# millions (of hectares or tonnes): whole numbers from 10 million, one decimal below
million <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) >= 1e7, number(x / 1e6), one(x / 1e6))
# a change in per cent, with its sign (the bold font of the charts has no minus sign: a dash there)
change_text <- function(x, minus = "−") paste0(ifelse(x >= 0, "+", minus), round(abs(x)), "%")
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}
# country names that take "the" in a sentence
with_the <- function(x) {
  ifelse(
    x %in% c("Central African Republic", "Democratic Republic of Congo", "United States", "Gambia"),
    paste("the", x),
    x
  )
}
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as this one
# without a trend
chance <- function(x, years) {
  p <- cor.test(years, x, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
  if (p < 0.01) "less than 1" else as.character(round(100 * p))
}
Code 
# the weekly figures: the year, and the week (the 53rd week of the years that have one counts as the
# 52nd, so that every year has the same weeks)
week_parts <- function(x) {
  x$year <- as.integer(substr(x$week, 1, 4))
  x$w <- pmin(as.integer(substr(x$week, 7, 8)), 52)
  x
}
weekly <- week_parts(weekly)
# the month of a week: that of its middle day, near enough
month_of <- function(w) as.integer(format(as.Date("2001-01-01") + 7 * (w - 1) + 3, "%m"))
first_week_year <- min(weekly$year)
last_season <- 2024 # the last year of the weekly figures and the carbon dioxide used here (below)
# for the world, the weekly figures of each year added up, against the yearly MODIS figures
weekly_world <- weekly[weekly$entity == "World", ]
agree <- weekly_world |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(weekly = sum(area_ha)) |>
  inner_join(world[, c("year", "all")], by = "year") |>
  mutate(ratio = 100 * weekly / all)
before <- agree[agree$year <= last_season, ]
# April to September: weeks 14 to 39
mid_year <- weekly_world[weekly_world$w %in% 14:39, ] |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(area = sum(area_ha))
mid_before <- mid_year$area[mid_year$year <= last_season]
modis_before <- world$all[world$year %in% before$year]

The continents are those of Our World in Data, with Russia on its own. Our World in Data counts all of Russia in Europe. But most of Russia is in Asia, and Russia burns 5 times as much land as the rest of Europe put together: as part of Europe, it would hide everything else.

The weekly figures, and the carbon dioxide, stop at 2024. From 2012 to 2024, the weekly figures of a year added up to between 93% and 120% of the yearly MODIS figure for the world; in 2025, to 81%. From April to September 2025 they add up to 141 million hectares, against 200 to 261 in the same months of the years before, while the yearly MODIS figure for 2025, 333 million hectares, is within the range of the years before it (331 to 454). The weekly figures may have changed the way they are made; until the two series agree again, this page uses them, and the carbon dioxide that comes with them, only up to 2024.

1. Where in the world does land burn?

Code 
mean_by_group <- yearly |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(burnt = mean(all)) |>
  mutate(world_share = 100 * burnt / mean(world$all))
# the share of its land, from the countries whose land area the World Bank has
group_land <- countries |>
  filter(!is.na(km2)) |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(land_share = sum(burnt) / sum(km2))
mean_by_group$land_share <- group_land$land_share[match(mean_by_group$group, group_land$group)]
in_group <- function(g, column) mean_by_group[[column]][mean_by_group$group == g]
world_burnt <- mean(world$all)
with_land <- countries[!is.na(countries$km2), ]
world_land_share <- sum(with_land$burnt) / sum(with_land$km2)
eu <- land[land$entity == "European Union (27)", ]
eu_hectares <- 100 * eu$ag_lnd_totl_k2[which.max(eu$year)]
in_country <- function(name, column) countries[[column]][countries$entity == name]
most_burnt <- countries |>
  filter(!is.na(km2)) |>
  arrange(desc(share)) |>
  head(4)
n_years <- last_year - first_year + 1
europe_rest <- countries[countries$group == "Europe without Russia", ]
ukraine_part <- 100 * in_country("Ukraine", "burnt") / sum(europe_rest$burnt)

Africa: two thirds of all the land that burns. From 2002 to 2025, fires burnt 397 million hectares of the world’s land in an average year, about as much as all the land of the European Union (399 million hectares), and 3.1% of the land of the world. 67% of it was in Africa: 267 million hectares a year, as much as 9% of the continent. Oceania, almost all of it Australia, had 11% of the world’s burnt land, South America 8% and Asia 7%. Russia had 3.1%, North America 2.2% and the rest of Europe 0.6%.

Code 
bars <- mean_by_group[order(mean_by_group$burnt), ] # the largest at the top
bars$group <- factor(bars$group, levels = bars$group)
bar_colors <- ifelse(bars$group == "Africa", red, gray)
left <- plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~ burnt / 1e6,
  y = ~group,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = bar_colors),
  text = ~ paste0(million(burnt), " (", percent(world_share), ")"),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f} million hectares a year<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
)
right <- plot_ly(
  bars,
  x = ~land_share,
  y = ~group,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = bar_colors),
  text = ~ percent(land_share, 1),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of its land a year<extra></extra>",
  showlegend = FALSE
)
hidden_axis <- list(title = "", showticklabels = FALSE, showgrid = FALSE, zeroline = FALSE)
panel_title <- function(text, axis) {
  list(
    text = text,
    xref = paste(axis, "domain"),
    yref = "paper",
    x = 0,
    y = 1,
    xanchor = "left",
    yanchor = "bottom",
    showarrow = FALSE,
    font = list(size = 13)
  )
}
# the left panel wider: its labels are longer
subplot(left, right, shareY = TRUE, margin = 0.04, widths = c(0.6, 0.4)) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Land burnt in an average year, ", first_year, "–", last_year),
    "GWIS (MODIS), via Our World in Data; land areas: World Bank.",
    x_axis = c(hidden_axis, list(range = c(0, 1.75 * max(bars$burnt) / 1e6))),
    xaxis2 = c(hidden_axis, list(range = c(0, 1.45 * max(bars$land_share)))),
    annotations = list(
      panel_title("Million hectares (and share of the world)", "x"),
      panel_title("Share of its own land", "x2")
    ),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 90, b = 50, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.06
  )

Interactive chart: Land burnt in an average year, 2002–2025

Some countries burn a large part of their land every year. In South Sudan, the land burnt in an average year adds up to 47% of the country: over the 24 years, 11 times the whole country, so the same land burns again and again. Zambia (31%), the Central African Republic (30%) and Angola (30%) come next, all in the belts of grassland and scattered trees north and south of Africa’s rainforest.

Code 
on_map <- countries[!is.na(countries$share), ]
classes <- c(0, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 20, Inf)
class_names <- c("Under 0.1%", "0.1–0.5%", "0.5–1%", "1–5%", "5–10%", "10–20%", "20% or more")
on_map$class <- as.integer(cut(on_map$share, classes, right = FALSE))
# a colour scale of seven steps, one colour for each class
steps <- do.call(c, lapply(seq_along(oranges), function(i) {
  list(list((i - 1) / 7, oranges[i]), list(i / 7, oranges[i]))
}))
plot_ly(
  on_map,
  type = "choropleth",
  locations = ~code,
  z = ~class,
  zmin = 0.5,
  zmax = 7.5,
  colorscale = steps,
  marker = list(line = list(color = "white", width = 0.3)),
  text = ~ paste0(
    entity,
    ": ",
    ifelse(share < 1, two(share), one(share)),
    "% of its land a year<br>",
    number(burnt),
    " hectares a year"
  ),
  hoverinfo = "text",
  colorbar = list(
    title = list(text = "Land burnt<br>each year"),
    tickvals = 1:7,
    ticktext = class_names,
    len = 0.8,
    thickness = 14
  )
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Land burnt in an average year, % of each country, ", first_year, "–", last_year),
    "GWIS (MODIS), via Our World in Data; land areas: World Bank. Grey: no land area in the World Bank's data.",
    geo = list(
      showframe = FALSE,
      showcoastlines = FALSE,
      showland = TRUE,
      landcolor = "#e8e8e8",
      projection = list(type = "natural earth"),
      lataxis = list(range = c(-57, 85))
    ),
    margin = list(t = 50, b = 40, l = 0, r = 0),
    note_y = -0.02
  )

Interactive chart: Land burnt in an average year, % of each country, 2002–2025

In Europe, most of it is Ukraine’s. Without Russia, Europe burnt 2.5 million hectares a year, 0.4% of its land, and 66% of that was in Ukraine, which burnt 2.9% of its own land every year, mostly fields (section 3). The countries of Europe’s south burn far less of their land: Portugal 1.39% a year, Greece 0.50%, Spain 0.23% and Italy 0.29%.

2. Is the world burning more than it used to?

Code 
changes <- with_world |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(
    start = mean(all[year %in% first_five]),
    end = mean(all[year %in% last_five]),
    chance = chance(all, year)
  ) |>
  mutate(change = 100 * (end / start - 1))
of_change <- function(g, column) changes[[column]][changes$group == g]
world_fall <- of_change("World", "start") - of_change("World", "end")
africa_part <- 100 * (of_change("Africa", "start") - of_change("Africa", "end")) / world_fall
north_america <- yearly[yearly$group == "North America", ]
without_2023 <- mean(north_america$all[north_america$year %in% setdiff(last_five, 2023)])
falls <- changes[changes$group != "World" & changes$change <= -30, ]

Less, by about a fifth. In 2002–2006 fires burnt 450 million hectares a year, in 2021–2025 353: 22% less. And the fall is not just a matter of a few good years at the end: a rank test of all the years finds it too (the chance of a pattern as strong as this one without a trend is less than 1 in 100).

The table compares the first and the last five years, million hectares a year. The last column is the chance, in 100, of a pattern as strong as that of all the years without a trend.

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    group = changes$group,
    start = million(changes$start),
    end = million(changes$end),
    change = change_text(changes$change),
    chance = changes$chance
  ),
  col.names = c(
    "",
    paste0(min(first_five), "–", max(first_five)),
    paste0(min(last_five), "–", max(last_five)),
    "Change",
    "By chance, in 100"
  ),
  align = "lrrrr"
)
2002–2006 2021–2025 Change By chance, in 100
World 450 353 −22% less than 1
Africa 299 238 −20% less than 1
Oceania 52 43 −18% 35
South America 37 31 −17% 20
Asia 36 20 −43% less than 1
Russia 15 8.7 −43% less than 1
North America 8.7 11 +28% 55
Europe without Russia 2.8 1.6 −42% 4

Most of the fall is Africa’s. 63% of the land that the world stopped burning was in Africa, which burnt 20% less. Asia, Russia and Europe without Russia burnt 42% to 43% less, but they burn far less land than Africa to begin with. Only North America burnt more, by 28%, and mostly because of 2023: the other four of its last five years burnt 6% more than its first five.

This is not new. Satellites found the same from 1998 to 2015: the land burnt in the world fell by about a quarter, most of all in the savannas, and mainly because farming spread and grew more intensive (Andela et al. 2017).

Code 
index <- with_world |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(index = 100 * all / mean(all[year %in% first_five])) |>
  ungroup()
late_lines <- changes |>
  mutate(level = 100 * end / start)
# the title of each panel: the group and its change
panel_names <- setNames(
  paste0(gsub("without ", "without\n", changes$group), "\n", change_text(changes$change, minus = "–")),
  changes$group
)
ggplot(index, aes(x = year, y = index)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(colour = dark_gray, linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(colour = dark_gray, size = 0.9) +
  geom_segment(
    data = late_lines,
    aes(x = min(last_five) - 0.4, xend = max(last_five) + 0.4, y = level, yend = level),
    colour = red,
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~group, ncol = 4, labeller = as_labeller(panel_names)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2005, 2015, 2025)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(50, 250, 50)) +
  labs(
    title = "Burning more or less?",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Land burnt each year, the average of ",
      min(first_five),
      "–",
      max(first_five),
      " = 100\nRed: the average of ",
      min(last_five),
      "–",
      max(last_five),
      ", and the change, under each name"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: GWIS (MODIS), via Our World in Data"
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0)
  )

3. What burns: forest, savanna, grassland or fields?

Code 
cover_totals <- with_world |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(names(covers)), sum))
cover_shares <- cover_totals
cover_shares[names(covers)] <- 100 * cover_totals[names(covers)] / rowSums(cover_totals[names(covers)])
of_cover <- function(g, k) cover_shares[[k]][cover_shares$group == g]
# the world, by kind of land: the first and the last five years, and the trend over all the years
world_covers <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(covers)[1:4], function(k) {
  data.frame(
    cover = covers[[k]],
    start = mean(world[[k]][world$year %in% first_five]),
    end = mean(world[[k]][world$year %in% last_five]),
    chance = chance(world[[k]], world$year)
  )
}))
world_covers$change <- 100 * (world_covers$end / world_covers$start - 1)
of_world_cover <- function(name, column) world_covers[[column]][world_covers$cover == name]
# the forest burnt in a group: the first and the last five years, and the trend
forest_in <- function(g, column) {
  x <- yearly[yearly$group == g, ]
  list(
    start = mean(x$forest[x$year %in% first_five]),
    end = mean(x$forest[x$year %in% last_five]),
    chance = chance(x$forest, x$year)
  )[[column]]
}
ukraine_crops <- 100 *
  in_country("Ukraine", "crops") /
  sum(countries$crops[countries$group == "Europe without Russia"])

Mostly savanna, shrubs and grass; forest is a small part. Of all the land that burnt in the world from 2002 to 2025, 44% was savanna, 40% shrubland and grassland, 8% cropland and 8% forest.

Code 
rows <- factor(cover_shares$group, levels = rev(c("World", groups)))
p <- plot_ly()
for (k in names(covers)) {
  p <- add_bars(
    p,
    x = cover_shares[[k]],
    y = rows,
    name = covers[[k]],
    orientation = "h",
    marker = list(color = cover_colors[[k]], line = list(color = "white", width = 1.5)),
    # a label only on the larger parts
    text = ifelse(cover_shares[[k]] >= 12, percent(cover_shares[[k]]), ""),
    textposition = "inside",
    insidetextanchor = "middle",
    textfont = list(color = if (k == "forest") "white" else "#1a1a1a"),
    hovertemplate = paste0("%{y}: %{x:.1f}% ", tolower(covers[[k]]), "<extra></extra>")
  )
}
p |>
  chart(
    paste0("What burnt, % of the land burnt, ", first_year, "–", last_year),
    "GWIS (MODIS burned area and land cover), via Our World in Data.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 100), ticksuffix = "%", showgrid = FALSE),
    barmode = "stack",
    legend = c(legend_top, list(traceorder = "normal")),
    uniformtext = list(minsize = 10, mode = "hide"),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 100, b = 70, r = 10),
    note_y = -0.1
  )

Interactive chart: What burnt, % of the land burnt, 2002–2025

What the satellites call savanna. GWIS lays the burnt land on NASA’s map of land cover, made from the same MODIS images (GWIS country profiles), and that map sorts land by how much of it trees cover, not by climate: forest is land where trees cover more than 60% of the ground, savanna land where they cover between 10% and 60% (MODIS land cover user guide). In Africa, South America and Australia that is the savanna of the word, grass under scattered trees. In Russia and Canada, where there is no tropical savanna, it takes in northern forest with gaps between the trees, which is why 49% of Russia’s burnt land and 49% of North America’s counts as savanna.

Europe burns fields. Without Russia, 76% of the land that burnt in Europe was cropland, 77% of it in Ukraine; forest, as the satellites define it, was 2.7%.

Savanna, grassland and fields burn less; forest, not clearly. In the world, by kind of land, million hectares a year:

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    cover = world_covers$cover,
    start = million(world_covers$start),
    end = million(world_covers$end),
    change = change_text(world_covers$change),
    chance = world_covers$chance
  ),
  col.names = c(
    "",
    paste0(min(first_five), "–", max(first_five)),
    paste0(min(last_five), "–", max(last_five)),
    "Change",
    "By chance, in 100"
  ),
  align = "lrrrr"
)
2002–2006 2021–2025 Change By chance, in 100
Forest 33 28 −14% 11
Savanna 193 155 −20% less than 1
Shrubland and grassland 183 144 −21% less than 1
Cropland 40 25 −37% less than 1

The burnt cropland fell the most, 37%, and savanna, shrubland and grassland by about a fifth, all with clear trends. The burnt forest fell by 14%, but a pattern like that would come up by chance 11 times in 100 without a trend. In North America the forest that burnt rose from 1.0 million hectares a year in 2002–2006 to 1.7 in 2021–2025 (by chance less than 1 in 100); in Russia it fell, from 1.1 to 0.5.

4. When does each continent burn?

Code 
seasons_of <- weekly[weekly$year <= last_season, ]
# each group: the share of the year's burnt land in each week, the average of the years
season <- by_group(seasons_of[, c("entity", "code", "week", "area_ha")], time = "week") |>
  week_parts() |>
  group_by(group, year, w) |>
  summarise(area = sum(area_ha), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = 100 * area / sum(area)) |>
  group_by(group, w) |>
  summarise(share = mean(share), .groups = "drop")
by_month <- season |>
  mutate(month = month_of(w)) |>
  group_by(group, month) |>
  summarise(share = sum(share), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(group, month)
# the three months in a row in which each group burns the most (December to February included)
three <- function(shares) sapply(1:12, function(m) sum(shares[(m - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1]))
best <- by_month |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(start = which.max(three(share)), share = max(three(share)))
months_of <- function(g) {
  s <- best$start[best$group == g]
  (s - 1 + 0:2) %% 12 + 1
}
season_text <- function(g) {
  m <- months_of(g)
  paste(month.name[m[1]], "to", month.name[m[3]])
}
season_share <- function(g) percent(best$share[best$group == g])
# the countries that burn the most of a group's land in its three months
countries_weekly <- seasons_of[seasons_of$code %in% country_codes, ]
countries_weekly$group <- group_of(countries_weekly$code)
leaders <- function(g, n = 2) {
  x <- countries_weekly[countries_weekly$group == g & month_of(countries_weekly$w) %in% months_of(g), ]
  s <- sort(tapply(x$area_ha, x$entity, sum), decreasing = TRUE)
  and_list(paste0(with_the(names(s)[1:n]), " (", percent(100 * s[1:n] / sum(s)), ")"))
}
# the share of a country's burnt land in some months
in_months <- function(name, months) {
  x <- countries_weekly[countries_weekly$entity == name, ]
  percent(100 * sum(x$area_ha[month_of(x$w) %in% months]) / sum(x$area_ha))
}

Each in its own dry season, and Africa in two. The chart shows, for each group, how the land it burns is spread over the year: the share of a year’s burnt land in each week, on average from 2012 to 2024.

Code 
season$class <- cut(
  season$share,
  c(-Inf, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, Inf),
  labels = c("Under 0.5%", "0.5–1%", "1–2%", "2–3%", "3–4%", "4% or more")
)
middle_of_month <- (as.integer(format(as.Date(paste0("2001-", 1:12, "-15")), "%j")) - 1) / 7 + 1
ggplot(season, aes(x = w, y = factor(group, levels = rev(groups)), fill = class)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = oranges[2:7], drop = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = middle_of_month, labels = month.abb, expand = c(0, 0)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "When each continent burns",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Share of the year's burnt land in each week, ",
      first_week_year,
      "–",
      last_season
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Data: GWIS (MODIS and VIIRS), via Our World in Data"
  ) +
  theme_page(13) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.8)))

Africa burns the most from July to September, 40% of the land it burns in a year, but it has two seasons, one on each side of the equator, each in its own dry months: 88% of South Sudan’s burnt land burns from November to February, and 88% of Angola’s from June to September. South America burns from August to October (61%), most of it in Brazil (71%) and Bolivia (13%), and Oceania from September to November (41%), almost all of it in Australia.

Asia burns from February to April (65%), mostly in Myanmar (27%), India (20%) and Laos (15%). North America burns most in spring too, from March to May (49%), mostly in Mexico (44%), the United States (20%) and Honduras (10%); Canada’s fires come later, 58% of its burnt land in July and August. Russia has a spring season and a summer one: 37% of its burnt land in April and May, 37% in July and August. So has Ukraine, which burns most of the rest of Europe: 26% of its burnt land in March and April, 67% from July to October.

5. Which were the worst years?

Code 
co2_groups <- by_group(co2)
co2_groups <- co2_groups[co2_groups$year <= last_season, ]
first_co2 <- min(co2_groups$year)
worst <- co2_groups |>
  group_by(group) |>
  summarise(average = mean(co2), worst_year = year[which.max(co2)], worst = max(co2)) |>
  mutate(times = worst / average) |>
  arrange(desc(times))
of_worst <- function(g, column) worst[[column]][worst$group == g]
co2_in <- function(g, year) co2_groups$co2[co2_groups$group == g & co2_groups$year == year]
canada <- cover[cover$entity == "Canada", ]
oceania <- yearly[yearly$group == "Oceania", ]
asia <- yearly[yearly$group == "Asia", ]
in_year <- function(x, year, column = "all") x[[column]][x$year == year]

Where fire is rare, the worst years stand out the most. Burnt land is one measure of a bad year; the carbon dioxide that the fires released is another, which counts the fires that burn forest and peat for more than those of grass. For each group, from 2003 to 2024, million tonnes of carbon dioxide:

Code 
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    group = worst$group,
    average = number(worst$average / 1e6),
    year = worst$worst_year,
    worst = number(worst$worst / 1e6),
    times = one(worst$times)
  ),
  col.names = c("", "A year on average", "Worst year", "That year", "Times the average"),
  align = "lrrrr"
)
A year on average Worst year That year Times the average
North America 560 2023 1,548 2.8
Russia 570 2003 1,304 2.3
Oceania 495 2012 1,009 2.0
Asia 811 2015 1,508 1.9
Europe without Russia 33 2007 54 1.6
South America 1,053 2007 1,679 1.6
Africa 2,907 2007 3,365 1.2
Code 
set.seed(2026)
strip <- co2_groups |>
  group_by(group) |>
  mutate(of_average = 100 * co2 / mean(co2), is_worst = co2 == max(co2)) |>
  ungroup()
order <- rev(worst$group) # the most extreme worst year at the top
strip$position <- match(strip$group, order) + runif(nrow(strip), -0.17, 0.17)
dots <- function(p, x, color) {
  add_markers(
    p,
    data = x,
    x = ~of_average,
    y = ~position,
    marker = list(color = color, size = 9, line = list(color = "white", width = 1)),
    text = ~ paste0(group, " ", year, ": ", number(co2 / 1e6), " million tonnes, ", round(of_average), "% of its average"),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  )
}
plot_ly() |>
  dots(strip[!strip$is_worst, ], gray) |>
  dots(strip[strip$is_worst, ], red) |>
  chart(
    paste0("CO₂ from fires, % of each group's average, ", first_co2, "–", last_season),
    "GWIS (MODIS and VIIRS), via Our World in Data. Dots: years; red: the worst year.",
    x_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero", ticksuffix = "%"),
    y_axis = list(
      tickvals = seq_along(order),
      ticktext = order,
      range = c(0.4, length(order) + 0.6),
      zeroline = FALSE
    ),
    annotations = lapply(seq_along(order), function(i) {
      list(
        x = 100 * of_worst(order[i], "times"),
        y = i,
        text = of_worst(order[i], "worst_year"),
        showarrow = FALSE,
        xanchor = "left",
        xshift = 8,
        font = list(size = 12, color = dark_gray)
      )
    }),
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line",
      x0 = 100,
      x1 = 100,
      yref = "paper",
      y0 = 0,
      y1 = 1,
      line = list(color = dark_gray, width = 1)
    )),
    margin = list(l = 150, t = 70, b = 90, r = 40),
    note_y = -0.14
  )

Interactive chart: CO₂ from fires, % of each group's average, 2003–2024

  • North America, 2023: 1,548 million tonnes, 2.8 times its average. Canada had the worst fire season in its records, about 15 million hectares by its own count, from mid-April to late October, after an early snowmelt and a drought, in a season 2.2 °C warmer than the average of 1991–2020 (Jain et al. 2024). MODIS mapped 13 million hectares in Canada that year, 5 times its average: the satellites miss part of what burns.
  • Russia, 2003: 1,304 million tonnes, 2.3 times its average.
  • Asia, 2015: 1,508 million tonnes, 1.9 times its average, though the land it burnt that year, 33 million hectares, was only 18% above its average. In September and October forests and peat burnt across the islands of South-East Asia, above all in Indonesia, after a long drought, and for those two months the fires released 11.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a day, more than the fossil fuels of the EU, 8.9 million tonnes a day (Huijnen et al. 2016). Peat is soil made of dead plants, full of carbon.
  • Oceania, 2012: its worst year for burnt land too, 90 million hectares, 90% of it shrubland and grassland. The fires that most people remember came later: between September 2019 and early January 2020, about 5.8 million hectares of mainly temperate broadleaf forest burnt in New South Wales and Victoria (Boer et al. 2020). In MODIS, 3.3 million hectares of forest burnt in Oceania in 2019, 6 times its average, but that is a small part of the 36 million hectares it burnt that year.
  • Africa, which burns the most, is the steadiest: its worst year, 2007, released only 1.2 times its average. And for the rest of Europe the worst year was 2007, the year of Greece’s worst fires (Greece Burning).

So, what does it mean?

  1. Most of the world’s fire is African. Africa has 67% of the land that burns; the land it burns in a year is as large as 9% of the continent. Europe without Russia burns 0.4% of its land a year.
  2. The world burns less than it did: 22% less in 2021–2025 than in 2002–2006, 63% of the fall in Africa.
  3. Forest is a small part of what burns, and it is not clearly burning less. In North America more of it burns.
  4. Every continent burns in its own dry months, and Africa has two seasons, one on each side of the equator.
  5. The worst years come where fire is rarer. North America released 2.8 times its average carbon dioxide in 2023; Africa’s worst year, only 1.2 times.

What this does not show. The satellites map the land that burnt, not what started the fire, and they miss small fires and fires under cloud or trees; the fires here include those that people set on purpose. A continent is large, and its average hides countries that burn far more or far less. The carbon dioxide is an estimate, from GWIS’s figures up to 2024. And hectares do not count the people, the homes and the animals lost in the fires, or the smoke that people breathe far from them.

For one country close up, see Greece Burning; for the heat that dries out the land, Athens Is Getting Hotter; for the temperature of the world, the NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly.

Sources

  • GWIS, the Global Wildfire Information System: the country profiles, with the land burnt each year by kind of land since 2002, from MODIS (MCD64A1 burned area, MCD12 land cover); the seasonal trends, with the land burnt each week and the carbon dioxide, from MODIS and VIIRS; data licence, CC BY 4.0.
  • Our World in Data, Wildfires: the GWIS figures by country and continent, from its charts annual-burned-area-by-landcover, weekly-area-burnt-by-wildfires and annual-carbon-dioxide-emissions; the land area of each country, from the World Bank; its continents (CC BY 4.0).
  • Giglio, L. et al. (2018), The Collection 6 MODIS burned area mapping algorithm and product, Remote Sensing of Environment 217, 72–85.
  • NASA LP DAAC, MODIS Collection 6.1 Land Cover Type Product User Guide (MCD12Q1: forest and savanna by tree cover).
  • Andela, N. et al. (2017), A human-driven decline in global burned area, Science 356, 1356–1362.
  • Jain, P. et al. (2024), Drivers and impacts of the record-breaking 2023 wildfire season in Canada, Nature Communications 15, 6764.
  • Huijnen, V. et al. (2016), Fire carbon emissions over maritime southeast Asia in 2015 largest since 1997, Scientific Reports 6, 26886.
  • Boer, M. M. et al. (2020), Unprecedented burn area of Australian mega forest fires, Nature Climate Change 10, 171–172.

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Greece Burning: How Much, When and Where Wildfires Burn
item.description: Wildfires in Greece in official and satellite data: the area burnt each year since 1980, the worst years, the fire season, a map of every large fire since 2016, and the neighbours.
item.content:encoded:
Wildfires in Greece in official and satellite data: the area burnt each year since 1980, the worst years, the fire season, a map of every large fire since 2016, and the neighbours.

What is this?

In August 2023 a fire near Alexandroupolis burnt more than 96,000 hectares, the largest single fire in Europe since the 1980s (JRC, 10 April 2024). A hectare is a square of 100 metres by 100; that fire burnt more than 960 square kilometres. Was it a sign that Greece burns more than it used to? This story asks five questions:

  1. Is Greece burning more than it used to?
  2. Which were the worst years, and why?
  3. Is the fire season getting longer?
  4. Where do the fires burn?
  5. How does Greece compare with its neighbours?

The data come from three places, besides the boundaries of the regions from GISCO and the area of each country from Eurostat (reg_area3):

  • National statistics: the area burnt and the number of forest fires in each country, every year since 1980, which the countries report and the Joint Research Centre (JRC) of the European Commission collects (country totals). Those of Greece count forest land, “wooded and non-wooded” (JRC 2025).
  • EFFIS, the European Forest Fire Information System, run by the JRC: satellites outline the land that burns. It has the area burnt in each country every year since 2006, in fires of about 30 hectares or more (statistics portal), and the outline of every fire mapped in Greece since 2016, at first of about 30 hectares or more and, since 2020, smaller ones too (rapid damage assessment).
  • NASA FIRMS: the hot spots that two satellites, Terra and Aqua, have seen in Greece since 2003 (FIRMS, with one file for each country and year).

They do not count the same things. The national statistics count forest land; the satellites outline all the land that burnt, farmland included, but miss the small fires. In 2007, for example, Greece counted 225,734 hectares of forest fires, and another 88,093 in fires outside forest land, 313,826 in all (JRC 2008); EFFIS mapped about 272,000 hectares, in fires of about 30 hectares or more. Where the two disagree, the page says which one it shows.

# the country totals: an Excel file with one sheet for the area burnt (hectares) and one for the
# number of fires, with a row for each year and a column for each country
totals_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".xlsx")
download.file(
  paste0(
    "https://forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu/effis/applications/data-and-services/",
    "report_2024.xlsx"
  ),
  totals_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE

read_greece <- function(sheet) {
  x <- as.data.frame(readxl::read_excel(totals_file, sheet = sheet, col_types = "text"))
  # numbers are written with spaces between the thousands, such as "32 965"
  data.frame(year = as.integer(x$Year), value = as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9.]", "", x$GRC)))
}
national <- data.frame(
  year = read_greece(1)$year,
  area = read_greece(1)$value,
  fires = read_greece(2)$value
)
Code 
# EFFIS's estimates for a country (its three-letter code): the area burnt each year, in hectares,
# and the number of fires of about 30 hectares or more, from satellite images
effis_annual <- function(code) {
  x <- jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(
    "https://api2.effis.emergency.copernicus.eu/statistics/v2/effis/",
    "estimatesbycountry?country=",
    code
  ))
  data.frame(code = code, year = x$year, area = x$ba, fires = x$nf)
}
countries <- data.frame(
  code = c("GRC", "PRT", "ESP", "ITA", "FRA", "CYP"),
  geo = c("EL", "PT", "ES", "IT", "FR", "CY"),
  name = c("Greece", "Portugal", "Spain", "Italy", "France", "Cyprus")
)
effis <- do.call(rbind, lapply(countries$code, effis_annual))
effis_greece <- effis[effis$code == "GRC", ]
# the area of each country, in square kilometres: for France, without its overseas departments
area_all <- get_eurostat(
  "reg_area3",
  filters = list(geo = c(countries$geo, "FRY"), landuse = "TOTAL", unit = "KM2"),
  time_format = "num",
  cache = FALSE
)
area_now <- area_all[area_all$time == max(area_all$time), ]
land <- setNames(area_now$values, area_now$geo)
countries$km2 <- land[countries$geo] - ifelse(countries$geo == "FR", land["FRY"], 0)

# the hot spots of one year: one file per country and year. Type 0 is a presumed vegetation fire,
# and frp is the fire radiative power of the hot spot, in megawatts
hot_spots_of <- function(year) {
  x <- read.csv(paste0(
    "https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/data/country/modis/",

    "_Greece.csv"

  x[x$type == 0, c("acq_date", "frp")]

  y_axis = list(),

1. Is Greece burning more than it used to?

Code 
area_in <- function(year) national$area[national$year == year]
last_total <- max(national$year)
worst <- head(national$year[order(-national$area)], 5)
decade_of <- function(year) {
  ifelse(year >= 2020, paste0("2020–", last_total), paste0(10 * (year %/% 10), "s"))
}
by_decade <- national |>
  mutate(decade = decade_of(year)) |>
  group_by(decade) |>
  summarise(
    years = n(),
    area_a_year = mean(area),
    fires_a_year = mean(fires),
    size_of_fire = sum(area) / sum(fires)
  )
of_decade <- function(decade, column) by_decade[[column]][by_decade$decade == decade]
last_decade <- tail(by_decade$decade, 1)
# a rank test of a trend over the years: the chance of a pattern as strong as this without one
trend_area <- cor.test(national$year, national$area, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
trend_fires <- cor.test(national$year, national$fires, method = "kendall", exact = FALSE)$p.value
# the area burnt by year, both sources side by side
both <- merge(national, effis_greece, by = "year", suffixes = c("_national", "_effis"))
ratio <- sum(both$area_effis) / sum(both$area_national)

Not steadily. The area burnt swings far more from one year to the next than it changes over the decades.

In the 45 years from 1980 to 2024, Greece’s forest fires burnt between 3,517 hectares (2003) and 225,734 (2007). Five years, 1988, 2000, 2007, 2021 and 2023, make up 36% of everything that burnt in those 45 years. The averages of the decades differ less:

Code 
knitr::kable(
  by_decade[, c("decade", "area_a_year", "fires_a_year", "size_of_fire")],
  digits = 0,
  format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
  col.names = c("Period", "Hectares burnt a year", "Fires a year", "Hectares a fire")
)
Period Hectares burnt a year Fires a year Hectares a fire
1980s 52,416 1,264 41
1990s 44,108 1,748 25
2000s 49,238 1,694 29
2010s 24,220 946 26
2020–2024 60,262 1,039 58

A rank test finds no trend in the area burnt from year to year (a pattern as strong as this one would come up by chance 16 times in 100), but a fall in the number of fires (4 in 100). The average fire grew from 25 hectares in the 1990s to 58 in 2020–2024, which is because the number of fires fell while a few of them were enormous. The number needs care, though: since 1998 the Fire Service has been responsible for forest fires, instead of the Forest Service, and the two did not count in the same way (European Commission 2001).
