Interactive chart: Area burnt by fires in Greece each year, thousand hectares

The 2010s were the quietest of the five periods, and the years from 2020 to 2024 the worst, 60,262 hectares a year, with two of the five worst years in them. But an average of five years says little when one of them burns 136,499 hectares and another 9,300.

The satellites agree, and go on to the present. EFFIS maps more land than the national statistics count, farmland included: 13% more in the years that both have, and their highs and lows are the same ones. After the country totals end, it has 47,819 hectares for 2025 and 35,454 for 2026, up to 21 November 2026. For 2025 the national figure, still provisional, is 41,540 hectares of forest land in 561 fires (JRC 2026).

2. Which were the worst years, and why?

Code 
largest <- st_drop_geometry(fires) |>
  arrange(desc(area)) |>
  head(10)
place_english <- c(
  Evvoia = "Evia",
  "Kalymnos, Karpathos, Kasos, Kos, Rodos" = "Rhodes and nearby islands",
  Ileia = "Ilia",
  "Dytiki Attiki" = "West Attica",
  "Lakonia, Messinia" = "Laconia and Messinia",
  "Anatoliki Attiki" = "East Attica",
  "Magnisia, Sporades" = "Magnesia and the Sporades"
)
latin <- places$NAME_LATN[match(largest$PROVINCE, places$NUTS_NAME)]
largest$place <- ifelse(latin %in% names(place_english), place_english[latin], latin)

Years of heat, drought or wind, when a few fires became huge. In the official record, the five worst years were:

  • 2007, the worst year for forest fires ever recorded in Greece: 225,734 hectares of forest land. Three heatwaves in a row, with more than 46 °C in some places, a long drought and strong winds; at the end of August five fires in the Peloponnese burnt 170,000 hectares and two in Evia 25,000. 69 civilians, 9 seasonal firefighters and 2 pilots died (JRC 2008).
  • 2000: 145,033 hectares, nearly three times the average of the two decades before (European Commission 2001).
  • 2023: 136,499 hectares, after the warmest July in 64 years and a heatwave from 12 to 26 July. In July there were fires in Attica, Rhodes, Evia, Corfu and near Volos, and from the middle of August in Evros and Rodopi. 23 civilians and one firefighter died (JRC 2024).
  • 1988: 110,501 hectares.
  • 2021: 108,418 hectares, in a summer that approached 46 °C, with the most notable heatwave, in length, for 35 years. Most of the large fires came between 3 and 11 August, among them those of Attica, Evia, Eastern Mani and Ancient Olympia (JRC 2022).

The deadliest fire was not among the largest. In July 2018 a fire of just over 1,000 hectares at Mati, in Attica, killed 100 people, in a year that was “relatively light” for the area burnt (JRC 2019).

Most fires are small: 80% of the outlined fires were under 100 hectares, and they made up 5% of the area. A year is bad because a few fires are huge, not because there are many.

3. Is the fire season getting longer?

Code 
# the heat that each day's fires gave off when the satellites passed, in megawatts: the sum of the
# fire radiative power of the day's hot spots
daily <- hot_spots |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(heat = sum(frp)) |>
  right_join(
    data.frame(
      date = seq(
        as.Date(paste0(min(hot_spot_years), "-01-01")),
        as.Date(paste0(max(hot_spot_years), "-12-31")),
        by = "day"
      )
    ),
    by = "date"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    heat = ifelse(is.na(heat), 0, heat),
    year = as.integer(format(date, "%Y")),
    day = as.Date(paste0("2001-", format(date, "%m-%d"))) # one calendar for every year
  )
big <- 2000 # a big-fire day: the fires gave off 2,000 megawatts or more when the satellites passed
big_days <- daily[daily$heat >= big, ]
big_days$j <- as.integer(format(big_days$date, "%j"))
big_days$summer <- as.integer(format(big_days$date, "%m")) %in% 6:9
# two periods of eleven years
periods <- list("2003–2013" = 2003:2013, "2015–2025" = 2015:2025)
period_numbers <- lapply(periods, function(years) {
  x <- big_days[big_days$year %in% years, ]
  first <- tapply(x$j, x$year, min)
  last <- tapply(x$j, x$year, max)
  list(
    per_year = nrow(x) / length(years),
    outside = 100 * mean(!x$summer),
    first = median(first),
    last = median(last)
  )
})
in_period <- function(k, what) period_numbers[[k]][[what]]
# the heat of a hot spot in each month (median of all years)
spot_heat <- tapply(hot_spots$frp, format(hot_spots$date, "%b"), median)

Not that the satellites can see. The chart shows every day since 2003, one row for each year and one square for each day. The colour is how much heat the fires of the day gave off when the satellites passed over, in megawatts: the sum of NASA’s fire radiative power of all the hot spots of the day, the presumed vegetation fires only (NASA’s description of the hot spots). The season of the big fires is the dark band of July and August. In the months around it there are many paler squares, especially in autumn, some of them probably farmers burning what is left in the fields: a hot spot gave off 10 megawatts in October and 46 in August (medians). The heat, not the number of hot spots, separates the big fires.

Code

A big-fire day here is one on which the fires gave off 2,000 megawatts or more. In 2003–2013 there were 7.4 of them a year, in 2015–2025 8.2; 6% and 4% of them came outside the months from June to September. The first big-fire day of the year came on 29 June in 2003–2013 and 12 July in 2015–2025, and the last on 27 August and 5 September (medians of the years). Nothing in these numbers says that the season has become longer.

That is not the last word. The authors of Greece’s chapter in the JRC’s report for 2025 write that climate change has “systematically extended the fire season” (JRC 2026), and hot days do come earlier and last later, at least in Athens, as Athens Is Getting Hotter shows. But the hot spots show what did burn, not how much could have: in years without a spark in a dangerous week, or with firefighters who put a fire out in time, a longer dangerous season leaves no trace in them. There are other limits too:

  • A hot spot is not a fire. It is a square about a kilometre across in which the satellite saw heat (NASA’s frequently asked questions): a big fire makes many, and farm burning and other sources of heat make some too.
  • The satellites see a fire only when they pass over, without cloud. Their orbits have changed as well: since 2020 NASA has not been able to keep Terra’s passing time from drifting earlier (NASA), so the two periods were not seen at exactly the same hours.
  • 23 years are few, and the fires of a year depend on the weather of a few weeks.

4. Where do the fires burn?

Code 
fires_area <- st_transform(fires, 3035) # an equal-area projection
regions_area <- st_transform(st_make_valid(regions), 3035)
burnt <- st_union(st_geometry(fires_area)) # the land burnt at least once
inside <- st_intersection(regions_area[, "NUTS_ID"], st_sf(geometry = burnt))
region_share <- data.frame(
  NUTS_ID = regions_area$NUTS_ID,
  land = as.numeric(st_area(regions_area)) / 1e4,
  burnt = as.numeric(st_area(inside))[match(regions_area$NUTS_ID, inside$NUTS_ID)] / 1e4
)
region_share$share <- 100 * region_share$burnt / region_share$land
region_share$name <- region_names[region_share$NUTS_ID]
region_share <- region_share[order(region_share$share), ]
in_region <- function(id, column) region_share[[column]][region_share$NUTS_ID == id]
all_land <- sum(region_share$land)
burnt_share <- 100 * sum(region_share$burnt) / all_land
# what burnt: EFFIS gives, for each fire, the share of its area that was each kind of land
cover <- c(
  BROADLEA = "forest",
  CONIFER = "forest",
  MIXED = "forest",
  SCLEROPH = "other natural land",
  TRANSIT = "other natural land",
  OTHERNATLC = "other natural land",
  AGRIAREAS = "farmland",
  ARTIFSURF = "other",
  OTHERLC = "other"
)
cover_share <- sapply(names(cover), function(column) {
  as.numeric(fires[[column]]) / 100 * fires$area
})
cover_share <- cover_share[!is.na(rowSums(cover_share)), ]
cover_total <- tapply(colSums(cover_share), cover, sum)
cover_percent <- 100 * cover_total / sum(cover_total)

Attica the most for its size, then the north-east and the Aegean. By 21 November 2026, EFFIS had outlined 1,793 fires in Greece since 2016. They burnt 5,518 square kilometres, some land more than once; 4.0% of Greece burnt at least once in those 11 years.

  coord_sf(datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Every fire that EFFIS outlined in Greece",
    subtitle = paste0(first_year, "–", last_year, ", the seven largest fires named"),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Data: EFFIS (Copernicus); boundaries: GISCO © EuroGeographics.",
      "Fires of about 30 hectares or more until 2019, smaller ones too since 2020.",
      sep = "\n"
    )
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )

Attica has burnt the most for its size: 22.7% of its land burnt at least once from 2016 to 2026, more than one square kilometre in five. The chart shows the same share for every region; that of the whole country was 4.0%. East Macedonia and Thrace has the fire of Evros, and the North Aegean, Central Greece with Evia and the South Aegean are next.

Code 
plot_ly(
  region_share,
  x = ~share,
  y = ~ factor(name, levels = name),
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "h",
  marker = list(color = ifelse(region_share$NUTS_ID == "EL30", red, gray)),
  text = percent(region_share$share, 1),
  textposition = "outside",
  cliponaxis = FALSE,
  hovertemplate = "%{y}: %{x:.1f}% of its land<extra></extra>"
) |>
  chart(
    paste0("Land burnt at least once, ", first_year, "–", last_year, ", % of the region"),
    "EFFIS outlines (Copernicus); regions: GISCO.",
    x_axis = list(range = c(0, 1.15 * max(region_share$share)), ticksuffix = "%"),
    margin = list(l = 190, t = 70, b = 70, r = 40),
    note_y = -0.1
  )

Interactive chart: Land burnt at least once, 2016–2026, % of the region

Code 
# the mainland of Attica and its neighbours: the region also has islands far to the south
window <- st_bbox(c(xmin = 22.95, ymin = 37.5, xmax = 24.2, ymax = 38.45), crs = st_crs(4326))
box <- st_bbox(st_transform(st_as_sfc(window), 2100))
# the years of the larger fires in the window, at the middle of their outlines
in_window <- st_intersects(fires_map, st_as_sfc(box), sparse = FALSE)[, 1]
attica_fires <- fires_map[in_window & fires_map$area >= 3000, ]
attica_xy <- st_coordinates(st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(attica_fires)))
attica_labels <- data.frame(x = attica_xy[, 1], y = attica_xy[, 2], label = attica_fires$year)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = regions_map, fill = "#ededed", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_sf(
    data = fires_map[order(fires_map$period), ],
    aes(fill = period, colour = period),
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = period_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = period_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = NULL), colour = "none") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = attica_labels,
    aes(x = x, y = y, label = label),
    size = 3.4,
    min.segment.length = 0,
    segment.colour = "grey40",
    label.size = 0.2,
    fill = "white",
    seed = 2
  ) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(box["xmin"], box["xmax"]),
    ylim = c(box["ymin"], box["ymax"]),
    datum = NA,
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Attica and its neighbourhood, close up",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Fires outlined ",
      first_year,
      "–",
      last_year,
      "\nLabels: the year of the fires of 3,000 hectares or more"
    ),
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Data: EFFIS (Copernicus); boundaries: GISCO © EuroGeographics."
  ) +
  theme_void(base_size = 14) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = rel(0.7), hjust = 0),
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )

What burns is mostly not forest: of the area inside the outlines, 23% was forest, 51% shrubland, grassland and other natural land, and 25% farmland; the rest, 2%, was built-up land or other cover. EFFIS gets these shares by laying the outlines on the EU’s CORINE map of land cover (EFFIS, fire damage assessment).

5. How does Greece compare with its neighbours?

Code 
compare <- effis[effis$year %in% 2006:2025, ]
compare <- merge(compare, countries[, c("code", "name", "km2")])
# 1% of a square kilometre is one hectare, so hectares per square kilometre are a percentage
compare$share <- compare$area / compare$km2
means <- compare |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(share), worst = max(share), worst_year = year[which.max(share)]) |>
  arrange(mean)
in_country <- function(name, column) means[[column]][means$name == name]
top_of_year <- compare |>
  group_by(year) |>
  slice_max(share, n = 1)
first_place <- table(top_of_year$name)
times_first <- function(name) {
  if (name %in% names(first_place)) first_place[[name]] else 0
}

Portugal burns the most for its size, and Greece is second. In the years from 2006 to 2025, the satellites found that fires burnt on average 1.14% of Portugal every year and 0.38% of Greece: 3.0 times as much. Greece was ahead of Cyprus (0.26%), Spain (0.19%), Italy (0.19%) and France (0.03%). In 3 of the 20 years Greece had the highest share of all six, in 16 Portugal.

Here EFFIS’s satellites measure all six countries in the same way, in fires of about 30 hectares or more, so the comparison does not depend on how each country counts.

Code 
set.seed(2026)
compare$position <- match(compare$name, means$name) + runif(nrow(compare), -0.17, 0.17)
plot_ly() |>
  add_markers(
    data = compare,
    x = ~share,
    y = ~position,
    marker = list(
      color = ifelse(compare$name == "Greece", red, gray),
      size = 9,
      line = list(color = "white", width = 1)
    ),
    text = ~ paste0(name, " ", year, ": ", two(share), "%"),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  add_markers(
    data = means,
    x = ~mean,
    y = ~ match(name, means$name),
    marker = list(
      color = ifelse(means$name == "Greece", red, dark_gray),
      symbol = "line-ns-open",
      size = 26,
      line = list(width = 4)
    ),
    text = ~ paste0(name, ", average 2006–2025: ", two(mean), "% a year"),
    hovertemplate = "%{text}<extra></extra>",
    showlegend = FALSE
  ) |>
  chart(
    "Land burnt each year, % of the country, 2006–2025",
    paste0(
      "EFFIS, fires of about 30 ha or more; areas of the countries: Eurostat, reg_area3. ",
      "Dots: years. Bars: averages."
    ),
    x_axis = list(rangemode = "tozero", ticksuffix = "%"),
    y_axis = list(
      tickvals = seq_len(nrow(means)),
      ticktext = means$name,
      range = c(0.4, nrow(means) + 0.6),
      zeroline = FALSE
    ),
    annotations = lapply(seq_len(nrow(means)), function(i) {
      list(
        x = means$worst[i],
        y = i,
        text = paste0(means$worst_year[i]),
        showarrow = FALSE,
        xanchor = "left",
        xshift = 8,
        font = list(size = 12, color = dark_gray)
      )
    }),
    margin = list(l = 80, t = 70, b = 90, r = 40),
    note_y = -0.14
  )

Interactive chart: Land burnt each year, % of the country, 2006–2025

The number beside each country’s row marks its worst year: 2017 in Portugal, 2007 in Greece, 2025 in Cyprus.

So, what does it mean?

  1. Greece does not burn steadily more, but it burns in bursts. Five years, 1988, 2000, 2007, 2021 and 2023, have 36% of everything that burnt from 1980 to 2024, and there is no trend in the total.
  2. A bad year is made of a few enormous fires. The ten largest fires made up 46% of the area of the 1,793 fires outlined since 2016.
  3. The satellites see no longer season of big fires, though the heat that makes a fire dangerous does last longer, and the Greek authors of the JRC’s report say that the season has.
  4. Attica burns the most for its size: more than a fifth of its land burnt at least once since 2016.
  5. Greece is second to Portugal. Every year it burns about 0.38% of its land on average, against 0.19% in Spain and 0.19% in Italy.

What this does not show. It does not say what started the fires, how well they were fought, or what the climate will do to the next ones. The national statistics and the satellites do not count the same things, the satellites miss the small fires, and the outlines show where a fire burnt, not how severely. And the fires are counted in hectares here, which do not measure the people, the homes and the animals lost in them.

For the heat that dries out the land, see Athens Is Getting Hotter; for the temperature of the world, the NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly.

Sources

  • JRC, country totals of the area burnt and the number of forest fires in each country, 1980–2024 (the file report_2024.xlsx of EFFIS, Data and services; CC BY 4.0).
  • EFFIS (Copernicus Emergency Management Service, JRC): the statistics portal, with the area burnt in each country every year since 2006; the outlines of the burnt areas in Greece since 2016, from its map service; how they are mapped, rapid damage assessment and fire damage assessment.
  • JRC (10 April 2024), Wildfires: 2023 among the worst in the EU in this century.
  • European Commission (2001), Forest fires in Southern Europe 2000 (the year 2000; who counts the fires in Greece).
  • JRC (2008), Forest fires in Europe 2007 (Greece in 2007).
  • JRC (2019), Forest fires in Europe, Middle East and North Africa 2018 (Mati).
  • JRC (2022), Forest fires in Europe, Middle East and North Africa 2021 (Greece in 2021).
  • JRC (2024), Forest fires in Europe, Middle East and North Africa 2023 (Greece in 2023).
  • JRC (2025), Forest fires in Europe, Middle East and North Africa 2024 (what Greece’s statistics count).
  • JRC (2026), Forest fires in Europe, Middle East and North Africa 2025 (what Greece’s authors say of the fire season).
  • NASA FIRMS, NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System, part of its LANCE: the hot spots of each country and year seen by MODIS on Terra and Aqua; what the attributes of the hot spots mean; and its frequently asked questions.
  • NASA, Terra’s orbital drift.
  • GISCO (European Commission), NUTS regions of 2024, © EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries.
  • Eurostat, reg_area3 (the area of countries and regions).

Rendered with R 4.6.2 · dplyr · ggplot2 · plotly · sf

item.title: The Greeks Who Left: How Many, Where To, and Who Came Back
item.description: Emigration from Greece since the debt crisis, in Eurostat data: how many left, who they were, where they went, who came back, and whether it was a brain drain.
item.content:encoded:
Emigration from Greece since the debt crisis, in Eurostat data: how many left, who they were, where they went, who came back, and whether it was a brain drain.

What is this?

From 2010 until August 2018, Greece lived on rescue loans, through three programmes (ESM). In those years many people left the country. This story asks five questions about them:

  1. How many people left Greece, and when?
  2. Who left? Their age and sex, and whether they were Greek citizens or foreigners.
  3. Where did they go?
  4. Did they come back?
  5. Was it a brain drain? Did those who left have more education than those who stayed?

Fewer and Older shows how births, deaths and migration change the size and the age of Greece’s population. This story follows the people who left.

The data come from Eurostat, the statistical office of the EU, and are downloaded when the page is rendered:

  • Greece’s figures on the people who leave the country and those who arrive, each year, from ELSTAT, the Hellenic Statistical Authority: by age and sex (migr_emi2), by citizenship (migr_emi1ctz, migr_imm1ctz), by country of birth (migr_imm3ctb) and by where they went (migr_emi5nxt); with the population (demo_pjan) and unemployment (une_rt_a).
  • The figures of the countries they moved to: the Greek citizens who arrive in each European country and those who leave it (migr_imm1ctz, migr_emi1ctz), and those who live there (migr_pop1ctz).
  • The Labour Force Survey, a survey of households in the countries of the EU and EFTA, which asks people where they were born and what education they have (lfst_lmbpcobed, edat_lfs_9912).

Most of these figures are estimates. In the statistics of the EU, an emigrant is someone who moves abroad for at least 12 months (Eurostat). Greece does not count them: nobody has to tell the authorities that they are leaving, so ELSTAT calls its data on emigration “essentially non-existent” and estimates it instead. For 2011 to 2021, emigration is the number of people who must have left for the population, as revised after the census of 2021, to add up with the births, the deaths and the people who arrived. Since 2022, it is worked out from the number of people that Germany counts arriving from Greece (ELSTAT). The countries the emigrants go to count the people who arrive, but not all in the same way: Norway, for example, counts as migrants the people who move for six months (Eurostat).

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("eurostat", "plotly", "jsonlite"))
library(eurostat)
library(plotly)

The data

Code 
# a Eurostat dataset, without its missing values, in the order of the years
eurostat_values<-function(id,filters) {
  x<-get_eurostat(id,filters=filters,time_format="num",cache=FALSE)
  x<-as.data.frame(x[!is.na(x$values),])
  result<-x[order(x$time),]
  return(result)
}
# the years that Eurostat flags as a break in one series (flag b); the eurostat package leaves the
# flags out when it filters, so they come from Eurostat's own API, in JSON-stat
breaks_in<-function(id,filters) {
  api<-"https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/api/dissemination/statistics/1.0/data/"
  query<-paste(paste0(names(filters),"=",unlist(filters)),collapse="&")
  x<-jsonlite::fromJSON(paste0(api,id,"?",query))
  years<-names(sort(unlist(x$dimension$time$category$index)))
  flags<-unlist(x$status)
  result<-as.numeric(years[as.integer(names(flags)[flags=="b"])+1])
  return(result)
}
# all ages, both sexes, age in completed years, numbers of people
everyone<-list(age="TOTAL",sex="T",agedef="COMPLET",unit="NR")
# Greece: the people who left each year, by sex and single year of age, and the breaks in the series
emigration<-eurostat_values("migr_emi2",list(geo="EL",agedef="COMPLET",unit="NR"))
breaks<-breaks_in("migr_emi2",c(list(geo="EL"),everyone))
# Greece: everyone (TOTAL) and the Greek citizens (NAT) among the people who left and among those
# who arrived; the people who arrived who were born in Greece (NAT); and the people who left, by
# group of country of next residence: another EU country, or a country outside the EU
left<-eurostat_values("migr_emi1ctz",c(list(geo="EL",citizen=c("NAT","TOTAL")),everyone))
came<-eurostat_values("migr_imm1ctz",c(list(geo="EL",citizen=c("NAT","TOTAL")),everyone))
came_born<-eurostat_values("migr_imm3ctb",c(list(geo="EL",c_birth="NAT"),everyone))
next_residence<-eurostat_values("migr_emi5nxt",list(geo="EL",unit="NR"))
# every country that reports them, but not Greece itself or the EU as a whole: the Greek citizens
# (EL) who arrived there each year, those who left, and those who lived there on 1 January
abroad<-function(x) {
  result<-x[!x$geo%in%c("EL","EU27_2020"),]
  return(result)
}
greeks_came<-abroad(eurostat_values("migr_imm1ctz",c(list(citizen="EL"),everyone)))
greeks_left<-abroad(eurostat_values("migr_emi1ctz",c(list(citizen="EL"),everyone)))
greeks_living<-abroad(eurostat_values("migr_pop1ctz",
                                      list(citizen="EL",age="TOTAL",sex="T",unit="NR")))
# Greece: the population on 1 January, by sex and single year of age, and unemployment, % of the
# labour force aged 15 to 74
population<-eurostat_values("demo_pjan",list(geo="EL",sex=c("T","M","F"),unit="NR"))
unemployment<-eurostat_values("une_rt_a",list(geo="EL",age="Y15-74",sex="T",unit="PC_ACT"))
# Labour Force Survey: the people born in Greece who live in another EU or EFTA country, by age
# group and education, thousands; and those who live in Greece, aged 15 to 64, by education, %
born_abroad<-eurostat_values("lfst_lmbpcobed",list(c_birth="EL",c_resid="EU27_2020_EFTA"))
born_home<-eurostat_values("edat_lfs_9912",list(geo="EL",c_birth="NAT",sex="T",age="Y15-64"))
# the names of the countries of the EU and EFTA, and of the United Kingdom
country_name<-c(setNames(eu_countries$name,eu_countries$code),
                setNames(efta_countries$name,efta_countries$code),UK="United Kingdom")
Code 
# one series of a dataset, in the order of the years
by_year<-function(x,years) {
  result<-x$values[match(years,x$time)]
  return(result)
}
# Greece, year by year: the people who left, all of them and the Greek citizens; the people who
# arrived, all of them, the Greek citizens and those born in Greece; and the population
total_left<-emigration[emigration$age=="TOTAL"&emigration$sex=="T",]
flows<-data.frame(year=total_left$time,left=total_left$values)
flows$left_greek<-by_year(left[left$citizen=="NAT",],flows$year)
flows$came<-by_year(came[came$citizen=="TOTAL",],flows$year)
flows$came_greek<-by_year(came[came$citizen=="NAT",],flows$year)
flows$came_born<-by_year(came_born,flows$year)
flows$net_greek<-flows$came_greek-flows$left_greek
everyone_living<-population[population$age=="TOTAL"&population$sex=="T",]
flows$population<-by_year(everyone_living,flows$year)
latest<-max(flows$year)
flow<-function(column,year) {
  result<-flows[[column]][match(year,flows$year)]
  return(result)
}
# the years of the rescue loans: the first programme started in 2010, and the third and last ended
# in August 2018 (ESM)
rescue<-c(2010,2018)
rescue_years<-rescue[1]:rescue[2]
Code 
greek_red<-"#d62728"
blue<-"#1f77b4"
orange<-"#ff7f0e"
gray<-"#9e9e9e"
light_gray<-"#ebebeb"
dark_gray<-"#6b6b6b" # also the color of the notes
# the source of a chart, as a note under it, and the common layout
chart<-function(p,title,source,y_title="",y_axis=list(),x_axis=list(),annotations=list(),
                margin=list(t=70,b=90),note_y=-0.16,...) {
  note<-list(text=paste("Source:",source),xref="paper",yref="paper",x=0,y=note_y,xanchor="left",
             yanchor="top",showarrow=FALSE,font=list(size=11,color=dark_gray))
  result<-layout(p,title=list(text=title,x=0.02,xanchor="left",y=0.97,yanchor="top"),
                 yaxis=c(list(title=y_title),y_axis),xaxis=c(list(title=""),x_axis),
                 margin=margin,annotations=c(annotations,list(note)),...) %>%
    config(displaylogo=FALSE)
  return(result)
}
legend_top<-list(orientation="h",x=0,y=1.02,yanchor="bottom")
# the years of the rescue loans, shaded behind the data
rescue_band<-list(type="rect",xref="x",yref="paper",x0=rescue[1]-0.5,x1=rescue[2]+0.5,y0=0,y1=1,
                  fillcolor=light_gray,line=list(width=0),layer="below")
shaded<-paste0("Shaded: the rescue loans, ",rescue[1],"–",rescue[2],".")
# numbers in the text
number<-function(x) {
  result<-format(x,big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
thousands<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,-3),big.mark=",",scientific=FALSE,trim=TRUE)
  return(result)
}
percent<-function(x,digits=0) {
  result<-paste0(format(round(x,digits),nsmall=digits),"%")
  return(result)
}
one<-function(x) {
  result<-format(round(x,1),nsmall=1)
  return(result)
}
and_list<-function(x) {
  if(length(x)<2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  result<-paste(paste(head(x,-1),collapse=", "),"and",tail(x,1))
  return(result)
}
# years as ranges: 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2019 give "2014–2016, 2019"
years_text<-function(years) {
  years<-sort(unique(years))
  starts<-years[c(TRUE,diff(years)>1)]
  ends<-years[c(diff(years)>1,TRUE)]
  result<-paste(ifelse(starts==ends,starts,paste0(starts,"–",ends)),collapse=", ")
  return(result)
}

1. How many people left Greece, and when?

Code 
in_2000s<-flows$left[flows$year%in%2000:2009]
peak_year<-flows$year[which.max(flows$left)]
per_1000<-function(year) {
  result<-1000*flow("left",year)/flow("population",year)
  return(result)
}
left_rescue<-sum(flows$left[flows$year%in%rescue_years])
left_greek_rescue<-sum(flows$left_greek[flows$year%in%rescue_years])
over_100k<-flows$year[flows$left>1e5]
# the last year in which more people left than the year before: the fall since goes on to the
# latest year
rose<-flows$year[c(FALSE,diff(flows$left)>=0)]
falling_since<-max(rose)
jobless<-function(year) {
  result<-unemployment$values[unemployment$time==year]
  return(result)
}
jobless_peak<-unemployment$time[which.max(unemployment$values)]
jobless_latest<-max(unemployment$time)

About 41,000 a year in the 2000s; more than 100,000 a year in 2011–2019.

From 2000 to 2009, between 37,433 and 46,993 people left Greece each year. Then came the crisis: 62,041 left in 2010, 106,398 in 2011 and 135,073 in 2012, the most since the figures start in 1991: 12.2 of every 1,000 people who lived in Greece. In the years of the rescue loans, from 2010 to 2018, 1,018,000 people left, 527,000 of them Greek citizens.

The number has fallen every year since 2018, to 78,014 in 2024, 1.9 times the average of the 2000s. It rose with unemployment, which went from 9.8% of the labour force in 2009 to 27.8% in 2013; both have fallen since, unemployment to 8.9% in 2025 (Eurostat, une_rt_a).

Code 
bars<-flows[!is.na(flows$left),]
rescue_label<-list(x=mean(rescue),y=1,xref="x",yref="paper",yanchor="bottom",
                   text=paste0("Rescue loans, ",rescue[1],"–",rescue[2]),showarrow=FALSE,
                   font=list(size=12,color=dark_gray))
plot_ly(bars,x=~year,y=~left/1000,type="bar",name="People who left",
        marker=list(color=greek_red,
                    pattern=list(shape=ifelse(bars$year%in%breaks,"/",""),fillmode="overlay",
                                 fgcolor="white")),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart("People who left Greece each year, thousands",
        "Eurostat, migr_emi2 (estimates of ELSTAT). Striped: a break in the series.","Thousands",
        annotations=list(rescue_label),shapes=list(rescue_band),showlegend=FALSE)

Interactive chart: People who left Greece each year, thousands

Eurostat marks a break in the series in 2002, 2008 and 2010 (the striped bars): the method changed, so the years before and after a break cannot be compared closely.

2. Who left?

Code 
# the age of a Eurostat age code: Y_LT1 is under one, Y_OPEN and Y_GE100 are the oldest, and the
# codes of totals, such as TOTAL, give NA
age_of<-function(code) {
  age<-suppressWarnings(as.numeric(sub("^Y","",code)))
  age[code=="Y_LT1"]<-0
  age[code%in%c("Y_OPEN","Y_GE100")]<-100
  result<-age
  return(result)
}
group_names<-c("0–14","15–19","20–24","25–29","30–34","35–39","40–44","45–49","50–54","55–59",
               "60–64","65+")
age_group<-function(code) {
  result<-cut(age_of(code),c(-1,14,19,24,29,34,39,44,49,54,59,64,Inf),labels=group_names)
  return(result)
}
# the people who left out of every 1,000 of the same sex and age group who lived in Greece on
# 1 January
rates<-function(year,sex) {
  out<-emigration[emigration$time==year&emigration$sex==sex,]
  living<-population[population$time==year&population$sex==sex,]
  result<-1000*tapply(out$values,age_group(out$age),sum)/
          tapply(living$values,age_group(living$age),sum)
  return(result)
}
rate<-function(year,sex,group) {
  result<-rates(year,sex)[[group]]
  return(result)
}
# the age that half of the people are younger than or as old as
median_age<-function(x) {
  x<-x[!is.na(age_of(x$age)),]
  x<-x[order(age_of(x$age)),]
  result<-age_of(x$age)[which(cumsum(x$values)>=sum(x$values)/2)[1]]
  return(result)
}
men_left<-emigration[emigration$age=="TOTAL"&emigration$sex=="M",]
men_share<-data.frame(year=men_left$time,
                      share=round(100*men_left$values/flow("left",men_left$time),1))
# the longest run of years in which the share of men is the same
runs<-rle(men_share$share)
run_end<-cumsum(runs$lengths)[which.max(runs$lengths)]
same_years<-men_share$year[(run_end-max(runs$lengths)+1):run_end]
middle_aged<-c("35–39","40–44","45–49","50–54")
men_to_women<-rates(peak_year,"M")[middle_aged]/rates(peak_year,"F")[middle_aged]

Mostly people in their twenties and thirties, and in the worst years, mostly men.

In 2012, 65% of the people who left Greece were men. Half of them were 32 or younger, while half of the people who lived in Greece were 41 or older.

The chart counts the people who left out of every 1,000 of the same sex and age who lived in Greece at the start of the year. In 2012, 44 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29 left, and 28 of every 1,000 women. From 35 to 54, men left at 2.3 to 3.5 times the rate of women. In 2024, fewer left: 31 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29, and 34 of every 1,000 women.

Code 
profile<-data.frame(group=factor(group_names,levels=group_names))
lines<-data.frame(year=c(peak_year,peak_year,latest,latest),
                  sex=c("M","F","M","F"),
                  name=paste(c("Men,","Women,","Men,","Women,"),
                             c(peak_year,peak_year,latest,latest)),
                  color=c(blue,orange,blue,orange),
                  dash=c("solid","solid","dot","dot"))
p<-plot_ly(profile,x=~group)
for(k in seq_len(nrow(lines))) {
  p<-add_trace(p,y=as.numeric(rates(lines$year[k],lines$sex[k])),type="scatter",
               mode="lines+markers",name=lines$name[k],
               line=list(color=lines$color[k],width=3,dash=lines$dash[k]),
               marker=list(color=lines$color[k]),
               hovertemplate=paste0("Aged %{x}: %{y:.1f} per 1,000<extra>",lines$name[k],
                                    "</extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("People who left Greece, per 1,000 of their sex and age",
        "Eurostat, migr_emi2 and demo_pjan (estimates of ELSTAT).","Per 1,000",
        y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=100,b=90))

Interactive chart: People who left Greece, per 1,000 of their sex and age

These shares are estimates too. ELSTAT does not measure the age and sex of the people who leave: it spreads its estimate of the total with fixed proportions (ELSTAT). In every year from 2016 to 2020, for example, 56.7% of those who left were men. So the chart shows the broad picture, not the changes from one year to the next.

Greek citizens and foreigners

Code 
citizens<-flows[!is.na(flows$left_greek),]
citizens$left_foreign<-citizens$left-citizens$left_greek
greek_share<-function(year) {
  result<-100*flow("left_greek",year)/flow("left",year)
  return(result)
}
mostly_greek<-citizens$year[citizens$left_greek>citizens$left_foreign]
most_greek<-citizens$year[which.max(citizens$left_greek/citizens$left)]
foreign<-function(year) {
  result<-citizens$left_foreign[citizens$year==year]
  return(result)
}

In 2008, 44% of the people who left Greece were Greek citizens; the rest were foreigners who had lived in Greece. In 2011–2017, most of those who left were Greek citizens: 58% in 2011, and 70,696 people in 2012. Foreigners left in larger numbers too, 64,377 in 2012 against 23,956 in 2008. In 2024, 32,141 Greek citizens left, 41% of all who left.

Code 
plot_ly(citizens,x=~year,y=~left_greek/1000,type="bar",name="Greek citizens",
        marker=list(color=greek_red),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Greek citizens</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~left_foreign/1000,name="Foreign citizens",marker=list(color=gray),
            hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Foreign citizens</extra>") %>%
  chart("People who left Greece, by citizenship, thousands",
        paste("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz (estimates of ELSTAT).",shaded),"Thousands",
        shapes=list(rescue_band),barmode="stack",legend=legend_top)

Interactive chart: People who left Greece, by citizenship, thousands

3. Where did they go?

Code 
next_year<-max(next_residence$time)
went<-function(partner) {
  result<-next_residence$values[next_residence$partner==partner&next_residence$time==next_year]
  return(result)
}
to_eu<-went("EU27_2020_FOR")
outside<-went("NEU27_2020_FOR")
# the years with figures for Germany, the main destination, after the gap of the crisis years
since<-min(greeks_came$time[greeks_came$geo=="DE"&greeks_came$time>2008])
window<-since:latest
counted<-greeks_came[greeks_came$time%in%window,]
destinations<-aggregate(values~geo,counted,sum)
destinations<-destinations[order(-destinations$values),]
left_window<-sum(flows$left_greek[flows$year%in%window])
counted_total<-sum(destinations$values)
not_counted<-left_window-counted_total
shown<-head(destinations,10)
other<-counted_total-sum(shown$values)
# a country's name, with the years it has figures for when they are not all the years
label<-function(geo) {
  name<-if(geo%in%names(country_name)) country_name[[geo]] else geo
  years<-counted$time[counted$geo==geo]
  if(length(years)==length(window)) name else paste0(name," (",years_text(years),")")
}
shown$label<-sapply(shown$geo,label)
share_of_counted<-function(geo) {
  result<-100*shown$values[shown$geo==geo]/counted_total
  return(result)
}
# the countries of the EU and EFTA without figures on Greek citizens arriving in these years
silent<-setdiff(names(country_name),c(unique(counted$geo),"EL","UK"))
uk_years<-counted$time[counted$geo=="UK"]
uk_rank<-function(year) {
  in_year<-counted[counted$time==year,]
  result<-sum(in_year$values>in_year$values[in_year$geo=="UK"])+1
  return(result)
}

Above all to Germany. But the countries they went to counted only 55% of them arriving.

Greece’s figures say only whether the people who left went to another EU country or outside the EU, not to which country: in 2024, 28,047 went to another EU country and 49,967 outside the EU, foreigners leaving Greece included (migr_emi5nxt).

So the chart looks from the other end, at the countries that count the people who arrive, by citizenship. It follows the 545,000 Greek citizens who left Greece from 2014 to 2024, the years with figures for Germany, to the countries that counted them arriving.

Code 
# where they went, from top to bottom: not counted, the countries from the most, the others
went_to<-data.frame(label=c(paste0("Not counted arriving in Europe: ",thousands(not_counted)),
                            paste0(shown$label,": ",thousands(shown$values)),
                            paste0("Other European countries: ",thousands(other))),
                    value=c(not_counted,shown$values,other),
                    color=c(gray,rep(blue,nrow(shown)+1)),
                    link=c("rgba(158, 158, 158, 0.35)",
                           rep("rgba(31, 119, 180, 0.3)",nrow(shown)+1)))
# the place of each node, as a share of the width and of the height (its middle), fixed so that
# plotly keeps this order: the nodes share the height of the plot, less a gap of `pad` pixels
# between two
pad<-10
margin<-list(t=60,b=80,l=10,r=10)
# opts_chunk has the dots per inch that set the height of a plotly chart; opts_current has them
# multiplied by fig.retina
dpi<-knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi")
plot_height<-knitr::opts_current$get("fig.height")*dpi-margin$t-margin$b
gap<-pad/plot_height
node_height<-went_to$value/sum(went_to$value)*(1-gap*(nrow(went_to)-1))
middle<-cumsum(node_height+gap)-gap-node_height/2
plot_ly(type="sankey",orientation="h",arrangement="fixed",valueformat=",.0f",
        textfont=list(size=12),
        node=list(label=c(paste0("Left Greece: ",thousands(left_window)),went_to$label),
                  color=c(dark_gray,went_to$color),x=c(0.001,rep(0.999,nrow(went_to))),
                  y=c(0.5,middle),pad=pad,thickness=16,line=list(width=0),
                  hovertemplate="%{label}<extra></extra>"),
        link=list(source=rep(0,nrow(went_to)),target=seq_len(nrow(went_to)),
                  value=went_to$value,color=went_to$link,
                  hovertemplate="%{target.label}<extra></extra>")) %>%
  chart(paste0("Where the Greek citizens who left went, ",since,"–",latest),
        paste0("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz (Greece's estimate) and ",
               "migr_imm1ctz (the countries' counts). ",
               "In brackets: the years with figures."),margin=margin,note_y=-0.04)

Interactive chart: Where the Greek citizens who left went, 2014–2024

Germany counted 153,000 Greek citizens arriving, 51% of all those counted in Europe, and the Netherlands 37,000, 12%. The United Kingdom has figures only for 2015, when 12,148 Greek citizens arrived there, the most after Germany; Eurostat’s figures for the United Kingdom stop with its withdrawal from the EU (Eurostat).

The other 247,000, 45% of those who left, were not counted arriving in any European country. They may have gone to countries outside Europe; to European countries that have no figures on Greek citizens arriving, Cyprus, Ireland, Malta, Poland, Portugal and Spain; or to countries in years without figures, such as the United Kingdom after 2015. And part of the gap is the difference between Greece’s estimate and the counts of the other countries. The figures cannot tell how much of each.

Code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(c(shown$label,"Other European countries"),number(c(shown$values,other))),
             col.names=c("Country (years with figures)",
                         paste0("Greek citizens who arrived, ",since,"–",latest)),align="lr")
Country (years with figures) Greek citizens who arrived, 2014–2024
Germany 153,421
Netherlands 36,650
United Kingdom (2015) 12,148
Sweden 12,123
Belgium (2014–2019, 2023–2024) 10,668
Switzerland (2014–2020) 10,566
France 10,250
Austria 9,371
Norway 6,176
Italy 5,976
Other European countries 30,707

Where they live now

Code 
living<-greeks_living[greeks_living$geo%in%names(country_name),]
newest<-do.call(rbind,lapply(split(living,living$geo),function(x) x[which.max(x$time),]))
newest<-head(newest[order(-newest$values),],15)
living_year<-max(newest$time)
newest$label<-ifelse(newest$time==living_year,country_name[newest$geo],
                     paste0(country_name[newest$geo]," (",newest$time,")"))
newest<-newest[order(newest$values),]
newest$label<-factor(newest$label,levels=newest$label)
lived<-function(geo,year) {
  result<-living$values[living$geo==geo&living$time==year]
  return(result)
}
uk_last<-max(living$time[living$geo=="UK"])
uk_place<-sum(living$values[living$time==uk_last]>lived("UK",uk_last))+1

The countries also count the people who live there, by citizenship. Germany had by far the most Greek citizens: 298,398 on 1 January 2025. Its Greek community was as large before the crisis, 297,668 in 2010: the number of people living in a country does not grow by all who arrive, as people also leave, die, or take the citizenship of the country. In the Netherlands, the number of Greek citizens grew from 7,781 in 2010 to 32,924 in 2025. The United Kingdom had 74,970 in 2019, its last year in the figures, the most after Germany.

Code 
plot_ly(newest,x=~values,y=~label,type="bar",orientation="h",marker=list(color=blue),
        text=number(newest$values),textposition="outside",cliponaxis=FALSE,
        hovertemplate="%{y}: %{x:,.0f}<extra></extra>") %>%
  chart(paste0("Greek citizens living elsewhere in Europe, 1 January ",living_year),
        "Eurostat, migr_pop1ctz. In brackets: the last year with figures.",
        x_axis=list(range=c(0,1.2*max(newest$values)),tickformat=","),
        margin=list(l=150,t=70,b=70,r=30),note_y=-0.08)

Interactive chart: Greek citizens living elsewhere in Europe, 1 January 2025

4. Did they come back?

Code 
turn<-min(flows$year[flows$year>rescue[1]&!is.na(flows$net_greek)&flows$net_greek>0])
after_turn<-flows$year[flows$year>=turn]
before_turn<-max(flows$year[flows$year<rescue[1]&!is.na(flows$net_greek)&flows$net_greek>0])
lost<--sum(flows$net_greek[flows$year%in%rescue[1]:(turn-1)])
gained<-sum(flows$net_greek[flows$year%in%after_turn])
born_elsewhere<-flow("came_greek",latest)-flow("came_born",latest)
germany<-data.frame(year=min(greeks_came$time[greeks_came$geo=="DE"]):latest)
germany$came<-by_year(greeks_came[greeks_came$geo=="DE",],germany$year)
germany$left<-by_year(greeks_left[greeks_left$geo=="DE",],germany$year)
both<-germany[!is.na(germany$came)&!is.na(germany$left),]
before<-both[both$year<rescue[1],]
restart<-min(both$year[both$year>rescue[1]])
since_restart<-both[both$year>=restart,]
peak_in<-since_restart$year[which.max(since_restart$came-since_restart$left)]
more_left<-since_restart$year[since_restart$left>since_restart$came]
# the years without figures between the last year before the crisis and the restart
gap_years<-(max(before$year)+1):(restart-1)
in_germany<-function(column,year) {
  result<-germany[[column]][germany$year==year]
  return(result)
}
left_germany_first<-length(more_left)==1&&more_left==latest

Some have. Since 2023, more Greek citizens move to Greece each year than leave it, by ELSTAT’s estimates, but they have made up only a small part of what the crisis took.

From 2010 to 2022, 328,000 more Greek citizens left Greece than moved to it. In 2023 and 2024, for the first time since 2009, more moved to Greece than left: 9,160 and 19,852 more. Together, that is 9% of what was lost from 2010 to 2022.

Not all the Greek citizens who move to Greece were born there: in 2024, 51,993 Greek citizens moved to Greece, but only 44,336 people born in Greece, of any citizenship, so at least 7,657 of the Greek citizens were born abroad. The people born in Greece who move to Greece are coming back to the country of their birth: 44,336 in 2024, against 27,604 in 2022 and 17,350 in 2008.

Code 
greek_flows<-flows[!is.na(flows$left_greek),]
plot_ly(greek_flows,x=~year,y=~left_greek/1000,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
        name="Greek citizens who left Greece",line=list(color=greek_red,width=3),
        marker=list(color=greek_red),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Greek citizens who left</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~came_greek/1000,name="Greek citizens who moved to Greece",
            line=list(color=blue,width=3),marker=list(color=blue),
            hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Greek citizens who came</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~came_born/1000,name="People born in Greece who moved to Greece",
            line=list(color=blue,width=2,dash="dot"),
            marker=list(color=blue,symbol="circle-open"),
            hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Born in Greece, came</extra>") %>%
  chart("Leaving Greece and moving to Greece, thousands a year",
        paste("Eurostat, migr_emi1ctz, migr_imm1ctz and migr_imm3ctb (estimates of ELSTAT).",
              shaded),"Thousands",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),shapes=list(rescue_band),
        legend=legend_top,margin=list(t=110,b=90))

Interactive chart: Leaving Greece and moving to Greece, thousands a year

These figures are ELSTAT’s estimates as well. Since 2022, it estimates the people who arrive, apart from those granted protection, such as refugees, with a model: from the number of the year before and the growth of the economy. It splits them by citizenship and country of birth as in the census of 2021 (ELSTAT).

A check from Germany

Germany counts the Greek citizens who move there and those who leave, and its figures point the same way. Before the crisis, more Greek citizens left Germany than moved there, in every year with figures from 1998 to 2008: in 2008, 16,079 left and 8,266 arrived. There are no figures for 2009–2013. In 2015, 18,970 Greek citizens moved to Germany and 5,796 left it. In 2024, 8,833 moved there and 9,025 left: for the first time since the figures restart in 2014, more left than came.

Code 
plot_ly(germany,x=~year,y=~came/1000,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
        name="Greek citizens who moved to Germany",line=list(color=greek_red,width=3),
        marker=list(color=greek_red),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Moved to Germany</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~left/1000,name="Greek citizens who left Germany",line=list(color=blue,width=3),
            marker=list(color=blue),
            hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>Left Germany</extra>") %>%
  chart("Greek citizens arriving in and leaving Germany, thousands",
        paste0("Eurostat, migr_imm1ctz and migr_emi1ctz (figures of Germany; none for ",
               years_text(gap_years),"). ",shaded),"Thousands",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),
        shapes=list(rescue_band),legend=legend_top)

Interactive chart: Greek citizens arriving in and leaving Germany, thousands

5. Was it a brain drain?

Code 
education_names<-c("ED5-8"="Higher education","ED3_4"="Upper secondary",
                   "ED0-2"="At most lower secondary")
education_colors<-c("ED5-8"=greek_red,"ED3_4"=gray,"ED0-2"=dark_gray)
adults_abroad<-born_abroad[born_abroad$age=="Y20-64"&born_abroad$time>=2005,]
level<-function(isced,year) {
  result<-adults_abroad$values[adults_abroad$isced11==isced&adults_abroad$time==year]
  return(result)
}
edu_latest<-max(adults_abroad$time)
# the share with higher education: abroad, of those whose education is known; in Greece, as Eurostat
# publishes it
working_age<-born_abroad[born_abroad$age=="Y15-64"&born_abroad$time>=2005,]
known<-working_age[working_age$isced11%in%names(education_names),]
share<-aggregate(values~time,known,sum)
names(share)<-c("year","known")
share$abroad<-100*by_year(known[known$isced11=="ED5-8",],share$year)/share$known
share$home<-by_year(born_home[born_home$isced11=="ED5-8",],share$year)
share<-share[!is.na(share$home),]
behind<-share$year[share$abroad<=share$home]
ahead_since<-max(behind)+1
first_share<-min(share$year)
last_share<-max(share$year)
higher<-function(where,year) {
  result<-share[[where]][share$year==year]
  return(result)
}

Partly. The people born in Greece who live elsewhere in Europe used to have less education than those at home; now they have more, and many more of them have a degree.

No statistic follows the people who left, so none can say exactly how much education they had. The nearest is Eurostat’s Labour Force Survey, which counts the people born in Greece, aged 20 to 64, who live in another EU or EFTA country, by the highest level of education they finished.

From 2010 to 2024, the number of them with higher education, a university degree or similar, rose from about 40,000 to 113,000: 2.8 times as many. The number with at most lower secondary schooling hardly changed: about 102,000 in 2010 and 98,000 in 2024.

Code 
p<-plot_ly()
for(k in names(education_names)) {
  p<-add_trace(p,data=adults_abroad[adults_abroad$isced11==k,],x=~time,y=~values,type="scatter",
               mode="lines+markers",name=education_names[[k]],
               line=list(color=education_colors[[k]],width=if(k=="ED5-8") 3 else 2),
               marker=list(color=education_colors[[k]]),
               hovertemplate=paste0("%{x}: %{y:.1f} thousand<extra>",education_names[[k]],
                                    "</extra>"))
}
p %>%
  chart("Greek-born aged 20 to 64 in other EU and EFTA countries",
        paste("Eurostat, lfst_lmbpcobed (Labour Force Survey), by education.",shaded),"Thousands",
        y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero"),shapes=list(rescue_band),legend=legend_top)

Interactive chart: Greek-born aged 20 to 64 in other EU and EFTA countries

So the Greeks abroad have changed. In 2005, 12% of the people born in Greece aged 15 to 64 who lived in another EU or EFTA country had higher education, against 18% of those who lived in Greece. In 2024, it was 36% against 32%, and those abroad have had more education than those at home in every year since 2017. To change the Greeks abroad so much, those who left in the crisis must have had much more education than those who had left before them. That they also had more than those who stayed is likely, but the survey cannot prove it: it counts the people who live abroad, not those who left. The share with higher education rose in Greece too, from 18% to 32%.

Code 
plot_ly(share,x=~year,y=~abroad,type="scatter",mode="lines+markers",
        name="Living in another EU or EFTA country",line=list(color=greek_red,width=3),
        marker=list(color=greek_red),
        hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>Living abroad</extra>") %>%
  add_trace(y=~home,name="Living in Greece",line=list(color=blue,width=3),
            marker=list(color=blue),
            hovertemplate="%{x}: %{y:.1f}%<extra>Living in Greece</extra>") %>%
  chart("Born in Greece, aged 15 to 64: share with higher education",
        paste("Eurostat, lfst_lmbpcobed and edat_lfs_9912 (Labour Force Survey).",shaded),
        "% of the age group",y_axis=list(rangemode="tozero",ticksuffix="%"),
        shapes=list(rescue_band),legend=legend_top)

Interactive chart: Born in Greece, aged 15 to 64: share with higher education

What the data cannot tell:

  • Who left when. The survey counts the people who live abroad, whenever they left, not those who left in a given year.
  • Where they studied. It does not say whether the degree was earned in Greece or abroad.
  • All the countries. It covers the EU and EFTA countries: not the United Kingdom, which is left out of this series, nor the countries outside Europe.
  • Exact numbers. The survey asks a sample of households, so its figures move from year to year more than the people do.
  • What it cost. No statistic here says whether those who left would have found work in Greece, or what their education cost the country.

So, what does it mean?

  1. The crisis drove a wave of emigration. By ELSTAT’s estimates, 1,018,000 people left Greece in the years of the rescue loans, 527,000 of them Greek citizens. In 2012, 12.2 of every 1,000 people who lived in Greece left.
  2. They were young, and many were men. In 2012, 44 of every 1,000 men aged 25 to 29 left.
  3. Germany took the most: 51% of the Greek citizens counted arriving in Europe from 2014 to 2024. For 45% of those who left, the figures do not say where they went.
  4. The flow has turned, a little. Since 2023, more Greek citizens come to Greece than leave it, and in 2024 more Greek citizens left Germany than moved there. But 29,012 more Greek citizens in 2023 and 2024 make up only 9% of the 328,000 lost from 2010 to 2022.
  5. It was partly a brain drain. The people born in Greece with higher education who live elsewhere in the EU and EFTA are 2.8 times as many as in 2010, and those abroad now have more education than those at home.

Most of these numbers are estimates: Greece does not count the people who leave, and the countries they go to count them in their own ways. The direction is clear; the exact numbers are not.

Sources

  • Eurostat, migration: migr_emi2 (emigration by age and sex), migr_emi1ctz (emigration by citizenship), migr_emi5nxt (emigration by group of country of next residence), migr_imm1ctz (immigration by citizenship), migr_imm3ctb (immigration by country of birth), migr_pop1ctz (population by citizenship), and the metadata of the migration statistics (definitions, breaks in the series, countries’ methods).
  • Eurostat, population and work: demo_pjan (population by age and sex), une_rt_a (unemployment).
  • Eurostat, Labour Force Survey: lfst_lmbpcobed (people born in an EU or EFTA country who live in another one, by education), edat_lfs_9912 (education by country of birth).
  • ELSTAT, Migration flows: Methodological note for the estimation of migration flows for the years 2022, 2023 and 2024 and population on 1st January of 2023, 2024 and 2025, and Short Methodological Note on Population Revision for the Intercensal years 2012 – 2021 and Estimation of Post-census Migration Models, both of 18 December 2025.
  • ESM: Greece successfully concludes ESM programme.

See also

  • golemeurostat: a Shiny app for exploring the Eurostat indicators of the countries and regions of Europe (open the app)

This post first appeared on Illustrations in R, with its interactive charts and the full R code.

item.title: Athens Is Getting Hotter: Hot Days, Tropical Nights and Heatwaves Since 1955
item.description: Daily temperatures at Athens Hellinikon since 1955 in NOAA’s GHCN-Daily: warming stripes, days of 35 °C, nights above 20 °C, a longer hot season and the worst heatwaves.
item.content:encoded:
Daily temperatures at Athens Hellinikon since 1955 in NOAA’s GHCN-Daily: warming stripes, days of 35 °C, nights above 20 °C, a longer hot season and the worst heatwaves.

What is this?

Summers in Athens feel hotter than they used to. This data story checks that feeling against the measurements of one weather station, which has measured the highest and the lowest temperature of the day since 1955, with some gaps, and asks five questions:

  1. Is Athens hotter than it used to be?
  2. How many hot days does a summer have?
  3. Do the nights still cool down?
  4. Is the hot season longer?
  5. Which were the worst heatwaves?

The station is at Hellinikon, on the coast south of the city centre, where Athens had its airport until 2001. Its record comes from NOAA, the US agency for weather and climate data, which publishes it in the Global Historical Climatology Network Daily (GHCN-Daily), an archive of daily measurements from weather stations around the world (Menne et al. 2012). It is downloaded when the page is knitted, so the charts show the latest days in NOAA’s archive.

The words of this page:

  • a hot day reaches 35 °C or more, and a very hot day 40 °C or more;
  • on a tropical night the temperature stays above 20 °C, as in the climate change indices of the ETCCDI, an international team of experts; on a very warm night it stays above 25 °C;
  • a heatwave is three days or more in a row above 37 °C (section 5 says why 37);
  • summer is June, July and August.

Packages

Code 
# install.packages(c("dplyr", "ggplot2", "RColorBrewer"))

The data

One station since 1955

GHCN-Daily lists its stations with where they are, and in the Athens area it has only one: Hellinikon, station GR000016716. It is also what this story needs, a long record from one place. The new airport, Eleftherios Venizelos, replaced Hellinikon in 2001 (Wikipedia), so its own record is much shorter, and joining the two would join two different places. The station at Hellinikon kept measuring after the airport moved.

NOAA keeps one file per station, with a row for each day:

Code 
station <- "GR000016716" # Athens Hellinikon
ghcnd_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/global-historical-climatology-network-daily/access/",
  station,
  ".csv"
)
raw <- read.csv(ghcnd_url)
head(raw[, c("DATE", "TMAX", "TMAX_ATTRIBUTES", "TMIN", "TMIN_ATTRIBUTES")])
        DATE TMAX TMAX_ATTRIBUTES TMIN TMIN_ATTRIBUTES
1 1955-01-01  185             ,,I  102             ,,E
2 1955-01-02  144             ,,I   70             ,,E
3 1955-01-03  158             ,,I   96             ,,E
4 1955-01-04  188             ,,I   73             ,,E
5 1955-01-05  179             ,,I   84             ,,E
6 1955-01-06  195             ,,I   90             ,,E

TMAX and TMIN are the highest and the lowest temperature of the day, in tenths of a degree. Each comes with three flags, separated by commas (NOAA’s description of the flags): how it was measured, whether it failed one of NOAA’s quality checks, and where NOAA got it. The values that failed a check are left out, and the days missing from the file are added as empty rows:

Code 
# the three flags of a value are "measurement,quality,source": a quality flag means that the value
# failed one of NOAA's checks, and the source flag says where NOAA got it
quality_flag <- function(attributes) sub("^[^,]*,([^,]*),.*$", "\\1", attributes)
source_flag <- function(attributes) sub("^.*,", "", attributes)
days <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(raw$DATE),
  tmax = raw$TMAX / 10,
  tmin = raw$TMIN / 10,
  tmax_source = source_flag(raw$TMAX_ATTRIBUTES),
  tmin_source = source_flag(raw$TMIN_ATTRIBUTES)
)
failed_max <- !is.na(days$tmax) & quality_flag(raw$TMAX_ATTRIBUTES) != ""
failed_min <- !is.na(days$tmin) & quality_flag(raw$TMIN_ATTRIBUTES) != ""
days$tmax[failed_max] <- NA
days$tmin[failed_min] <- NA
cbind(left_out = c(maximum = sum(failed_max), minimum = sum(failed_min)))
        left_out
maximum       12
minimum       13
Code 
# every day from the first to the last day with a temperature, the missing ones as empty rows
measured <- days$date[!is.na(days$tmax) | !is.na(days$tmin)]
first_day <- min(measured)
last_day <- max(measured)
days <- merge(data.frame(date = seq(first_day, last_day, by = "day")), days, all.x = TRUE)
days$year <- as.integer(format(days$date, "%Y"))
days$month <- as.integer(format(days$date, "%m"))
# for the text: "1 January 1955" in English, whatever the language of the computer, numbers with
# one or two decimals, and lists such as "2021, 2024 and 2025"
date_text <- function(d) {
  paste(as.integer(format(d, "%d")), month.name[as.integer(format(d, "%m"))], format(d, "%Y"))
}
one <- function(x) format(round(x, 1), nsmall = 1)
two <- function(x) format(round(x, 2), nsmall = 2)
and_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) {
    return(paste(x))
  }
  paste(paste(head(x, -1), collapse = ", "), "and", tail(x, 1))
}

So the record runs from 1 January 1955 to 24 August 2025, the latest day that NOAA has for this station. NOAA checks the values but does not correct them for new instruments or new ways of measuring (NOAA): the record is what the station measured.

Three sources, one record

NOAA put the record together from three sources:

Code 
source_names <- c(
  I = "NOAA's International collection",
  E = "European Climate Assessment & Dataset",
  S = "Global Summary of the Day"
)
# from when to when each source gives a measure, and for how many days
from_source <- function(value, source, measure) {
  data.frame(date = days$date, value = value, source = source) |>
    filter(!is.na(value)) |>
    group_by(source) |>
    summarise(from = min(date), to = max(date), days = n()) |>
    arrange(from) |>
    mutate(measure = measure, source = source_names[source])
}
sources <- rbind(
  from_source(days$tmax, days$tmax_source, "Maximum"),
  from_source(days$tmin, days$tmin_source, "Minimum")
)
knitr::kable(
  sources[, c("measure", "source", "from", "to", "days")],
  col.names = c("Measure", "Source", "From", "To", "Days")
)
Measure Source From To Days
Maximum NOAA’s International collection 1955-01-01 2000-12-31 16800
Maximum Global Summary of the Day 2001-01-01 2025-08-24 6510
Minimum European Climate Assessment & Dataset 1955-01-01 2022-12-31 24414
Minimum Global Summary of the Day 2023-01-01 2025-08-23 788
Code 
# the first day of each measure from the Global Summary of the Day, and the year before it
gsod_from <- c(
  maximum = min(days$date[days$tmax_source %in% "S" & !is.na(days$tmax)]),
  minimum = min(days$date[days$tmin_source %in% "S" & !is.na(days$tmin)])
)
year_before <- as.integer(format(gsod_from, "%Y")) - 1
names(year_before) <- names(gsod_from)

Until 2000 the maximum comes from NOAA’s International collection, data that weather services sent to NOAA, and until 2022 the minimum from the European Climate Assessment & Dataset (Klein Tank et al. 2002). After that, both come from the reports that the station sends every hour or every few hours to the weather services of the world, as NOAA’s Global Summary of the Day (GSOD) collects them.

A change of source can put a step into a record, the same as moving a station. But GSOD also has the station’s reports for the years before, so in the last year before each change the two can be compared, day by day:

Code 
# GSOD of the same station (167160 99999) for a year: degrees Fahrenheit, 9999.9 when missing. A
# "*" flag marks a value worked out from the readings of the day instead of reported: left out
gsod <- function(year) {
  x <- read.csv(paste0(
    "https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/global-summary-of-the-day/access/",
    year,
    "/16716099999.csv"
  ))
  reported <- function(value, flag) ifelse(value > 9000 | trimws(flag) == "*", NA, value)
  data.frame(
    date = as.Date(x$DATE),
    gsod_max = (reported(x$MAX, x$MAX_ATTRIBUTES) - 32) * 5 / 9,
    gsod_min = (reported(x$MIN, x$MIN_ATTRIBUTES) - 32) * 5 / 9
  )
}
gsod_years <- lapply(setNames(unique(year_before), unique(year_before)), gsod)
# the two sources on the days that both have: the average gap between them, and the days on
# which they are more than 1 °C apart
compare <- function(measure) {
  year <- year_before[[measure]]
  both <- merge(days, gsod_years[[as.character(year)]], by = "date")
  gap <- if (measure == "maximum") both$gsod_max - both$tmax else both$gsod_min - both$tmin
  data.frame(
    measure = measure,
    year = year,
    days = sum(!is.na(gap)),
    average_gap = mean(abs(gap), na.rm = TRUE),
    apart = sum(abs(gap) > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}
overlap <- rbind(compare("maximum"), compare("minimum"))
knitr::kable(
  overlap,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Measure", "Year", "Days in both", "Average gap (°C)", "Days over 1 °C apart")
)
Measure Year Days in both Average gap (°C) Days over 1 °C apart
maximum 2000 290 0.07 6
minimum 2022 256 0.03 1

They are the same measurements: on the days that both have, they differ by 0.07 °C or less on average, and by more than 1 °C on 7 days out of 546. The change of source is not a step in the record.

A check without gaps: ERA5-Land

One station can mislead: the place around it changes, and it misses days. So this story also downloads ERA5-Land, a reconstruction of the weather of every day since 1950 by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (Muñoz-Sabater et al. 2021; data: Muñoz Sabater 2019). It is a model of the land surface, driven by the weather of ERA5, the Centre’s reconstruction of the weather of the whole world, and it does not use the measurements of any station directly. It describes squares of land 9 km across, so it cannot see what happens around one station: it is a check on the station, not a replacement for it. It comes through the historical weather API of Open-Meteo (Zippenfenig 2023), for the nearest point of its grid that Open-Meteo counts as land:

Code 
# ERA5-Land through Open-Meteo, from the station's first day to yesterday, as one CSV file: two
# lines about the point of the grid, an empty line, then the days
era5_url <- paste0(
  "https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive",
  "?latitude=",
  raw$LATITUDE[1],
  "&longitude=",
  raw$LONGITUDE[1],
  "&start_date=",
  first_day,
  "&end_date=",
  Sys.Date() - 1,
  "&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min",
  "&timezone=Europe%2FAthens&models=era5_land&format=csv"
)
era5_lines <- readLines(era5_url)
era5_point <- read.csv(text = era5_lines[1:2])
era5 <- read.csv(text = era5_lines[-(1:3)], col.names = c("date", "tmax", "tmin"))
era5 <- era5[!is.na(era5$tmax) & !is.na(era5$tmin), ] # the last few days are not ready yet
era5$date <- as.Date(era5$date)
era5$year <- as.integer(format(era5$date, "%Y"))
era5$month <- as.integer(format(era5$date, "%m"))
era5_point[, c("latitude", "longitude", "elevation")]
  latitude longitude elevation
1     37.9      23.8        62
Code 
# the average temperature of each whole summer, day and night together
era5_summers <- era5 |>
  filter(month %in% 6:8) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(summer = mean((tmax + tmin) / 2), days = n()) |>
  filter(days == 92)

Missing days

Code 
enough <- 0.8 # the share of a season's days that must have a measurement
# for each year: the share of its summer days with a maximum, with both a maximum and a minimum,
# and of its days from May to October with a minimum; the average temperature of its summer, and
# its hot days, very hot days, tropical nights and very warm nights
years <- days |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    summer_max = sum(!is.na(tmax[month %in% 6:8])) / 92,
    summer_both = sum(!is.na(tmax[month %in% 6:8] + tmin[month %in% 6:8])) / 92,
    warm_season_min = sum(!is.na(tmin[month %in% 5:10])) / 184,
    summer = mean((tmax[month %in% 6:8] + tmin[month %in% 6:8]) / 2, na.rm = TRUE),
    hot = sum(tmax >= 35, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_hot = sum(tmax >= 40, na.rm = TRUE),
    tropical = sum(tmin > 20, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_warm = sum(tmin > 25, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    summer = ifelse(summer_both >= enough, summer, NA),
    hot = ifelse(summer_max >= enough, hot, NA),
    very_hot = ifelse(summer_max >= enough, very_hot, NA),
    tropical = ifelse(warm_season_min >= enough, tropical, NA),
    very_warm = ifelse(warm_season_min >= enough, very_warm, NA)
  )
# the year with the fewest days with a maximum
max_days <- days |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(days = sum(!is.na(tmax)))
fewest <- max_days[which.min(max_days$days), ]
left_out <- function(x) and_list(years$year[is.na(x)])
dropped <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Summer average", "Hot days", "Tropical nights"),
  needs = c(
    "June to August, maximum and minimum",
    "June to August, maximum",
    "May to October, minimum"
  ),
  kept = c(sum(!is.na(years$summer)), sum(!is.na(years$hot)), sum(!is.na(years$tropical))),
  left_out = c(left_out(years$summer), left_out(years$hot), left_out(years$tropical))
)

The weak point of the record is its gaps. The station’s reports often leave out the maximum of the day: in 2013, only 4 days have one. A year with many missing days would seem to have fewer hot days than it had, so a year counts only if at least 80% of its days in the season that matters have a measurement: June to August for the summer average and the hot days, May to October for the warm nights, when almost all of them come. Of the 71 years from 1955 to 2025, this leaves out 9 for the summer average, 9 for the hot days and 4 for the tropical nights:

Summer average June to August, maximum and minimum 62 2001, 2002, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2023
Hot days June to August, maximum 62 2001, 2002, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2016, 2017, 2019 and 2023

Code 
# ERA5-Land has every day: for each summer kept, its average over the days that the station has,
# against its average over all the days of the summer
measured_summer <- days$date[days$month %in% 6:8 & !is.na(days$tmax + days$tmin)]
shift <- era5 |>
  filter(month %in% 6:8, year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$summer)]) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    all_days = mean((tmax + tmin) / 2),
    station_days = mean(((tmax + tmin) / 2)[date %in% measured_summer])
  )
largest_shift <- max(abs(shift$station_days - shift$all_days))

How much can the missing days change the average of a summer? ERA5-Land has every day, so it can tell: for each summer kept, its average over the days that the station has is at most 0.2 °C away from its average over all the days of that summer. Counts are another matter: a missing day may hide a hot day or a tropical night, so the counts of the years with missing days are, if anything, too low.

1. Is Athens hotter than it used to be?

Code 
# three periods: 1961-1990, the usual reference for the climate of a place, and the two after it
last_year <- max(years$year)
recent <- paste0("2011–", last_year)
period_of <- function(year) {
  cut(year, c(1960, 1990, 2010, last_year), labels = c("1961–1990", "1991–2010", recent))
}
years$period <- period_of(years$year)
by_period <- years |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    summers = sum(!is.na(summer)),
    summer_average = mean(summer, na.rm = TRUE),
    hot_years = sum(!is.na(hot)),
    hot_days = mean(hot, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_hot_days = sum(very_hot, na.rm = TRUE),
    night_years = sum(!is.na(tropical)),
    tropical_nights = mean(tropical, na.rm = TRUE),
    very_warm_nights = mean(very_warm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
base <- by_period$summer_average[1]
now <- by_period$summer_average[3]

Yes. The summers of 2011–2025 were 2.4 °C warmer than those of 1961–1990.

Each stripe below is one summer, from 1955 on the left to 2025 on the right, coloured by its average temperature, day and night together: blue for the cooler summers, red for the warmer ones. They follow Ed Hawkins’ warming stripes (#ShowYourStripes), which show in the same way how the world, a country or a city has warmed. As there, the colours change from blue to red at the average of 1961–2010, and reach their darkest three standard deviations away from it, a measure of how much summers differ from one another (theirs is that of 1901–2000, here it is that of 1961–2010): here 2.8 °C below and above 26.6 °C. Grey stripes are the summers with too many missing days.

In 1961–1990, a summer at Hellinikon averaged 26.2 °C, day and night together. The 8 summers of 2011–2025 that can be counted averaged 28.5 °C. The five warmest summers since 1955 were those of 2008, 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025, and the warmest of all, 2024, averaged 31.0 °C, 4.8 °C more than the summers of 1961–1990. station_warming <- mean(years$summer[years$year %in% recent_kept]) - station_base

  sum(era5_summers$summer >= era5_summers$summer[era5_summers$year == year])
}

  data.frame(year = years$year, station = years$summer - station_base),

place_text <- function(k) {
  if (k == 1) {
    return("the warmest")
  }
  words <- c("second", "third", "fourth", "fifth", "sixth", "seventh", "eighth", "ninth", "tenth")
  if (k <= 10) paste("the", words[k - 1], "warmest") else paste0("the ", k, "th warmest")
}

The station and ERA5-Land agree. The warm and the cool summers are the same in both (their correlation is 0.94, where 1 would be a perfect match), and both have warmed: compared with 1961–1990, the summers of 2011–2025 that the station can count were 2.4 °C warmer at the station and 1.6 °C warmer in ERA5-Land. The summers that the station cannot count do not change the picture: over all the summers of 2011–2025, ERA5-Land was 1.6 °C warmer.

The station warmed by 0.8 °C more. Part of the difference may come from the place around it. Cities cool more slowly than the countryside at night (Founda and Santamouris 2017), and the station’s own surroundings have changed: the airport around it closed in 2001, and since 2020 the old airfield has been a building site (Wikipedia). NOAA’s file gives the station the same place for the whole record, so it does not say whether the station itself moved within the old airport. ERA5-Land cannot see any of this, and it warmed too: the warming is not only the station’s.

ERA5-Land also has the summer of 2026, which NOAA’s record of the station does not reach yet: it was 1.5 °C warmer than its summers of 1961–1990, the 13th warmest of its 72 summers since 1955.

Code 
hottest <- days[which.max(days$tmax), ]
summer_2024 <- days[days$year == 2024 & days$month %in% 6:8, ]
above_37_2024 <- sum(summer_2024$tmax > 37, na.rm = TRUE)
missing_2024 <- sum(is.na(summer_2024$tmax))

Many more. In 1961–1990 Hellinikon had 5 hot days a year on average, in 1991–2010 15, and in the 8 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted 30. The most were in 2024: 70 days of 35 °C or more.

Very hot days, of 40 °C or more, were rare and still are, but less so: 2 in the 30 years of 1961–1990, 6 in the 8 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted. The hottest day of the record was 3 August 2021, at 43.0 °C.

Can the station be trusted for a summer like that of 2024? The National Observatory of Athens has its own stations, and counted the days of that summer above 37 °C: 45 at Harokopio University in Kallithea and 30 in Piraeus (meteo.gr, 3 September 2024). Hellinikon had 32, with 8 days of the summer missing: in the same range.

Less and less. At Hellinikon, by the sea, a summer night often stays above 20 °C anyway: in 1961–1990 there were 86 tropical nights a year on average. In the 11 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted there were 102, and the most were in 2012: 118. The change is larger for the very warm nights, above 25 °C: from 9 a year in 1961–1990 to 28 in 2011–2025, with 49 in 2024. The warmest night of the record was that of 26 July 2025, when the temperature did not fall below 31.7 °C.

4. Is the hot season longer?

Each row of the chart below is one year, from 1955 at the bottom to 2025 at the top, and each small square one day from May to October, coloured by the maximum of that day. A season that starts earlier or ends later shows as colour spreading to the left or to the right; grey squares are the days with no measurement.

# the share of hot days in two parts of the season, in each period
share_between <- function(from, to) {
  days |>
    filter(year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$hot)], !is.na(tmax)) |>
    mutate(period = period_of(year), md = format(date, "%m-%d")) |>
    filter(!is.na(period), md >= from, md <= to) |>
    group_by(period) |>
    summarise(share = 100 * mean(tmax >= 35)) |>
    pull(share)
}
late_june <- share_between("06-16", "06-30")
late_august <- share_between("08-16", "08-31")
# the first and the last tropical night of each year that can be counted, as days of the year,
# and their average in each period, as a date
warm_nights <- days |>
  filter(year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$tropical)], tmin > 20) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(
    first = as.integer(format(min(date), "%j")),
    last = as.integer(format(max(date), "%j"))
  ) |>
  mutate(period = period_of(year)) |>
  filter(!is.na(period)) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(first = mean(first), last = mean(last))
day_text <- function(d) {
  x <- as.Date(round(d) - 1, origin = "2001-01-01")
  paste(as.integer(format(x, "%d")), month.name[as.integer(format(x, "%m"))])
}
season_length <- warm_nights$last - warm_nights$first
longer <- season_length[3] - season_length[1]

Yes: it starts earlier and ends later. In 1961–1990 a day in the second half of June reached 35 °C in 1% of the years; in 2011–2025, in 26%. In the second half of August the share went from 5% to 30%.

The nights tell the same story. In 1961–1990 the first tropical night of the year came, on average, on 31 May, and the last on 6 October. In 2011–2025 the first came on 19 May and the last on 13 October: the season of warm nights is 19 days longer.

5. Which were the worst heatwaves?

Code 
# runs of days above 37 °C. A single missing day between two such days does not end a run, and a
# run counts as a heatwave if at least three of its days were measured above 37 °C
above <- days$tmax > 37
bridge <- is.na(above) &
  c(FALSE, head(above, -1) %in% TRUE) &
  c(tail(above, -1) %in% TRUE, FALSE)
in_run <- above %in% TRUE | bridge
run <- cumsum(in_run & !c(FALSE, head(in_run, -1)))
heatwaves <- days |>
  mutate(run = run) |>
  filter(in_run) |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(
    start = min(date),
    end = max(date),
    days = n(),
    measured = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    hottest = max(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    warmest_night = if (all(is.na(tmin))) NA else max(tmin, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(measured >= 3) |>
  mutate(year = as.integer(format(start, "%Y")), period = period_of(year))
# how rare a day above 37 °C was in the summers of 1961-1990
summers_1961_1990 <- days$tmax[days$year %in% 1961:1990 & days$month %in% 6:8]
share_above_37 <- 100 * mean(summers_1961_1990 > 37, na.rm = TRUE)

Why 37 °C? At Hellinikon, in the summers of 1961–1990, only 1.1% of the days were warmer than 37 °C, about one in 89; the National Observatory of Athens, too, counts the days above 37 °C in its reviews of the summer (meteo.gr, 3 September 2024). Three such days in a row are a heatwave here. Each dot below is one heatwave, as high as it was long:

when <- function(start, end) {
  day <- function(d) as.integer(format(d, "%d"))
  month <- function(d) month.name[as.integer(format(d, "%m"))]
  ifelse(
    month(start) == month(end),
    paste0(day(start), "–", day(end), " ", month(end), " ", format(end, "%Y")),
    paste0(day(start), " ", month(start), " – ", day(end), " ", month(end), " ", format(end, "%Y"))
  )
}

  filter(!is.na(period), year %in% years$year[!is.na(years$hot)]) |>
  count(period, .drop = FALSE)

More of them, and longer. In the 30 years of 1961–1990 Hellinikon had 4 heatwaves; in the 8 years of 2011–2025 that can be counted, 8. Before 2021 no heatwave that the station measured lasted a week. The longest, of 17 days, was that of 8–24 July 2024, with 3 days missing in it; the hottest day of a heatwave was 43.0 °C, in that of 27 July – 5 August 2021.

What these numbers mean for people is clearest in July 1987: in that month, when a major heatwave hit Greece, almost twice as many people died in Athens (97% more) as in July of the six years before (Katsouyanni et al. 1993). At Hellinikon, by the sea, the heatwave lasted 3 days, 22–24 July 1987, and reached 41.6 °C.

Some heatwaves are missing. The station has a maximum for only 3 days of July 2023, when the National Observatory of Athens counted, in Greece as a whole, a heatwave of 15 days, the longest until then; that of July 2024 beat it, with 16 (meteo.gr, 25 July 2024). And it has a maximum for only 11 of the 92 days of the summer of 2012, the second warmest of the 72 in ERA5-Land.

So, what does it mean?

Athens is getting hotter, by day and by night. At Hellinikon, comparing 1961–1990 with the years of 2011–2025 that can be counted:

Code 
measures <- rbind(
  "Summer average (°C)" = by_period$summer_average,
  "Hot days a year" = by_period$hot_days,
  "Very hot days a year" = by_period$very_hot_days / by_period$hot_years,
  "Tropical nights a year" = by_period$tropical_nights,
  "Very warm nights a year" = by_period$very_warm_nights,
  "Heatwaves a year" = per_period$n / by_period$hot_years
)
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(rownames(measures), measures),
  row.names = FALSE,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Measure", as.character(by_period$period))
)
Measure 1961–1990 1991–2010 2011–2025
Summer average (°C) 26.2 27.3 28.5
Hot days a year 5.4 14.7 29.6
Very hot days a year 0.1 0.3 0.8
Tropical nights a year 85.7 93.0 102.2
Very warm nights a year 8.6 14.6 27.5
Heatwaves a year 0.1 0.4 1.0
  1. Summers are warmer: 2.4 °C warmer than in 1961–1990, and ERA5-Land, which cannot see the city, warmed too.
  2. Hot days are much more common: 30 a year instead of 5.
  3. The nights cool down less: 28 very warm nights a year instead of 9.
  4. The hot season is longer: its warm nights start earlier and end later, 19 days longer in all.
  5. Heatwaves come more often and last longer: the longest at Hellinikon lasted 17 days, in 2024.

What this does not show. It is one station, at the edge of the city and by the sea; the centre of Athens and the plains inland are hotter by day, and some of the station’s warming may come from the city around it, which this record cannot separate from the climate. NOAA’s record of the station has gaps, worst in the 2010s, and ends on 24 August 2025; ERA5-Land, which goes on to the present, is a model, not a measurement.

For the world as a whole, see the NASA GISS Global Temperature Anomaly; for more of what a weather station measures, hour by hour, the Airport Weather Analysis of the new Athens airport; and for the fires that burn in Greek summers, Greece Burning.
